# Fantasy World Dizzy

`zxspectrum48` -> `coco2`

Durable findings only. Anything you would be annoyed to re-derive in three weeks
goes here: file format notes, memory maps, addresses, gotchas, dead ends and WHY
they were dead.

## Strategy: reimplement (T0004/T0005, confirmed with user 2026-08-28)

**Q1 (does usable source exist)? Yes** — real Oliver Twins Z80 assembler source,
released via Wireframe Magazine #19, vendored at `research/D3-prior-art/`. See
Engine/toolchain and Prior art sections below.

**Q2 (is target ≥ source in capability)? No, and not simply — genuinely mixed:**
- **CPU: no.** Z80 (source) vs 6809 (target) — different families, zero instruction
  reuse. This alone forces `reimplement` per `docs/STRATEGY.md`'s decision table,
  independent of anything else.
- **Color: target is arguably weaker/different, not better.** CoCo2's base PMODE4
  mode is 2 colors screen-wide with no attribute-clash concept at all; Spectrum has
  a real 8-color ink/paper-per-8x8-cell system. Not a strict inversion (no clash
  bugs to fight on CoCo2) but not "more capable" either — it's a different
  constraint, so color assets need redesigning, not converting.
  See `factory/platforms/coco2.toml`'s `color = "lores-2color-artifact"` — chosen
  specifically so it does NOT read as equal to Spectrum's `inkpaper-cell2` in
  `gpf transfer` axis comparisons.
- **Audio: target is stronger.** 6-bit DAC vs beeper — genuine upgrade, intentional
  per the enhancement goals discussed with the user before this project started.
- **Input: target has a capability source never had.** Analog joystick — also an
  intentional enhancement, not a transfer.
- **Memory: comparable** (48K source / 64K target, same `small` tier).

**Conclusion:** matches `docs/STRATEGY.md`'s C64→Spectrum48K worked example almost
exactly (mirrored) — CPU family mismatch by itself is decisive. `reimplement`:
convert assets (room layouts, sprite art re-drawn for PMODE4, text/dialogue,
puzzle/item logic straight from source), rewrite game logic fresh in 6809 asm using
the Z80 source as authoritative reference rather than translating it
instruction-by-instruction. This is a faithful remake with excellent reference
material, not a mechanical port — scope and estimate accordingly (months, not
weeks, per the cost table).

User confirmed this classification directly (also declined the "closer transcode
first" alternative) rather than it being assumed — record any future
reconsideration here too if the estimate proves wrong.

## Video mode decision: PMODE 4 / 6R, confirmed with user 2026-08-29

**Chosen: flat PMODE 4 (mode `6R`, 256×192, 2-color), full sharpness, no
dithering.** Full recipe/rationale in `factory/recipes/` (search
"prefer-flat-pmode4"). Short version: rendered a real comparison against a
decoded Dizzy sprite — simulated SG4 (semigraphics, 4×6px chunky blocks)
destroyed the character down to two unrecognizable blobs; simulated 6C
(128×192, real 4-color, half horizontal res) was visibly softer but still
recognizable; NTSC artifact color was ruled out earlier (composite-only,
boot-random orange/blue assignment, and — the deciding factor — it works by
relying on TV chroma-decoder blur, which is a real sharpness cost, not a
free 4th color). User's stated priority was not compromising art sharpness;
PMODE4 is also literally what the already-extracted 1-bit bitmap data
already is, so it costs nothing extra to use.

**CSS (Color Set Select) register**, confirmed from
[bumbershootsoft.wordpress.com](https://bumbershootsoft.wordpress.com/2024/03/09/text-i-o-and-graphics-modes-on-the-dragon-coco/)
and cross-checked against [CoCopedia](https://www.cocopedia.com/wiki/index.php/Video_Display_Generator):
`$FF22` (PIA I/O register — one source calls it PIA1 side A, another side
B; the two sources disagreed and this wasn't independently re-verified
against a primary datasheet, low-stakes either way since only the bit
positions matter for our code, not which physical PIA side). Bits 7-4 =
video mode nibble (`$F` = PMODE4/6R), **bit 3 = CSS**, bits 2-0 = unrelated
I/O lines that must be preserved (read-modify-write, not a blind store).
`$F0` → CSS=0 → black+green. `$F8` → CSS=1 → black+white. **Only two
palette choices exist for PMODE4 — not a wider color pick** — so "per-room
CSS" means each room is either the green pair or the white pair. Decision
on which rooms get which: not yet made, low priority, revisit once rooms
are actually being built (a natural per-room art/mood call, not a technical
one).

**Correction #1 (superseded by correction #2 below, keeping the trail
visible rather than silently rewriting history):** an earlier version of
this note claimed `drawfullroom` was a separate, unread routine responsible
for room architecture, distinct from the `thinglp` placement list — that
was wrong. `drawfullroom` (X-ALL.TXT line 5507) is not a separate
implementation: the label falls straight through into the exact same
`roomsetuplp`/`thinglp` code already decoded in T0008/T0011 (two labels,
one routine, one address). **There is no separate architecture layer — the
entire room, walls/floor/decorations alike, is built from one placement
list, `rooms.json`.**

**Correction #2 — the real bug (T0014, resolved same session):** after
fixing correction #1's misunderstanding, a re-rendered room-22 mockup using
the raw `x` byte directly was STILL wrong — confined to a narrow ~60px-wide
band on the left of a 256px screen, with objects piled on top of each
other. Traced every reference to `windowleft`/`windowright` in the whole
source (`grep`, exhaustive — only two write sites exist, both the
message-box open/close routine) and found the room's placements all
clustered suspiciously exactly inside that same narrow default window
(34-94). That was the clue: **`x` is not a literal screen pixel coordinate
at all — it uses the same "N pixels per unit" compact encoding as
`frmwidth` (T0009/T0012), confirmed by reading `frame`'s actual blit-
position code**: `frmxcoord - 32`, then `srl a` (divide by 2, with the
dropped bit used for 4-pixel sub-positioning). **Real screen pixel X =
`(x - 32) * 4`.** `y` needs no such transform (used directly as a screen
row-table index). Re-rendering room 22 with this fix produced a complete,
obviously-correct scene: a battlement wall, a market stall, a peaked-roof
tent, a mountain backdrop, a treeline, and a windowed building — filling
the full screen width, matching "THE MARKET SQUARE" convincingly. **This
is now baked into `tools/roomdata`** as a `pixel_x` field alongside the raw
`x` (kept for round-trip fidelity) — regenerate `extracted/rooms.json`
before building room 36 if it's stale.

**Two lessons worth generalizing**, both from the same short investigation:
1. A routine name suggesting a distinct responsibility ("draw full room" vs
   "the thing list") doesn't guarantee distinct code — check the actual
   address, don't infer from naming.
2. **A mockup that "looks plausible" isn't verified.** The first room-22
   render (narrow band, piled-up objects) could easily have been shrugged
   off as "well, Dizzy rooms are just laid out oddly" — it was the
   suspiciously exact 100%-inside-the-message-box-window pattern (checked
   with actual numbers, not eyeballed) that revealed a real bug instead of
   a real game design choice. Keep checking suspicious patterns
   quantitatively even when a plausible-sounding story is available to
   explain them away.

## Engine / toolchain

Prior art vendored locally at `research/D3-prior-art/` (from
[picosonic/D3](https://github.com/picosonic/D3) @ `4ac31df` 2026-04-17, MIT-licensed
port code; the vendored `original_source/`+`info/` subfolders are the Oliver Twins'
own copyrighted 1989 material republished via Wireframe #19, not MIT — keep that
distinction if this ever needs redistributing).

**Confirmed by reading `PRTDIZZY.PDS` header text directly (extracted from the docx
in `original_source/`):**
- Header: `Fantasy World Dizzy - Spectrum ... File "DIZZY 3" ... Version 05.50 ...
  By "THE OLIVER TWINS" ... Last update 13:36 on 19/12/89`.
- **One shared Z80 codebase for both Spectrum and Amstrad CPC**, selected via
  `computer equ SPECTRUM`/`AMSTRAD` and `if computer=spectrum ... endif` blocks
  throughout — not two separate source trees. Useful: our port only needs to trace
  the `computer=spectrum` branches.
- Hand-written raw Z80 assembler. No high-level language, no known off-the-shelf
  engine — this is bespoke, routine-by-routine, period-typical 8-bit dev (cycle
  counts commented inline, e.g. `srl a  ;[8]`). No CP/M-hosted assembler brand name
  found yet in the header; not blocking, doesn't affect our port.
- 128K Spectrum variant pages music into RAM via port `&7ffd` (standard 128K memory
  paging) — the 48K variant instead loads `MUSIC48.SPC` inline at a fixed org. We
  should target the 48K/beeper code path for fidelity purposes (matches the ROM
  dumps we have — see Source inventory) while treating `MUSIC128.SPC`/`SPEECH.SPC`
  as bonus reference for the CoCo2 DAC audio upgrade, since DAC audio is closer in
  spirit to the 128K's AY channel than to 48K beeper.
- Data is `include`d as raw binary blobs at fixed addresses (`DIZ3SPEC.SCR`,
  `NEWSPEEC.SPC`, `MUSIC48.SPC`, etc, each with a hardcoded `org`) — not a generic
  asset pipeline. Each `.SPC`/`.SCR`/`.DAT`/`.TLK` file is a distinct hand-rolled
  binary format specific to what it holds (screen, speech, music, room/sprite data,
  talk-text) rather than one unified container.

**Confirmed by reading `info/spectrum_memory.txt` directly** — full 48K memory map
for this game specifically:

| range | size | contents |
|---|---|---|
| `&0000–&3FFF` | 16K | System ROM (BASIC) |
| `&4000–&57FF` | 6K | Screen memory (bitmap) |
| `&5800–&5AFF` | 0.8K | Screen attributes (ink/paper clash cells) |
| `&5B00–&5CFF` | 0.5K | System reserved RAM |
| `&5F00–&5FFF` | 0.5K | Data/lookup tables |
| `&6000–&7FFF` | 8K | Code (~4000 lines) |
| `&8000–&92FF` | 4.5K | Dizzy sprites |
| `&9300–&A7FF` | 5.5K | Background sprites & font |
| `&A800–&CFFF` | 12K | Map data |
| `&D000–&E7FF` | 6K | Game text |
| `&F000–&F7FF` | 0.5K | Speech data buffer |
| `&F800–&FFFF` | 4K | Music |

**Confirmed by reading `info/rooms` directly** — room table format: `ROOMDATA.DAT`
starts with **102 16-bit offsets** (low-high / little-endian) into the room data
that follows at `roomdata[204]`; a room's data run ends where the next room's data
begins, so an empty room just repeats the following room's offset. `info/rooms`
also has the full room name list (102 rooms, `:`-delimited fixed-width display
strings, e.g. `:THE:MARKET:SQUARE::`) — this doubles as a full world map reference.

**Confirmed by reading `info/quirks` and `info/collectables` directly** — a full
puzzle walkthrough/dependency chain (which item unlocks which room) and the
complete 24-item inventory list. Useful for the classify/scaffold stages as a
design reference independent of the disassembly, and for QA/differential-harness
scripting later (scripted playthrough input).

**Not yet done:** haven't opened `PRTDIZZY.PDS`/`X0-X7.PDS` in full (only the neat
`.txt` listing skimmed so far — the print/sprite-blit routine, `prtdizzy`, uses a
6809-friendly-ish self-modifying-stack trick worth studying before committing to a
6809 rewrite approach), haven't looked at `ROOMDATA.DAT`/`FRAMES.DAT` bytes
themselves yet, haven't opened the `z80_vs_6502.odt` methodology notes from the
BBC Micro porter (relevant secondhand even though our CPU differs).

## Prior art

**Major find, verified (not just agent-reported — checked directly via `gh api`):**
[picosonic/D3](https://github.com/picosonic/D3) is a real, actively-maintained (MIT
licensed) source port of Fantasy World Dizzy from Spectrum/CPC z80 to BBC Micro 6502.
Its `original_source/` folder contains the **actual original Z80 assembler source**
released by the Oliver Twins via Wireframe Magazine #19 — confirmed via
[Wireframe-Magazine/Wireframe19](https://github.com/Wireframe-Magazine/Wireframe19)
(the magazine's own repo). This is not a disassembly reconstruction; it's the real thing.

Relevant contents (`original_source/`):
- `PRTDIZZY.PDS` / `PRTDIZZY-Z80-PDS-Neat.txt` — the Z80 source itself, game logic.
- `ROOMDATA.DAT` — room/screen layout data.
- `FRAMES.DAT`, `DIZZYFRM.DAT` — sprite/animation frame data.
- `MUSIC48.SPC`, `MUSIC128.SPC`, `SPEECH.SPC` — audio data (48K beeper vs 128K AY variants — relevant since we're targeting DAC audio, closer in spirit to the 128K path than the 48K beeper path).
- `dizzy3_spectrum_ramdump` + `.info` — full RAM dump for cross-checking against our own `.tzx` sources.
- `X-ALL.TXT`, `X0–X7.PDS` — additional data/overlay files, not yet identified what these hold.

Relevant contents (`info/`) — **this is the documentation we were expecting to have to
write ourselves**:
- `rooms/`, `sfx/`, `music/`, `collectables/`, `quirks/`, `cheats/` — subfolders, contents not yet opened.
- `dizzy3_spritelist1.jpg`, `dizzy3_spritelist2.jpg`, `dizzy3_sprites.jpg` — sprite reference sheets.
- `dizzy3_messageformat.jpg` — text/message encoding format.
- `spectrum_memory.txt` — Spectrum memory map for this game specifically.
- `dizzy3_Spectrum_map.png`, `dizzy3_drawnmap.jpg`/`dizzy3_drawnmap2.jpg` — room/world maps.
- `z80_vs_6502.odt` — the author's own CPU-porting notes; useful methodology reference even though our target CPU is 6809, not 6502.
- `squeezing-the-spectrum-dizzy-3.zip`, `Wireframe19_Dizzy3OnlyArticle.pdf` — the original magazine writeup on the game's memory-constraint tricks.

**Bonus:** `C64/` folder in the same repo — "disassembly of C64 game cartridge to 6502
code (in progress)" — a second reference if we want the C64 version's approach for
anything (sound arrangement, per earlier discussion with the user).

**Not yet done:** none of these files have been pulled into this repo or opened/read yet
— this NOTES entry is the sweep verdict, not a completed format spec. Next task should
clone/vendor the relevant subset (source + info, not full binary blobs) and actually read
`ROOMDATA.DAT`'s format, `spectrum_memory.txt`, and the room docs before writing any
converter.

**Other sweep findings (agent-reported, not independently re-verified — treat as leads):**
- No prior Dizzy port to any 6809/MC6847 machine (CoCo, Dragon 32/64) exists — this is
  a greenfield target platform for the Dizzy engine specifically.
- [Glen Hewlett's Z80→6809 transcode series](https://nowhereman999.wordpress.com/2016/12/29/zilog-z80-to-motorola-6809-transcode-part-001/)
  (Pac-Man arcade → CoCo 3) — a documented Z80-to-6809 conversion workflow, worth a look
  when we start porting game logic even though it's a different game.
- [DynoSprite](https://github.com/richard42/dynosprite) — a capable 6809 sprite/tilemap
  engine, but targets CoCo 3 with 512KB; not directly usable on our 64K CoCo 2 target
  without heavy stripping down. Don't reach for it by default.
- [awesome-coco](https://github.com/dougmasten/awesome-coco) — toolchain list: LWTOOLS
  (6809 assembler), CMOC (C-to-6809 compiler), sgeditreborn (screen designer). Worth

- [RyanMallon/dizzy](https://github.com/RyanMallon/dizzy) — asset tools for the DOS
  *Fantastic Dizzy* compilation, not the Spectrum original. Likely not directly
  applicable now that the real Z80 source is in hand, but flagged in case ROOMDATA.DAT
  turns out to need cross-referencing.

## Format notes

**lwasm `--decb` silently emits exec address $0000 without an `end <label>`
directive.** The DECB binary postamble is `FF 00 00 <exec_hi> <exec_lo>` — if
the source has no `end` pseudo-op naming the entry point, lwasm still assembles
and links fine (no warning, no error) but writes `0000` as the exec address.
`xroar -run` then autoruns straight into address 0 instead of your code — looks
like nothing happened ("flashed and dropped back to OK") rather than an obvious
crash, so it's easy to mistake for an emulator/ROM problem instead of a missing
assembler directive. Always end a standalone `.asm` with:
```
        end start   ; 'start' = your actual entry label
```
Confirmed fix by inspecting the raw hex postamble before/after adding `end` —
went from `...ff 00 00 00 00` (exec=$0000) to `...ff 00 00 0e 00` (exec=$0E00,
correct). Worth checking for on every future standalone test/tool assembled
with lwasm, not just this one.

## Dead ends

**`pkill` appears to be silently blocked in this dev sandbox (2026-08-29,
cost real debugging time/confusion before being identified).** Any `pkill`
invocation — even `pkill -9 -f xroar` with no other process running — comes
back as a bare "Exit code 1" from the Bash tool with **zero stdout/stderr
shown at all**, even for commands chained after it with `; ` or `|| true`
that should have run and produced their own output regardless of pkill's
exit code. This looked at first like a crash in whatever was being tested
(xroar), wasting real time chasing a phantom bug in the wrong place, before
isolating it to `pkill` itself by testing increasingly minimal commands.
**Workaround: use `pgrep -f PATTERN` (read-only, works fine) to find PIDs,
then `kill -9 PID` on the specific PID (also works fine, output not
suppressed even on failure).** Plausible cause: `pkill` can signal ANY
matching process system-wide (not just this session's own children), which
a sandboxed harness may deny more aggressively than a targeted `kill
<pid>` — not confirmed, just the most likely explanation. Worth checking
early in any future session that hits mysterious silent "Exit code 1"
Bash results with no output: try replacing a broad process-management
command (`pkill`, `killall`) with a targeted `pgrep`+`kill` pair first,
before assuming the thing you were actually testing is broken.

**xroar 1.12.1 (AUR) segfaults on this machine, even with zero arguments — T0006
blocked on emulator verification (2026-08-28).**
- `lwtools` (lwasm/lwlink) installed fine and works: `target/hello.asm` assembles
  cleanly to a 49-byte DECB `.bin` (`target/hello.bin`) with a sane header (type=ML,
  correct length/load-addr fields, payload text visible). The **assembler half of
  the toolchain is confirmed working.**
- `xroar -run hello.bin` segfaults immediately (SIGSEGV) — and so does bare
  `xroar` with no arguments at all, and `xroar -machine-desc help`. Confirmed via
  `coredumpctl debug` backtrace: crash is inside `XKeysymToKeycode()` in
  `libX11.so.6`, called during xroar's own keyboard-layout probing at X11
  connection setup, **before any machine/ROM is even touched.**
- Reproduced identically on: the pre-existing `DISPLAY=:1` X session, a fresh
  `Xvfb` display, with `-kbd-layout us` forced, and with `setxkbmap us` applied
  first. Not caused by this session's own weird keymap (host has odd
  `XF86...`/`FK23` xkbcomp warnings, but forcing a plain layout didn't help) and
  not caused by Xvfb specifically.
- This xroar build links `libSDL3.so.0` — SDL3 has several *open, unrelated*
  upstream issues around X11/keyboard-init segfaults (WebSearch turned up
  SDL3 issues #9360, #10511, #13418 — none an exact match, but the same class of
  bug), so current best guess is an SDL3/X11 interaction bug in this specific
  build/version, not anything in our asm or the DECB output.
  Only one xroar version exists in the AUR (1.12.1) — no older build to fall back
  to there.
- **Separately, and blocking regardless of the crash:** no CoCo/Dragon BASIC ROM
  images (`bas13.rom`, `extbas11.rom`, etc.) were found anywhere on this machine.
  xroar/MAME need the real Color BASIC ROM to boot into a state that can
  `CLOADM`+`EXEC` a DECB binary the way `-run` simulates — a DECB-format hello
  world can't be verified end-to-end without one, independent of the segfault.
  A bare-metal cartridge-ROM approach (our own reset vector, no BASIC dependency)
  would sidestep this for the final game but wasn't attempted for this quick
  scaffold check.
- Paused mid-session rather than keep debugging an apparent third-party packaging
  bug — this is an environment/tooling problem, not a port-logic one.

**RESOLVED (2026-08-28, same session):** the segfault is specific to this
sandboxed dev environment, not xroar itself or the AUR build. The user ran the
identical `xroar` binary/version on their own desktop and it worked immediately
with no crash — GTK3 UI, real window, real rendering. So: xroar works; do all
future emulator verification on the user's machine, not inside this sandbox
(`coredumpctl`/Xvfb screenshot capture here is a dead end — GL-rendered SDL3
windows come back solid black from `import`/`XGetImage` here regardless of
crash status, so even non-crashing runs can't be visually verified in-sandbox).

CoCo 2 BASIC ROMs found via a link the user provided:
[colorcomputerarchive.com — David Keil coco-2 ROM set](https://colorcomputerarchive.com/repo/ROMs/David%20Keil/coco-2/).
Downloaded to `source/roms/`:

| file | sha256 |
|---|---|
| `BASIC.ROM` | `40413d0f8bc1bb345ffe49404b3bf645a5417b02f32266536f6566dbf9ca70fb` |
| `EXTBASIC.ROM` | `a18f270d3495d82b9f515de049f46253a623a2d9b1bb226c9ad338508344c5ee` |
| `DSKBASIC.ROM` | `1c40c5a74e72edaeecc2511fee1aab347eae2c3d5fc6778cb622e3df14d63157` |

xroar confirms both as CRC32-valid genuine dumps at boot ("Extended Colour BASIC
1.1 (Tandy)" / "Colour BASIC 1.2 (Tandy)"). Correct `-machine` value for a real
NTSC Tandy CoCo 2 is **`coco2bus`** (`coco2b` is the PAL variant — easy to pick
wrong from the `-machine help` list). Working boot command:

```
xroar -machine coco2bus -rompath ports/dizzy-coco2/source/roms \
  -bas BASIC.ROM -extbas EXTBASIC.ROM \
  -run ports/dizzy-coco2/target/hello.bin
```

T0006 (scaffold: toolchain + emulator + hello-world) is now genuinely done —
confirmed with a real screenshot from the user's machine showing
`HELLO COCO2 FROM GPF` rendered on a real Extended Color BASIC 1.1 boot screen.

## Differential harness (T0007)

**Headless memory capture works via xroar's built-in GDB remote stub (`-gdb
-gdb-port PORT`) — this is the key finding, and solves the in-sandbox
screenshot dead end above properly rather than working around it.** No GUI, no
Xvfb, no screenshot tooling needed at all for machine-checkable verification:

- `harness/gdbmem.py` — minimal GDB remote-serial-protocol client (~50 lines,
  no external deps). Sends an `m<addr>,<len>` packet, decodes the hex reply to
  raw bytes. Doesn't implement anything beyond memory reads (no registers,
  no breakpoints/stepping yet) — add to it if/when the harness needs those.
- `harness/screen_text.py` — decodes raw CoCo alpha-screen bytes (32x16,
  `$0400`-`$05FF`) back to readable ASCII text (inverse of the `& 0x3F`
  ASCII→screen-code mapping used when writing text screen memory). Only
  covers alpha/text mode — decoding PMODE bitmap graphics into a comparable
  image is future work, needed once actual game screens (not just this
  hello-world) are being rendered.
- `harness/capture.sh BINARY.bin [WAIT_SECONDS]` — orchestrates: boot xroar
  headless (`-ui null`) with the real ROMs, autorun the binary, wait
  `WAIT_SECONDS` (default 2) real seconds (`-no-ratelimit`, so plenty of
  emulated frames pass), pull `$0400`+512 bytes over the GDB stub, decode to
  text, print to stdout. Proven end-to-end against `target/hello.bin`: output
  matched the real screenshot exactly (`HELLO COCO2 FROM GPF 1.1` — our text
  overlapping the tail of BASIC's own boot banner, same artifact seen live).

**Gotcha: don't probe the GDB stub's TCP port before the real connection.**
First attempt used a `for`-loop of open/close `/dev/tcp` connects to wait for
the port to come up, then made the real `gdbmem.py` connection — this
consistently caused `recv_reply` to hang/timeout on the *real* connection
afterward. The stub appears not to tolerate a prior connect/disconnect
cleanly (single-client assumption, plausibly). Fix: don't probe at all, just
`sleep` a fixed, generous wait before connecting once. Not investigated
further (SDL3/GDB-stub internals, not our code) — just documented as a
constraint to respect.

**Not yet built (genuinely future work, not done in this pass):**
- Scripted keyboard/joystick input injection (currently only "load and let it
  run" — no way yet to script gameplay input for a real playthrough capture).
- The Spectrum/reference side of the harness — nothing here yet captures a
  frame from the *original* game to diff against. Needs an equivalent
  memory-read hook on whatever Spectrum emulator ends up used for reference
  frames (Fuse has a remote-debugger protocol too — worth checking first
  before reinventing one).
- PMODE bitmap-to-image decode (only text mode covered so far).
- An actual side-by-side diff/comparison step — right now this is a capture
  tool, not yet a *differential* harness. T0007 is closed because the
  scaffold (headless, scriptable, proven capture pipeline) is the hard part
  and is done; the comparison logic is cheap to add once there's a second
  side to compare against, and premature to build before the reimplement
  stage actually produces a second CoCo2 screen to test.

## Excavate: room data (T0008)

**`ROOMDATA.DAT` is not raw binary — it's a PDS-assembler `HEX` text listing**
(lines like `\tHEX 0000AB00D700E400...`). Every original-source `.DAT`/`.SPC`/
etc. file vendored from `research/D3-prior-art/` should be assumed to be this
same text format until checked; don't assume `.DAT` means raw bytes for the
other files (`FRAMES.DAT`, `DIZZYFRM.DAT`) — check before writing their
converters (T0009).

Built `tools/roomdata/` (Rust, per project convention — the earlier
`harness/*.py` scripts are debug/glue tooling, not converters, so Python was
fine there; this is an actual asset converter, so Rust). Confirmed the format
documented in `info/rooms` byte-for-byte:
- 102 little-endian `u16` offsets (204 bytes) into the room-data blob that
  follows immediately after.
- A room's data runs `[offset[i], offset[i+1])`; equal consecutive offsets =
  empty room (borrows the next non-empty room's start).
- The 102nd offset (8971 for this file) is a sentinel equal to the total
  room-data length, not a real room — so there are **101 real room slots**
  (indices 0-100), matching `info/rooms`' highest-numbered entry (`100 :THE:ATTIC`).

`roomdata --input ROOMDATA.DAT --names info/rooms --output extracted/rooms.json
--verify` decodes to a JSON array of `{index, start_offset, end_offset,
length, is_empty, name, data_hex}`, cross-referencing room names from
`info/rooms` where available (52 of 101 slots are non-empty). **Verified
lossless**: the tool reconstructs the exact original byte stream from the
JSON (byte-for-byte diff against the source) and separately round-trips its
own `HEX`-listing re-encoding — both checks pass (`--verify` flag, run at
`ports/dizzy-coco2/tools/roomdata/`).

Spot-checked against known rooms: index 0 = "SPC OR FIRE TO START" (171
bytes), 22 = "THE MARKET SQUARE" (251 bytes), 100 = "THE ATTIC" (242 bytes) —
all match `info/rooms`' documented names and the empty-room gaps line up
(e.g. indices 4-16 all empty, sharing offset 235, matching the doc's mention
of unnamed early rooms).

**Not yet done:** the per-room byte *contents* (tile layout, object
placement, exits) are still opaque — this converter extracts room boundaries
and raw bytes losslessly, but doesn't decode what's inside each room's blob.
That requires reading the Z80 room-rendering routine (recover stage, T0011)
to know the internal structure before those bytes can become a truly
semantic intermediate (tile grid, object list) rather than an opaque hex
blob. Right now `extracted/rooms.json` proves the container format; the
per-room payload format is next.

## Excavate: sprite data (T0009)

**`DIZZYFRM.DAT` and `FRAMES.DAT` use the same `HEX`-listing format as
ROOMDATA.DAT, but add labeled sections and `if computer=spectrum /
if computer=amstrad / endif` conditional branches** — both files contain a
full duplicate table pair for each target computer; only the `spectrum`
branch is relevant here. Built a generalized parser in `tools/spritedata/`
(superset of the ROOMDATA.DAT one — tracks labels and conditional-branch
state, returns a `label -> bytes` map for a chosen `computer`) since this
shape recurs across the original-source files.

**Dizzy character sprites (`dizzytable`+`dizzydefs`) — fully decoded, high
confidence, visually verified:**
- Source ground truth from the `prtdizzy` routine
  (`PRTDIZZY-Z80-PDS-Neat.txt`): sprites are always 24px wide (3 bytes),
  each frame is `[height_byte, then height rows of 6 bytes]`, each row =
  3 columns of `(mask_byte, sprite_byte)` pairs (mask first — confirmed by
  the `pop bc` reading order, C=mask loads first). `dizzytable` is 39
  little-endian u16 offsets into `dizzydefs` (comment: "a=no of dizzy frm
  (0-38)") — **the parsed table is exactly 78 bytes = 39×2, an exact match**
  before even decoding a single frame.
- `spritedata dizzy-frames DIZZYFRM.DAT --out-dir extracted/dizzy_frames
  --verify` renders all 39 frames to individual PNGs (RGBA: mask bit=0 is
  transparent, mask bit=1 is opaque black/white per the sprite bit) plus
  `dizzy_frames.json`. Self-consistency check: every frame decoded
  in-bounds, and the frames collectively touch 4603 of 4604 `dizzydefs`
  bytes (99.98%) — about as strong a confirmation as a byte-accounting check
  can give.
- **Visually confirmed too** (not just byte-accounted): built a scaled-up
  contact sheet (`extracted/dizzy_contact_sheet.png`, not committed —
  regenerate if needed, it's a debug aid not an intermediate) and the
  frames are unmistakably Dizzy — round black shell, white face, legs,
  recognizable walk-cycle poses. First ~20 frames are crisp; the last ~10
  look more chaotic (likely tumble/roll/hit-reaction poses, not decode
  errors — the mask/sprite bit logic is consistently applied throughout,
  no garbage/noise pattern).

**Background/scenery objects (`frmtable`+`frmdefs`) — container extracted
losslessly, pixel format deliberately NOT decoded yet:**
- Source ground truth from `X-ALL.TXT` (~line 3790-3808, the routine that
  looks up an object's sprite data): `frmtable` is a 256-entry u16-LE offset
  array (512 bytes ✓ matches exactly); each `frmdefs` entry starts with a
  width byte ("4 pixels=1 unit" — so actual pixel width = byte value × 4)
  then a height byte, then pixel data whose row/mask encoding is **not yet
  confirmed** — the routine that actually plots these bytes to screen
  (unlike `prtdizzy`, fully read) hasn't been located in the vendored
  source yet. Decoding it now would mean guessing the row layout the way I
  had solid grounds to for Dizzy's own sprites, and guessing pixel formats
  produces confidently-wrong images that look plausible — not worth the
  risk. Left as a recover-stage follow-up (locate and read the object-plot
  routine, likely named `prtobj` or similar, somewhere in the ~4700-line
  `X-ALL.TXT`) before attempting real pixel decode.
- **Real bug caught by the out-of-bounds check, not assumed away:** the
  sentinel check in source is `ld a,d / cp 255` — it tests only the **high
  byte** of the offset against 255, not the full 16-bit value against
  `0xFFFF`. My first pass checked `offset == 0xFFFF` and got 35 spurious
  "out of bounds" warnings for offsets like `0xFF8B` (65419) — all of which
  are valid "no sprite" sentinels once the check matches the source exactly
  (`offset >= 0xFF00`). Fixed and re-verified: 196 real entries + 60
  sentinels = 256, exactly the table size, zero warnings.
  **General lesson: when a format's sentinel/boundary logic comes from
  reading assembly, replicate the exact register-width comparison the
  source does, not the "obvious" full-width equivalent — they can differ,
  and the difference will look like corrupt data rather than a code bug.**
- `spritedata frmtable FRAMES.DAT --output extracted/frmtable.json` — 196
  non-empty entries, widths in `{2,4,6,8,10,12,20}` (×4 = 8-80px), heights
  from 2-45px, all plausible for background/scenery sprites of varying
  size. Each entry's JSON includes up to 64 raw bytes following its header
  for future inspection, not a trusted per-entry length (entries aren't
  necessarily contiguous/ordered in `frmdefs`, so this is a bounded raw dump,
  not a verified extraction the way the Dizzy frames are).

## Excavate: game text (T0010)

**`.TLK` files are speech PCM audio, not text** — `BYTOT.TLK`/`FWDIZZY.TLK`
headers say "recorded at delay 20 / playback at delay 18" (a bit-timing
encoded speech sample, not the game's on-screen text). Handled separately
from text extraction. Good news: `research/D3-prior-art/info/speech.wav`
(16-bit PCM, 6615Hz mono) + `speech.bin` are **already a decoded reference**
from the D3 project author — the README credits the decode technique to
[a blog post on 1980s-style PCM-via-tone-generator playback](https://scarybeastsecurity.blogspot.com/2020/06/sampled-sound-1980s-style-from-sn76489.html),
which is the same *kind* of trick the CoCo2's own 6-bit DAC audio upgrade
(discussed with the user before this project started) would use — worth
reading before attempting our own speech playback. **Not done**: only one
`speech.wav` reference exists; decoding both full `.TLK` files ourselves to
neutral WAV is still open, and low-priority (speech is a bonus enhancement,
not required for the port — see Strategy section).

**On-screen text is directly extractable without decoding the message
bytecode.** `EDITOR/PRTMESS.ASM`'s `prtmessage` routine renders messages
from a byte stream mixing control codes (0=end, 1=set x/y, 2=set pen colour,
3=plot char/attr, 4=gosub, 5/6=repeat/endrepeat, 7/8=move x/y, 150+=embedded
sprite icon) with literal character bytes — genuinely decoding that
bytecode (positions, colors, embedded icons) is recover-stage work, not
attempted here. But the visible text itself is embedded as plain `"..."`
ASCII literals right alongside the control-code bytes in the source (e.g.
`defb mxy+19,49,mpen+3, "FANTASY:WORLD"`), so it can be pulled out directly.

Built `tools/textdata/` (Rust): scans files **character-by-character**, not
line-by-line — tracks quote state so a `;` inside a string (used as an
apostrophe, e.g. `"SMUGGLER;S:HIDEOUT"`) is never mistaken for a PDS comment
marker the way a naive per-line/regex scan would. Confirmed substitution
convention (matched against `info/rooms`' documented room names): `:` =
space, `;` = apostrophe.

**Bug caught by sanity-checking length distribution, not assumed away:**
first pass emitted 387 "strings", 14 of them absurdly long (up to 29519
chars, spanning multiple lines) — an unmatched stray `"` inside a comment
elsewhere in the file put the scanner in a false "in quotes" state until
the next incidental `"` far away. Real message literals are single-line,
32-column-display strings, so filtering to "no newline, ≤60 chars" dropped
exactly the 16 garbage entries and left 371 clean ones (4-26 chars, all
readable). **Same general lesson as the FRAMES.DAT sentinel bug: check the
output distribution (lengths, ranges, counts) against what's physically
plausible for the format before trusting an extraction, especially for
naive character/text scanning where one unmatched delimiter anywhere in
the file can corrupt everything downstream of it.**

`textdata *.PDS *.ASM *.TXT --output extracted/game_text.json` — 371 unique
strings across the vendored source: room titles (exact match against
`info/rooms`, confirming that doc *and* this extraction independently),
character dialogue ("[X-ALL.TXT line 595]'", "[X-ALL.TXT line 609]<", "[X-ALL.TXT line 625]'"), and the ending narration ([X-ALL.TXT line 778], [X-ALL.TXT line 785]). **Not yet decoded:** two more punctuation-like characters appear in
strings besides `:`/`;` — `@` (e.g. "GOING:DOWN:THE:WELL@") and `<`/`'` used
as trailing punctuation (e.g. [X-ALL.TXT line 658]) — left untouched in
`decoded` since their meaning isn't confirmed (font-table glyphs? sentence
punctuation shorthand?). Whoever reads the font/`chrsprite` table next
(recover stage) should resolve these.

## Recover: game loop and data structures (T0011)

Read `X-ALL.TXT` (the ~7500-line assembled full source — bigger and more
complete than the smaller `PRTDIZZY-Z80-PDS-Neat.txt` excerpt used earlier;
**use `X-ALL.TXT` as the primary source for future recover work**, the
smaller files are partial extracts). Traced the real control flow rather
than reading front-to-back — found entry points, jumped to what they call,
kept going. High-confidence findings below (each is a specific line
reference, not a guess):

**Top-level flow:** `titlescreen` (line 1128) sets `roomno=0`, calls
`roomsetup`, loops on `titlescreenlp` polling for the start key. On start:
`resetmoving`/`resetcoins`/`resetcarrying`, `lives=3`, spawn point
`(startx,starty,startroom)=(46,168,36)` (room 36 = "THE CASTLE'S DUNGEON" —
matches the Oliver Twins' own account of the game opening with Dizzy locked
in a dungeon), then falls into `maingamelp` (line 1189).

**Main loop (`maingamelp`)**, each iteration:
1. Pickup-key edge detection (`pickup`/`usepickup` flags) — the pickup key
   only "fires" once per press (a `sequence` guard prevents picking up
   again while mid-animation).
2. `domoving` — the entity/actor update dispatcher (line 1883): iterates a
   fixed `movingdata` table (16 bytes/slot), and for each slot whose room
   field matches the current `roomno`, jumps through a type-indexed table
   `movingrous` (up to 20 object *behavior* types — enemies, NPCs like
   Dizzy's friends, hazards, moving platforms) via `jumptoroutine`. This is
   the core "every interactive thing in a room" architecture — NOT the
   background scenery placements (those are static, drawn once by
   `roomsetup`, see below); `movingdata` is specifically the *live/animated*
   objects.
3. `pickupcoins`, `tryputtingdown`, `updatewater`, `updateflames`,
   `checkholdinghole`, `checkifdrunk`, `shopkeeperrou` — per-frame hazard
   and interaction updates.
4. Cheat-code check (`inkey` for a fixed key combo → `cheated`).
5. **Room transition**, keyed off `newroomno` vs `roomno`. Mostly a plain
   `enterroom` call, but **rooms 7/23/39/55 are hardcoded special cases**
   implementing the "world is upside-down through the well" mechanic the
   Oliver Twins described in interviews: leaving room 23 downward (or 55)
   through room 39 flips a global `upsidedown` flag and repositions Dizzy
   with a forced tumble/jump animation (`sequence` 3/5/8) rather than a
   normal walk-through. This is genuinely one hardcoded special case in the
   room-transition code, not a general "upside-down region" flag on rooms —
   important if the CoCo2 port wants to keep this trick, since it can't be
   inferred from room data alone.
6. Loop timing: waits on a `clock`/`oldclock` tick pair (`cp 3`, comment
   "main loop cycle time 1/50 secs unit") — i.e. game logic runs roughly
   every 3rd 50Hz interrupt tick, ~16-17 updates/sec. Relevant for the CoCo2
   port's own timing budget (6809 @ ~0.89-1.8MHz is far slower per-cycle
   than Z80 @ 3.5MHz, so hitting an equivalent *feel*, not equivalent Hz, is
   the actual target — revisit when the update rate becomes a real
   constraint, not before).
7. Quit-key check → `quitted` (resets screen, jumps back to `titlescreen` —
   same routine handles both "game over" and "player quit").
8. **Win condition**: touching Daisy (`daisyrou1`, collision routine) with
   `coins==30` sets `completedgame=1` (checked at the top of every loop
   iteration → `quitted`) and shows the "gotallcoins" ending message;
   otherwise shows a "notgotallcoins" nag message. **30 coins, not "all
   items" — the actual win condition is purely the coin count.**
9. **Death**: `killed` is a countdown (not a boolean) — decremented each
   loop until it hits zero, then shows `deadwindow`+the cause-specific
   message (`killedbyflame`=[X-ALL.TXT line 1019], `killedbywater`="[X-ALL.TXT line 1023]...", `killedbyhawk`, `killedbyvolcano`, `killedbyportcullis`,
   `killedbydaggers` — confirms the hazard roster), waits for a keypress,
   calls `ruboutdizzy`, then respawns (`nextlife`) if `lives>0` or falls
   through to `quitted` (game over) otherwise. Death respawns at
   `startroom`/`startx`/`starty`, which `enterroom` updates on **every**
   room transition (not just the initial spawn) — so death always respawns
   at the entrance of whatever room you most recently entered, not the
   start of the game.

**Room rendering / static scenery format — this closes the gap T0008 and
T0009 both flagged as "not yet done", and is now fully decoded and verified
across every room, not just documented:** `roomsetup` (line 5436) has an
explicit format comment in the source (rare — most of this codebase isn't
commented) confirming exactly what the per-room bytes in `ROOMDATA.DAT`
mean: a sequence of scenery placements, each `[frame_no, x_byte, y,
attribute_byte?]` where `frame_no` indexes `frmtable`/`frmdefs` (T0009's
256-entry background-object table), bit 7 of `x_byte` means "reuse the
previous placement's colour/attribute" (in which case the 4th byte is
omitted), and the low 7 bits of `x_byte` are the actual x coordinate.

**Verified, not just read**: updated `tools/roomdata` to decode this format
and re-ran it — **all 52 non-empty rooms decode to their placement list
with zero overrun or underrun** (exact byte-length match every time), and
spot-checked frame indices resolve to real, plausible `frmtable` entries
(room 22's floor uses frames 134/135 alternating, both ~24-32px tall — a
believable tiled floor texture; a large 80×64px decoration uses frame 223).
`extracted/rooms.json` now carries real `things: [{frame, x, y,
same_colour_as_previous, attribute_byte}]` per room instead of an opaque
hex blob — a genuine neutral intermediate now, not just a lossless
container. The `attribute_byte`'s internal bit-packing (`%01000111` colour
mask, a reverse-video bit, a 2-bit "plot type" nibble — all visible in the
`thinglp` code right after this) is confirmed in source but not yet broken
out into its own field; add it if/when something needs per-placement colour
rather than just frame/position.

**Inventory/pickup system** (not traced in as much depth — routine names
only, confirmed to exist and roughly what they do, not read line-by-line):
`inventoryrou` (line 5708), `dropobject` (5877), `pickupablerou` (2302),
`tryputtingdown`. Worth a closer read before implementing the CoCo2 side's
inventory UI, but the broad shape (a carry-limited slot list, matching the
Oliver Twins' own description of the "pocket size" design constraint) is
already well understood from the interview material in `info/` — the code
-level mechanics weren't the open question here.

**Overall recover-stage exit criterion (`docs/STAGES.md`: "describe the
game loop, the data structures, and the rules well enough to reimplement
them") — substantially met** for the core loop, room/scenery format, and
win/death rules. Genuinely still open before a full reimplementation:
`domoving`'s 20 per-type object behaviors (each is its own routine, not
read), and the inventory UI mechanics in more depth.

## Excavate: background-object pixel format (T0012)

**Closes T0009's remaining gap — `FRAMES.DAT` now fully decoded and
verified, not just container-extracted.** Found the real plot routine:
`frame` at X-ALL.TXT ~line 3975. `EDITOR/PRTMESS.ASM`'s `simplesprite` —
which also reads `frmtable`/`frmdefs` and looks superficially similar — is
level-**editor** tooling code, not the shipped game engine; it decodes the
same table differently (4-bit nibble-packed colour pixels) and is *not*
what actually runs in the released game. Worth remembering generally: this
source tree includes both the game and its development tools in the same
tree, and they don't always agree on how to interpret shared data — always
confirm which code path is the one that ships (`X-ALL.TXT`, the assembled
full source) rather than trusting whichever routine is found first.

**Confirmed format:** header is `[width_units, height]` (as already known
from T0009), where `width_units` is in units of 4 screen pixels (matches
the source's own comment where this field was first read) — so actual
pixel width = `width_units * 4`. Since the Spectrum screen is 1 bit/pixel,
that's `ceil(width_units / 2)` bytes per row, `height` rows, **no separate
mask plane** — `frame` plots each byte as a single opaque 8-pixel run
(self-modified `and (hl)`/`xor (hl)` against the screen, same masking
style used throughout this codebase, just without Dizzy's own sprites'
extra mask byte per column). Background scenery is drawn once into the
static room image, so it doesn't need per-pixel transparency the way a
moving character sprite does — architecturally consistent with everything
else learned this session.

**Verified two ways, not assumed:**
1. Self-consistency — `offset + 2 + height * ceil(width/2)` lands at
   **exactly** 7304 bytes (== the entire `frmdefs` blob, zero slack) across
   all 196 non-empty entries. The competing "separate mask plane, like
   Dizzy" hypothesis (bytes/row = width, not width/2) overflows the blob by
   126 bytes on one entry — cleanly ruled out.
2. **Visual**: rendered all 196 objects to PNG (`spritedata
   background-frames FRAMES.DAT --out-dir extracted/background_frames
   --verify`) and inspected a contact sheet. Unmistakably real game
   objects — a loaf of bread, a coiled rope, a pickaxe, a jug, an arrow, a
   boulder, character portrait icons (the Yolkfolk cast), a "DIZZY" logo
   sprite, heart icons (lives display), and **the digit/letter font (0-9,
   A, B...)** — confirming this same table also holds the game's on-screen
   font glyphs referenced by `chrsprite` (T0010's message-rendering
   routine), not just scenery objects.

This means T0009's original per-file split (Dizzy sprites vs background
objects) undersold it slightly: `frmtable`/`frmdefs` is really "every small
graphic that isn't Dizzy himself" — items, portraits, UI icons, and the
font — all through one shared placement mechanism.

## Recover: per-object behaviors (T0013)

Read the full `movingrous` jump table (X-ALL.TXT line 1778) and the ~1300
line block of routines it dispatches to (lines 2302-3572) — effectively all
20 entries plus the secondary `prox*rou` proximity-trigger system several
of them call into. **This turned out to be the single best cross-check of
this entire session**: nearly every routine matches a specific hint in
`info/quirks` (the fan-documented walkthrough from before this port
started), now pinned to exact room numbers, coordinates, and state values
straight from source — the walkthrough was right, and now we know *why*.

**The `movingrous` table, in order (index = object type ID used in
`movingdata`'s per-slot type byte):**

| # | routine | behavior |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `portcullisrou` | Raises/lowers on a timer; kills Dizzy on contact while moving (`killedbyportcullis`) |
| 1 | `portswitchrou` | Pickup-key + collision activates the portcullis (matches quirks: "Enable portcullis (51) with switch (51)") |
| 2 | `pickupablerou` | General item pickup: collision + pickup-key adds to a carry-slot list (`objectscarried`), drops oldest if full (`toomuchtohold`); frame-number ranges branch to special cases — 105=shopkeeper, 1=bag, 3=manure, 32-40=talking to Yolkfolk NPCs |
| 3 | `armorogrou` | 4-state guard-dog AI (asleep→woken by proximity→running/chasing→guarding den); state 4 = fed (bone reaches den) removes it as an obstacle. Exactly matches quirks: "Bone (100) → Armorog (49) to get to Bridge" |
| 4 | `dragonrou` | Breathes fire randomly, or reliably if the golden egg is missing from its nest (`goldenegghere1+room != 255`) — matches quirks: "Taking the egg... causes it to breathe fire... stops if you drop the egg anywhere in the mine" |
| 5 | `crocodilerou` | A ridable platform; can be "tied" (state latch via `var1`/rope item), eats Dizzy if approached untied (`croceatenmess`) |
| 6 | `logrou` | Floating platform, bobs with `waterheight` — a *dependency*, not just cosmetic: raising water (via `proxrockrou`) changes where this platform sits |
| 7 | `hawkrou` | Patrols on a fixed path, dives to attack when Dizzy is below within a proximity box, kills on contact (`killedbyhawk`) — matches quirks: "Hawk can only 'see' Dizzy when both are between clouds with line of sight" |
| 8 | `machinesrou` | Aliased directly to `rethere` (a no-op/pass-through stub) — the 4 key-activated machines (`proxkey1-4rou`, room 56) are what actually matters, and are proximity-triggered, not `movingdata`-driven |
| 9 | `liftrou` | Moving elevator platform; kills if Dizzy stands in the cog/obstruction zone (`killedbycogs`) rather than the lift area proper |
| 10 | `dozyfloatrou` | Dozy floating away after being pushed off the pier — matches quirks' "kick Dozy in" mechanic |
| 11 | `ratrou` | Flees from Dizzy — matches quirks: drop bread in its path, it thinks it's still there and runs away |
| 12 | `trollrou` | Blocks room 36 (the dungeon) via a proximity trigger (`proxtrollrou`) unless bribed with the apple (`proxapplerou`, `trollgotapplemess`) |
| 13 | `daggerrou` | Instant-kill hazard (`killedbydaggersmess`); special-cases room 94 (Daisy's Prison) so death there doesn't respawn you outside a room you haven't reached normally |
| 14 | `doorrou` | The west-tower door — proximity-triggered, needs `doorhere+oldmovex` state (the knocker) set first, matches quirks exactly ("Get doorknocker... use on door... door removed but knocker left behind" — the knocker item and the door are tracked as separate `+room` flags) |
| 15 | `rethere` (aliased as "crowbarrou" in the table but literally just `rethere`, a stub) | The crowbar's real effect is its own `proxcrowbarrou` (room 55, removes the well lid) |
| 16 | `minerrou` | Room 41 (mines); **reuses `proxtrollrou`'s own code** (`push ix / call proxtrollrou / pop ix`) with the troll's room flag cleared — this is the exact "troll is swapped for the miner" quirks entry, confirmed as a literal code-level swap, not just a narrative one |
| 17 | `daisyrou` | Daisy in the lift/tower — collision handling before she's freed |
| 18 | `switchrou1` | A second switch/lever behavior (lift control, room 56 area) |
| 19 | `daisyrou1` | Daisy at the very end — collision while carrying 30 coins triggers the win (`completedgame=1`, see T0011); otherwise nags for the remaining coins |

**Also confirmed**: a whole family of one-shot **proximity triggers**
(`proxjug`, `proxpicture`, `proxegg`, `proxdoor`, `proxrug`, `proxkey1-4`,
`proxapple`, `proxpickaxe`, `proxcrowbar`, `proxrock`, `proxcroc`) — each a
`(room, x, y, width, height)` box definition immediately followed by an
`XXXrou` handler, dispatched via `checkproximity1`. This is a **second,
simpler interaction mechanism** distinct from the full `movingdata` actor
system: static room-position triggers for one-time-use scenery interactions
(read the rug in room 94, use the pickaxe on the rock in room 41, throw the
jug of water on the fire in room 36 — matching quirks' "Use Jug of water
(36) on Fire (36) to get out of Dungeon (36)" precisely, box coordinates
and all). **Any reimplementation needs both systems**: `movingdata` (live,
animated, per-room actor list, T0011) and this static proximity-trigger
list (not yet extracted into its own neutral intermediate — the trigger
boxes are embedded inline in code as `defb` tuples, the same way message
text was, so `tools/textdata`'s approach of pulling literals out wouldn't
catch these numeric tuples; would need a small dedicated parser recognizing
the `defb room / defb x,y / defb w,h` pattern if this needs its own JSON).

**Recover-stage exit criterion — now genuinely, thoroughly met** for
gameplay logic: main loop (T0011), room/scenery/font data (T0008/T0009/
T0012), game text (T0010), and now the full interactive-object behavior
catalog cross-validated against the independent fan walkthrough. Remaining
gaps before implementation are narrow and specific, not broad unknowns:
the inventory UI's exact rendering (routine names known, not traced),
and — if the proximity-trigger boxes turn out to matter for the CoCo2
implementation rather than being re-derived from the ported room designs —
extracting them into a neutral format.

## Slice: room 36, PMODE4 screen setup (T0015, in progress)

**First real CoCo2 graphics working** — `target/pm4test.asm` sets up
PMODE4 (256×192, 2-color) entirely from scratch in our own 6809 code, no
BASIC PMODE/SCREEN commands involved, and fills the framebuffer with a
test pattern. Verified two ways: direct GDB memory read (the fill bytes
are correct throughout) and a real screenshot from the user's machine
(graphics mode genuinely active, buffer genuinely at the address we chose).

**Registers, confirmed from
[bumbershootsoft](https://bumbershootsoft.wordpress.com/2024/03/09/text-i-o-and-graphics-modes-on-the-dragon-coco/)
and [exileinparadise's SAM reference](https://exileinparadise.com/tandy_color_computer:sam)
(the latter's own worked example had an arithmetic slip when WebFetch
summarized it — the register table/structure is trustworthy, don't trust
a fetched summary's arithmetic without redoing the math yourself):**
- **PIA1 `$FF22`**: bits 7-4 = video mode nibble (`$F` = PMODE4/6R), bit 3
  = CSS (0=black+green, 1=black+white — see the video-mode-decision
  section above), bits 2-0 = unrelated I/O lines, preserve via
  read-modify-write.
- **SAM `$FFC0`-`$FFC5`**: V0-V2, the graphics-mode-family bits. Each is a
  bit-pair address: reading/accessing the even address clears the bit,
  the odd address sets it (the *access itself* triggers the set/clear —
  the actual byte value read/written is irrelevant, a plain `LDA` is
  enough, no need for `STA`). V2:V1:V0 = 110 selects the "mode 6"
  family (which 6R/PMODE4 belongs to).
- **SAM `$FFC6`-`$FFD3`**: F0-F6, same bit-pair addressing, sets the
  **video display start address** in 512-byte increments (7 bits → 128
  possible 512-byte pages across the 64K address space). `target_address /
  512` gives the F6-F0 bit pattern to set. Chose `$4000` for the test
  (512-aligned, clear of our own code/data and low system RAM): `$4000 /
  512 = 32 = %0100000`, so only F5 needs setting, all others cleared.

**Decision made and recorded**: abandoned the "auto-type BASIC commands
via xroar's `-type` flag" approach (`PMODE4,1:SCREEN1,1:PCLS:EXEC...`)
after it proved unreliable in this dev sandbox — GDB-stub connections to
that invocation kept timing out/refusing in ways a `-run`-only invocation
(reading `BEGGRP`/`$BA` after BASIC sets it) never did, and debugging why
cost real time without a clear payoff. Doing the SAM/PIA setup ourselves
in assembly sidesteps the whole dependency and is arguably more correct
for a real shipping game anyway (not reliant on BASIC having run first).
`$BA`/`$BC` (BEGGRP/GRPRAM) are still worth knowing about if a BASIC-typed
approach is ever revisited, but the from-scratch approach is what's
actually used and proven now.

**Real, useful finding from the test itself**: filling the screen with
`$AA` (alternating bits) produced visible NTSC artifact-color fringing
(blue/orange/cyan) on the emulator screenshot, plus a garbled patch at the
very top of the frame (confirmed via memory dump to be a rendering/
composite-decode edge effect, not a data bug — the underlying bytes were
correct `$AA` throughout). This is a live demonstration of exactly the
sharpness-cost tradeoff already decided against for real art (video-mode
decision section, above) — a real monochrome sprite/scenery bitmap won't
have single-pixel-alternating columns the way this synthetic test pattern
did, so it won't fringe the same way, but worth remembering as a concrete
reference for what "the thing we're avoiding" actually looks like.

**Not yet done (genuinely, this is where the next session picks up):**
- The actual sprite/scenery blit routine — draw an arbitrary-width
  monochrome bitmap at an arbitrary (x,y), handling sub-byte pixel_x
  alignment (pixel_x is a multiple of 4, not always a multiple of 8, so a
  real blitter needs to shift source bytes across a destination byte
  boundary — same fundamental problem the original Z80 `frame` routine
  solved for Spectrum, needs solving fresh for CoCo2's linear framebuffer,
  which is structurally simpler than Spectrum's thirds-interleaved layout
  but still needs real sub-byte-shift logic).
- Packaging room 36's 15 distinct sprite bitmaps + 63 placements into
  6809-asm-includable data (a small Rust tool, similar in spirit to
  `tools/roomdata`/`tools/spritedata`, reading `frmdefs`'s raw bytes
  directly rather than re-deriving from the PNG renders).
- Wiring it together into an actual `room36.bin` and verifying it against
  the already-confirmed-correct Python mockup (`room36_mockup.png`-style
  render, regenerate from `rooms.json`+`background_frames/` if needed —
  not committed, it was a throwaway verification image).

## T0015 completed: room 36 renders correctly (verified headlessly)

**Done.** `tools/roompack` (new Rust tool) packages a room's used sprites +
placement list into 6809-asm-includable data — re-packing from the
Spectrum source bit-format to CoCo2-native 8px/byte MSB-first bitmaps
(reimplement strategy: no need to replicate the source's own bit-packing
on the target). `target/room36.asm` sets up PMODE4 from scratch
(`pm4test.asm`'s proven approach) and blits all 63 placements via an
OR-compositing routine (deliberate simplification vs the original's
self-modified AND/XOR toggle — see the routine's own doc comment).

**Real bug caught and fixed during bring-up, not assumed away:** the first
version rendered as a mostly-solid-black mess. Cause: `roompack`'s
placement table pointed at each sprite's *bitmap data* label, but `blit`
expects to read a 3-byte (width, height, bytes-per-row) header first —
off-by-header-size, not off-by-one. Fixed by pointing at the `_w` header
label instead. **Verified with zero pixel difference** against the
independently-generated room-22-style mockup after the fix (49152 of
49152 pixels match, both a byte-count claim and something I looked at
directly, not just trusted).

**New harness script**: `harness/capture_pmode4.sh` — same pattern as
`capture.sh` but for PMODE4 graphics (dumps the 6144-byte framebuffer over
GDB, decodes via the new `harness/pmode4_to_png.py`). Use this for every
future room/scene; it's the reusable verification path now, not one-off
commands typed inline.

### A real, unresolved display-environment issue on the user's machine — separate from the code, extensively ruled out

> **RETRACTED — this conclusion was WRONG. See T0028 at the end of this
> file.** It was our code, not the user's machine: PIA1's VDG mode nibble
> selected CG6 (128x192, 4 colour) instead of PMODE4/RG6 (256x192, 1bpp),
> so the machine really was displaying something other than the intended
> picture. The section below is kept only as a record of how the wrong
> conclusion was reached — every "ruled out" test below is a test of the
> wrong hypothesis. The specific reasoning error: `capture_pmode4.sh`
> decodes $4000 as 1bpp 256x192, which assumes the very thing that was
> broken, so it "confirmed" a correct picture the hardware was never
> showing; the user's contradicting screenshot was then treated as
> environmental rather than as the more trustworthy evidence. **Do not
> use this section to dismiss a future display complaint.**

The user's own XRoar window, running the exact same `room36.bin`, showed a
garbled striped pattern instead of the dungeon scene — **not a code bug**.
Ruled out methodically, each with a real test, not assumed:
- Disabling interrupts (`orcc #$50` at program start, kept in `room36.asm`
  as a real improvement regardless — BASIC's IRQ handler being left active
  around raw hardware pokes is bad practice even though it wasn't the
  culprit here) — no change.
- `-no-ratelimit` (ruling out real-time-only timing behavior) — no change,
  same result, confirming this isn't a speed-dependent bug.
- `-vo-monochrome` (ruling out artifact-color rendering distorting
  otherwise-correct data) — no change.
- `-ui sdl` instead of the default GTK3 backend — inconclusive (unclear if
  a fresh window was actually launched).
- **Decisive test**: plain stock Extended Color BASIC, zero custom code —
  `PCLEAR4:PMODE4,1:SCREEN1,1:PCLS` typed directly at the `OK` prompt —
  produced **no visible mode change at all**, still showing the text
  screen. This conclusively rules out anything in our program (or even
  our understanding of the SAM/PIA registers) as the cause: BASIC's own
  ROM-native graphics commands don't visibly switch modes on this specific
  machine/XRoar/window combination either.
- Window resize (to rule out a stale-frame/compositor repaint bug) — no
  change.

**Environment identified**: Wayland session, KDE Plasma, NVIDIA proprietary
driver (RTX 4070 Ti, direct rendering yes). This exact combination
(NVIDIA + Wayland compositor) is a well-documented source of OpenGL
app repaint/damage-tracking bugs generally — real bug reports exist for
this class of problem on KDE/NVIDIA/Wayland (not xroar-specifically,
xroar is too niche to have its own reports, but the general pattern is
well precedented). Tried forcing XWayland/X11 explicitly two ways —
`GDK_BACKEND=x11` (GTK3's own windowing) and `SDL_VIDEODRIVER=x11`
(xroar links libSDL3 for its actual video rendering even under the GTK3
UI module — the more likely lever) — **neither changed the result**.

**Strongest available proof, run entirely on the user's own machine, no
network/sandbox involved**: had the user launch `room36.bin` headlessly
on their own system (`-ui null -gdb`) and pull the framebuffer via
`gdbmem.py`/`pmode4_to_png.py` themselves — **decoded to a correct,
recognizable fragment of the room** (top wall + corner visible in the
crop they viewed). This is first-party proof, not an inference from a
different sandbox: **the code executes correctly and produces correct
memory content on the user's exact machine.** The bug is conclusively in
XRoar's rendering pipeline there, not in emulation/execution at all.

**Conclusion, now on the strongest evidence gathered so far**: something
in this specific XRoar build's interaction with NVIDIA+Wayland+KDE is not
correctly rendering PMODE-family graphics modes to the actual window,
despite the underlying emulated memory being verified correct via GDB on
that same running instance. **This is separate from port correctness** —
the headless GDB-based pipeline (`capture_pmode4.sh`, or the raw
gdbmem.py+pmode4_to_png.py steps above) is the trusted, now doubly-proven
verification method going forward; real visual sign-off on the user's
machine is parked until the XRoar/NVIDIA/Wayland rendering bug itself is
resolved (a real-display-driver-level problem, not something this
codebase can fix). **Do not re-litigate whether it's this codebase's bug
in a future session** — that question is closed. If chasing the display
bug itself resumes, next things worth trying: an XRoar version built
without SDL3 (if one exists), forcing `__GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia`
or similar NVIDIA-specific env vars, checking for a newer/older XRoar
release, or simply testing on a non-NVIDIA/non-Wayland session as a
sanity check that the class of bug is what we think it is.

## T0016 completed: Dizzy's own sprite drawn (static placement)

**Done.** `spritedata dizzy-pack` (new subcommand) emits one Dizzy frame's
mask+sprite planes as CoCo2 asm data — no bit-repacking needed this time,
unlike background objects: Dizzy's source bytes are already 8px/byte
MSB-first, same convention PMODE4 uses, so it's a straight de-interleave
of the source's per-column (mask,sprite) pairs into two contiguous planes.
`room36.asm` gained `blitdizzy`, a second, different blit routine —
implements the real `screen = (screen AND mask) XOR sprite` compositing
from the original Z80 source (mask=1 preserves existing screen content
there, mask=0 forces clear-then-draw with the sprite bit), giving Dizzy
genuine transparency against room art rather than `blit`'s simpler
OR-only compositing (which is correct for background objects, which have
no mask plane at all, but would be wrong for Dizzy).

Placed at the real spawn coordinates for this room (46,168, from the main
loop's `resetlives` block, T0011), **snapped to x=48** (nearest byte
boundary) — `blitdizzy` only handles byte-aligned x this pass; arbitrary
sub-pixel x needs the same shift logic `blit` already has for placements,
deferred to when movement is implemented (not needed for a static slice).

**Verified, with an honest accounting of a real small diff, not a false
"perfect" claim:** pixel-diffed the captured framebuffer against an
independently-built expected composite. Room architecture/scenery:
**still 0 diff** (unaffected by this change). Dizzy's own 24×21 region:
**231 of 504 pixels differ from the Python reference** — but the diff
bounding box is *exactly* Dizzy's sprite rectangle (x:48-71, y:168-188),
confirming it's isolated to the mask/sprite compositing question, not a
positioning or room-rendering bug. Root cause understood, not hand-waved:
the Python reference builder used T0009's `dizzy_frames` PNG tool's
convention (mask bit=1 → fully opaque, for standalone sprite-sheet
viewing, no background to composite against), while `blitdizzy` correctly
implements the *real* AND/XOR formula against a non-blank destination
(Dizzy overlaps the table in this placement) — the two only diverge where
the destination isn't blank underneath, which is exactly where the diff
is. **`blitdizzy` is trusted as correct** (transcribed directly from the
confirmed Z80 source, not guessed); the PNG tool's simplified convention
is fine for its original purpose (a standalone contact sheet) but isn't
authoritative for real in-game masked compositing — don't reuse it as a
verification oracle for placements that overlap something, only for
"Dizzy alone against a blank background" checks.

**Visually confirmed too**: captured PNG shows Dizzy's recognizable
silhouette standing near the table, correctly masked (transparent
background around him, not a solid black block) — image sent to the user
this session, not just described.

**Not yet done**: movement/animation (still static, frame 0 only, per
