Tried `-state <file>` (the CLI-level equivalent, restoring before the
autoboot script's own periodic registration runs at all) as a workaround
-- same result, zero ticks. Whatever `--from-tape` itself does differently
(it never calls `load()` -- it boots from tape and calls `save()` at the
very end, in ONE continuous run with periodic registered once at genuine
machine start) is why THAT script still works fine even under
`-nothrottle`. This looks like a real MAME/lua-plugin interaction on this
system (the "attempt to assign to const variable 'info'" `load_dat.lua`
error appears on EVERY run in this environment, savestate-related or not
-- plausibly related, not confirmed).

**What this means for finishing T0037**: the fast savestate-resume path
is not usable for scripted movement testing as currently built. The real
path forward is extending `--from-tape`'s OWN approach -- one continuous
run, full tape boot, `natkeyboard`/ioport-driven navigation to room 36,
THEN the actual x=106 test -- never calling `load()` mid-script. Real
cost: ~7 minutes per run (the tape load alone), so budget for it rather
than assuming the 5-second turnaround the savestate trick was supposed to
give.

**Real, reusable finding from this session's work, despite not reaching
an answer**: decoded the original's actual key mapping from
`X-ALL.TXT`'s `keyboardkeys`/`getkeybyte` (traced the self-modifying
`inkey` routine's bit-packing by hand, then confirmed the row assignment
against MAME's own `:LINE0`/`:LINE6`/`:LINE7` ioport field names for this
driver) -- **LEFT = Z, RIGHT = X, JUMP = SPACE, FIRE/pickup = ENTER**.
Not recorded anywhere in this project before now; needed by any future
`zx_orig.sh` scripted-input work, this task included.

Task left `todo`, not `doing` -- genuinely not answered, don't mark T0031's
open question resolved based on this entry.

### T0040: room 52's picture message

X-ALL.TXT's `proxpicturerou`/`lookatpicturemess` (~848/~3270), ported
directly now that T0041 gave room 52 real headroom. Real text, real box
geometry, byte-for-byte.

**The real gating, reproduced exactly, not simplified**: this is NOT a
plain "walk near it to see a tooltip" trigger. `tryputtingdown`
(X-ALL.TXT's real caller) returns immediately if `pickup==0` -- i.e. the
picture only shows while the player is CARRYING something and presses
DOWN, checked BEFORE the inventory-screen fallback that same key path
falls through to otherwise. Confirmed from the source, not guessed --
plausibly a real quirk of how the original's DOWN-key dispatch is
structured (drop-zone checks first, inventory second), not something
worth "fixing" to be more permissive. Reproduced in `try_pickup`
(`actors.asm`): after scanning for a pickupable actor underfoot and
finding none, a new check (holding something + `cur_room==52` +
`aabb_hit` against `PICTURE_BOX_*`) runs BEFORE the existing "open
inventory" fallback, showing `msg_picture` and returning without opening
the inventory or touching what's held -- matching `proxpicturerou`
never consuming the carried item either.

**Verified** with a scripted MAME test (poke `cur_room=52`, position
inside the box, `inv[0]=17` to simulate carrying the apple, drive DOWN
then SPACE via real ioport keys): message box renders with correct,
readable, centred text over room 52's real background; `inv[0]` is
still 17 after dismissal (nothing consumed); normal gameplay resumes
cleanly. Full regression clean: address-range audit 0 in every
protected region, `verify_verbatim.py` 134/134, playtest script clean,
room 36's own boot pixel-unchanged.

**Still not wired** (unchanged from T0036's own note): room 52's two
actor-table entries (the "railingmess" pickupable prop, and this same
`proxpicture` trigger's OWN entry in `actors.json` -- the message is now
implemented directly in `try_pickup`, not through the general actor/prox
system this port uses for apple/jug/loaf, since `proxpicture` isn't
attached to a droppable item at all). `--actor-rooms` stays at `35,36`.

### T0042-T0049: a batch of real playtest findings, and one root cause behind four of them

Eight items from one play session. Two turned out to share nothing, four
shared a single root cause, and one was a misdiagnosis worth recording.

**T0045-T0048 (room 52's railings/painting/sword, and its "missing"
left railing) were ONE bug**: bit 7 of a placement's colour byte is the
original's `frmreverse` flag -- X-ALL.TXT `thinglp` (~5553) decodes it
(`ld a,(ix+0) / rlca / and 1 / ld (frmreverse),a`) and `frame` consumes
it by walking the sprite's bytes right-to-left instead of left-to-right
(~4072/4103). It is a plain horizontal MIRROR of the drawn sprite, and
this port had ignored it since the very first room was converted.

18 of room 52's 91 placements have that bit set (room 36 has 2; rooms
2/35/53 none), and they are exactly the things the playtest called out:
the right-hand stair railings (frame 195 x6, 193), the painting
(164/165), the top-right sword (166/168 -- "tip split from the bottom
and displayed further to the left" is precisely what half a mirrored
sprite drawn unmirrored looks like), and the left balustrade (192 x4).
`roompack` now carries the flag into the sprite variant key (so a frame
and its mirror are two distinct, separately-deduplicated bitmaps, `_m`
suffix) and flips the finished grid before packing. `verify_verbatim.py`
learned the `_m` suffix too, so mirrored sprites are checked against the
MIRROR of the source bitmap rather than reported as corrupt: 147/147
byte-exact.

**The `_m` variants cost room** -- room 52 grew from 15 to 22 sprite
variants and actor_data.asm grew by four sprites once rooms 52/53's
actors were wired, which left the $5800 gap with 43 bytes free. Moved
`actor_data.asm` down to the $7800 block (it's pure data, referenced
only by absolute `ldx #label`). Headroom now: low 197, gap1 691, gap2
564, $8000+ 29796.

**T0048/T0049 were the same omission, not art bugs at all**: the
"missing" railing section is a PICKUPABLE ACTOR (frame 192 at x=216,
`railingmess`) filling the gap between the static railing pieces at
x=184/200/232, and room 53's gator is likewise an actor. Neither room
was in `--actor-rooms`, so neither was ever drawn. Now `35,36,52,53`.
The gator renders; its `crocodile` behaviour routine is still unported
(it is drawn and inert -- disclosed, not hidden).

**T0044 (walking on top of the wall) -- the transition threshold was
simply unreachable.** `TOP_TRANSITION_Y` was 40, but the rat corridor's
floor is the slab top at y=80 and a jump rises 32px (measured), so the
apex is y=48 at best: the up-transition could NEVER fire. Dizzy instead
apexed level with the y=48 wall row, drifted out of the x=192-231
ceiling gap, and landed ON the wall. 66 is the source's own value
(`checktopside`: `cp 66 / jp c,goneup`) and works unchanged because
this port's dizzy_y is feet-anchored exactly like the source's `y`.
Verified: jumping in the gap now flips to room 52 at y=65; under the
solid wall he bonks at y=73 and never reaches the threshold at all.
The earlier "sized generously, not derived from the source's raw
values" note above T0035 was the mistake -- the raw value was right.

**T0043 (rat ghost) was a MISSING ERASE, not a stuck actor.** The
playtest already contained the diagnosis: "if you go up a level and
then climb down, the rat is gone and that is correct" -- state right,
pixels wrong. `draw_actors` only ever clears an actor's CURRENT
position, so an actor that stops being drawn never gets its last frame
erased. `ur_flee_gone` now forces both buffers to do one full redraw,
the same one-line fix `try_pickup` already used for picked-up items.
Confirmed by capture: the rat walks to x=224 (its 32px sprite's right
edge exactly meets the screen edge -- RAT_FLED_X can't go higher
without blit wrap) and leaves nothing behind.

**T0042 (apple/troll gating the loaf/rat) -- NOT REPRODUCIBLE as an
ordering dependency, and there is no code path that imposes one.**
Tested directly: with `troll_bribed=0`, carrying the loaf, standing in
`proxloaf`'s box on the rat ledge, dropping it arms `rat_target_active`,
the rat walks to it, eats it (`loaf_room=255`), and flees -- the entire
chain, apple untouched. `check_drop_triggers`' loaf branch checks only
frame id, room and box; the only `troll_bribed` test in the file is
inside the APPLE branch and the troll's own knockback.

What DOES gate things is geometry, and two findings are worth recording:
- The rat corridor is unreachable from room 36's floor. Brute-forced it
  (walk the full width both ways, jumping constantly, bribed and not):
  the highest Dizzy's feet ever reach is y=144, and the slab at y=80-100
  is solid from x=8 to x=247. The corridor is entered from room 35's
  top-right ledge (walking right at y=80 arrives in room 36 at x=8,
  y=80) or by dropping in from room 52.
- Getting left into room 35 at floor level walks straight through the
  fireplace, which kills -- i.e. the JUG/fire puzzle, not the apple/troll
  one, is what actually gates the westward route. A plausible source of
  the "there is an order" impression, along with T0044: dropping the
  loaf while standing on top of the wall (where T0044 wrongly allowed
  Dizzy to be) silently does nothing, because the drop lands at y=36,
  far outside proxloaf's y=64-80 box.
Left open pending the user's own re-test rather than closed as "works
for me" -- if it still happens after T0044, the next thing to capture is
where exactly Dizzy is standing when the loaf is dropped.

### T0050: polish pass against the original source -- Dizzy's x unit, and the checkpoint

A deliberate "compare everything against X-ALL.TXT" round rather than a
bug report. Two real findings, one of them long-standing.

**Dizzy's `x` in the original is in FOUR-PIXEL units, not pixels.**
`PRTDIZZY.PDS` settles it: `ld a,(dizx)` then `srl c` makes x/2 the
screen BYTE column, so one unit is 8/2 = 4 pixels, with the low bit
selecting the 4px sub-byte shift this port's blit already implements.
The routine's own header comment says `e=x (0=left 255=right)`, which is
simply stale -- and believing it is what put several derived constants
into this port in pixel units when the source's numbers were units.

Four independent cross-checks agree, which is why this is not a guess:
- `cp 1 / jp z,goneleft` and `cp 57 / jp z,goneright` bound movement --
  meaningless as pixels (a 57-pixel-wide room), exact as units: the
  walkable span is x=2..56 == 8..224 px, which is precisely a 24px
  sprite kept fully on a 256px screen.
- `goneright` sets x=2 (8px, the left edge) and `goneleft` sets x=56
  (224px, the right edge) -- both nonsense read as pixels, both exactly
  right read as units.
- Movement is `x +/- 1` per tick == 4px/tick, which is what this port
  has always used.
- A real ZX capture of room 36 has Dizzy resting at ~84px, exactly one
  troll knockback west of 184px.

What changed as a result:
- **Spawn and first respawn: x 46 -> 184, y 170 -> 168.** `resetlives` seeds
  startx=46 (units) = 184px; `starty`=168 needs no conversion (y is
  plain pixels and already the FEET -- prtdizzy does `ld a,(dizy) / sub
  c` "giving the top corner ... rather than the bottom corner"). The old
  170 matched neither the source nor the "168+21=189" its own comment
  claimed. **184px puts Dizzy inside the troll's proximity box, so a new
  game now opens with "[X-ALL.TXT line 976] [X-ALL.TXT line 977]?" and a shove
  west -- that is the original's own opening beat**, and it is what the
  ZX capture shows.
- **Edge triggers**: leftmost standing x is now 8 (source x=2) and
  rightmost 224 (source x=56); stepping off either is the transition.
  DIZZY_MAXX was 232 ("256-24"), which let Dizzy stand two 4px steps
  further right than the original can.
- **Arrival positions**: 224 for a westward transition (goneleft's own
  56 units), 8 for an eastward one (goneright's 2). T0036's x=48 arrival
  into room 53 is reverted to 8 -- the flame it was dodging only burned
  Dizzy because that test forced an arrival from high above room 52's
  floor; walking east off the floor arrives at y=168 and the flame's box
  is y=114-126.
- **The WALK_STEP saga is resolved, and NOTES/room36.asm were wrong for
  a long time**: 4px/tick IS the source's real speed. The
  "source-faithful" 1px/tick that felt stuttery when tried was four
  times too slow. The old comment is kept in place, explicitly marked as
  history, because the playtest reasoning around it is still useful --
  it just reached the right answer for the wrong reason.

**Death respawn is a per-room CHECKPOINT in the original, not a fixed
point.** `enterroom` (~6787) runs on every single room change and stores
the arrival position: `ld (startroom),a`, `ld a,(x) / ld (startx),a`,
`ld a,(y) / ld (starty),a`; `starteggres` (~6751) copies those back on
losing a life. `resetlives` only seeds them for the first life of a new
game. This port had RESPAWN_ROOM/X/Y as constants, so every death dumped
you back in the dungeon regardless of where you had got to -- which,
once rooms 52/53 existed, made dying up there a far bigger setback than
the original intends. Now `set_checkpoint` (gameplay.asm) is enterroom,
called from all six transitions and from the initial spawn. Verified:
walk west to room 35, die -- respawn is room 35 at its own entry point
(224,168), not room 36.

**Known divergence, recorded not fixed: the placement PLOT TYPE.** Bits
3-4 of a placement's colour byte select how the sprite combines with the
screen (`doplottype`, ~4693): 0 = plain STORE (overwrite, blanks erase),
1 = XOR, 2/3 = OR. This port always ORs. Distribution across all rooms:
2484 STORE, 284 XOR, 15 OR -- and the rooms currently built use STORE
exclusively (35/36/52) or nearly (53 has 3 XOR at x=200-224,y=152-168;
room 2's four XOR placements are all frame 115, the flame, which this
port animates separately anyway). STORE and OR are identical wherever
sprites don't overlap, which is why the rooms verify correct against the
original today; the difference would only show as ink that should have
been erased by a later overlapping placement. Worth doing if a future
room looks "too full"; not worth rewriting the blit for speculatively.

### T0051: frame pacing -- the loop was free-running, not paced

Real playtest: "there is a noticeable change in framerate and
responsiveness depending on the complexity of the scene. The first
scene for example, as soon as the fire on the left is out, everything
speeds up, and when you cross to the room on the left, it gets
noticeably much faster."

**There was no pacing at all.** `redraw` ended with a single
`wait_vsync`, which looks like pacing but isn't: it waits for PIA0's
60Hz pulse FLAG, and that flag is a LATCH. Once a frame's work has
overrun one field -- which it always has here -- the flag is already
set when the wait is reached, so it returns immediately and the loop
free-runs at exactly whatever rate the scene's own cost allows.

**Measured** (counting `rng_ctr` advances, which happen exactly once per
mainloop pass -- a far better metric than timing Dizzy's walk, which
silently reports walls, steps, troll knockbacks and deaths as "slow"):

|                     | before | after |
|---------------------|-------:|------:|
| room 36, fire lit   |   15.0 |  15.0 |
| room 36, fire out   |   15.0 |  15.0 |
| room 35             |   18.0 |  14.0 |

and walking past the fireplace, where the fire's tiles fall inside the
damage rect: 15.0 lit / 17.4 out before, 14.4 / 15.6 after.

**The fix is the original's own approach.** X-ALL.TXT's main loop waits
on `clock`, a counter its 50Hz interrupt drives, for 3 ticks -- 16.7
updates/sec, scene-independent. This port can't use an interrupt for it
(IRQs stay masked, and in all-RAM mode the vector area at $FFF0 is
uninitialised RAM), so `tick_poll` polls the flag from inside the
frame's own long-running loops -- the damage-rect clear, the placement
scan, `blit` itself, and each draw/update loop -- consuming and counting
each boundary as it happens. `redraw`'s tail then holds the frame until
`FRAME_FIELDS` (4 fields = 15/sec, the closest whole-field match to the
original's 16.7) have passed.

**Two things had to be right, both found by measuring rather than
reasoning:**
- *Carry the surplus, don't clear the counter.* Clearing throws away the
  fraction of a field the frame overran by, so the frame's phase against
  the 60Hz field drifts and constant work straddles 4 boundaries
  sometimes and 5 others. That alone held room 35 at 13.7 against a 15.0
  target while room 36 hit 15.0 exactly. Subtracting the budget (clamped
  to one frame of credit, so a room change's full-screen redraw can't
  buy several unpaced frames afterwards) keeps the long-run average at
  exactly FRAME_FIELDS.
- *Check the budget before waiting, not after.* Waiting first costs a
  whole extra field whenever the work already met the budget -- room 36
  dropped to 12.0 that way.

**Cost and layout**: ~15 `jsr tick_poll` sites, ~22 cycles each against a
field's ~15000. That was enough to leave the $0E00-$4000 region with 50
bytes of headroom, so `message.asm` moved down into the $5800 gap (pure
code, absolute calls only): low region back to 582 bytes free, gap1 159,
gap2 564.

**Residual, disclosed**: room 35 lands at 14.0 against 15.0, and the
fireplace corner at 14.4 against 15.6 while moving. Both are far inside
the ~20% swing that prompted the report, and the fire-lit/fire-out
change specifically is gone, but this is "much more even", not "exactly
even". Closing the rest means either a bigger `FRAME_FIELDS` (5 gives
11.7/11.7/11.3 -- more even, and uniformly slower) or making the
heaviest frames cheaper. `draw_actors` is the biggest single phase
(~20% of a frame in room 36, measured by ablation against a build with
pacing off), then the fire overlay and the placement scan at ~12% each.
Profile with `lwasm -DPACING=0` (which disables the pacing wait) and
ablate a phase by replacing its `jsr` with `nop` -- that is how these
numbers were taken.

### T0052: making the frame cheap enough to beat the original's own pace

"If the ZX Spectrum can draw this with its Z80, we can do it as well on
the CoCo." Correct -- and the reason we couldn't was not the CPU, it was
that this port did far more work per frame than the original ever does.

**Room 36, walking, main-loop passes/sec (frame sync stripped so the
numbers are continuous rather than quantised to whole video fields):**

| | passes/sec | frame |
|---|---:|---:|
| before | 19.0 | 52.6ms |
| + blit inner loops | 19.8 | 50.5ms |
| + placement-scan rewrite | 24.8 | 40.3ms |
| + rat save-under | 27.8 | 36.0ms |

**a) The placement scan (the big one, +25%).** `redraw_placements_dmg`
walks EVERY placement in the room (63 in room 36) on every redraw, and
almost all of them are rejected -- so the reject path is the hot path.
It was computing four bounds through memory (8 stores, 10 loads) and
then loading them back to compare: ~130 cycles to say "no", 63 times a
frame. Now it keeps x/y/header in registers, tests cheapest-first, and
writes the blit's inputs out only once a placement has actually passed:
~40 cycles for a reject.

**b) Save-under for the rat (+12%).** The rat used to clear the union of
its old and new positions and then rescan all 63 placements to repaint
whatever static art lived there -- a second full scan every frame, 14%
of the frame. The original never does anything like this: `PRTDIZZY.PDS`
saves the screen bytes it is about to cover into `storescreen`, and
`ruboutdizzy` puts them straight back. Now so do we.
*The ordering is the subtle part*: the restore happens at the TOP of
redraw, before the damage-rect clear, not next to the draw. Restoring
next to the draw would repaint the rat's old background over a Dizzy who
had moved into that spot, flickering him for a frame. Restoring first
means the buffer is pure static art before anything is drawn into it;
the save can then legitimately capture Dizzy's pixels where they overlap,
because that area sits inside his own damage rect and gets repainted next
frame anyway.

**c) blit's inner loops (+4%).** Both loops kept their byte counter in
memory (`inc blit_c / ldb blit_c / cmpb blit_bpr` -- 18 cycles of
bookkeeping per byte) and the shifted path moved a nibble with eight
shift instructions plus a pshs/puls to keep a copy. Now: a register
countdown for the aligned path, and a nibble-swap table for the shifted
one (`nibswap[s] = ((s & $0F) << 4) | (s >> 4)`, so `& $0F` yields s>>4
and `& $F0` yields (s & $0F) << 4). Pointers also stay live in X and U
across rows instead of being reloaded and stored back every row, which
mattered because this port's sprites are 2-4 bytes wide but 13-21 rows
tall -- the row overhead was most of the routine.
The table is built at boot rather than assembled in (no load-file cost)
and is stored ROTATED BY 128, because the 6809 SIGN-EXTENDS the
accumulator offset in `lda b,y`: with Y = nibswap+128, source byte s
lands on nibswap[(s+128) & 255] across the whole 0..255 range.

**Result: FRAME_FIELDS is now 3, i.e. 20 passes/sec, and it holds.**
Measured with pacing on: room 36 fire lit 20.0, fire out 20.0, room 35
19.0, walking in room 36 19.0. That is a 5% spread where the original
complaint was a 20% one -- and it is FASTER than the Spectrum original's
own 16.7/sec (3 ticks of its 50Hz clock).

**Every step was checked for pixel-identical output** (`capture_display`
of the boot frame diffed against the pre-optimisation build: no
difference at any stage), plus `verify_verbatim.py` 147/147 and the
playtest regression. The rat was specifically checked for trails after
several seconds of patrolling -- clean.

**A real bug I made and caught, worth recording**: the save-under blocks
were first placed at `org $7F00`, which put nibswap's 256 bytes at
$7F00-$7FFF and pushed the save buffers to $8000 -- straight through the
relocated room 52 sprite data. The standing address-range audit did not
flag it, because it only asks "is anything at $8000+" and room 52's data
is legitimately there. The audit now needs the stronger question: **is
anything at $8000+ that is NOT an r52_/r53_ symbol?** Everything T0052
adds lives in the $7800 gap ($7E00 nibswap, $7F00 save blocks), with 206
bytes still free there.

**What is left, if more is ever wanted** (frame now 36.0ms, measured by
ablation): redraw is 54% of it and the game logic 46%. Inside redraw no
single phase now dominates -- blit 7%, the placement scan 7.5%, actors
7.5%, the fire overlay 7.5% -- so the next real step would be
save-under for DIZZY too, which would remove the damage-rect clear and
his placement rescan the same way the rat's went.

### T0053: the proximity boxes were a quarter of their real width

Reported twice: "there seems to be a mandatory sequence of events, for
example the rat won't eat the bread if I don't give the troll the apple,
that should not be the case." The first investigation wrongly cleared it
("no code path imposes that order") -- which was true and beside the
point. There is no ordering; there is a box so narrow that whether the
drop works depends on exactly where you happen to be standing, which in
play is indistinguishable from a sequence requirement.

**The bug**: a proximity box's WIDTH is in the same 4-pixel units as its
x, and only x was ever transformed. `joinprox` (X-ALL.TXT ~1991) proves
it -- it moves DIZZY into the box's coordinate space with `ld a,(x) /
add a,32`, and the comparison immediately below uses `eggwidth equ 6` as
his width there. Six units for a sprite that is 24 pixels wide: one unit
is 4 pixels, so `w` needs the same *4 as x. `h` does NOT: the vertical
half of the same routine uses `eggheight equ 18`, plain pixels, matching
y (the same x-is-scaled/y-is-not split T0050 found for Dizzy himself).

So every box in this port has been a quarter of its real width since
T0024:

| box | was | correct |
|---|---|---|
| proxloaf | x=56 w=40 | x=56 **w=160** |
| proxtroll | x=200 w=8 | x=200 **w=32** |
| proxapple | x=176 w=20 | **x=184** w=16 |
| proxjug | x=40 w=24 | **x=48** w=24 |
| proxpicture | x=120 w=5 | x=120 **w=20** |

The loaf's is the one that bites: 40px instead of 160px meant only a
narrow band of the rat's corridor armed it at all. Measured before and
after by sweeping the drop position across the corridor: previously NO
tested position from x=100 eastward armed the rat; now every position
from x≈48 to x≈204 does, and the two outside the real box correctly
don't.

It also explains T0032's own note about the apple and jug boxes being
"unreachably narrow" and needing hand-widening -- they were never 4px
and 6px wide, they were 16px and 24px. Those hand-tuned numbers are
reverted to the source's own here.

**A second bug fell out of fixing the first**: with the apple box at its
real x=184..200 and a drop landing 4px ahead of Dizzy, every position
that could land the apple in its box (180-196) already overlaps the
troll's box, so he launches you before you can let go -- the puzzle
would have become unsolvable. `dropobject` (~5877) is explicit about
where an item goes: `ld a,(x) / and %11111110 / add 34`, which in this
port's pixels is "round down to a multiple of 8, then add 8" -- up to
12px ahead, not 4. With that, standing at x=176 (which clears the
troll's box exactly) puts the apple at 184, inside its own box.
Verified with the troll's knockback ACTIVE, not suppressed.

The y half of `dropobject` (`(y & $F8) - 8`) is deliberately NOT adopted:
standing on room 36's floor at y=176 it yields exactly 168, the apple
box's own bottom edge, which this port's point-in-box test treats as
outside. The original never compares an object against these boxes --
it re-tests DIZZY (see below) -- so the question doesn't arise there.

**Recorded, not changed**: the original's proximity checks are always
DIZZY-vs-box (`joinprox` reads `(x)`/`(y)`), never dropped-item-vs-box.
This port tests the dropped item's position instead, a T0032 decision
with its own playtest evidence behind it (the jug/fire outcome was wrong
in a way that check fixed). Now that the boxes are the right size the
two are much closer in practice, but they are not the same mechanic, and
a future session chasing a puzzle that fires at the wrong moment should
start here.

### T0054: the item puzzles were testing the wrong thing

Straight after T0053 widened the boxes: "I have to drop the apple on top
of the troll for it to work, and if I get a pixel or 2 closer to the gate
I get a knock back", and then "the water jug seems to not be working now
as well".

T0053 fixed the box SIZES but left the mechanic wrong, and with the
correct sizes the wrongness became obvious. This port fired a puzzle at
the moment of the drop, testing **where the dropped item landed** against
the box. The original tests **Dizzy** against the box:
`proximitycollide`/`joinprox` (X-ALL.TXT ~1923/1991) load `(x)` and `(y)`
-- Dizzy's -- and compare them using `eggwidth`/`eggheight`.

Why that matters so much for the apple: its box is x=184-200 and the
troll's own box starts at 200. An ITEM is a point, so it had to come to
rest inside those 16 pixels, which meant standing at 180-196 -- and Dizzy
is 24px wide, so every one of those positions already overlaps the troll,
who launches you first. Exactly the reported "drop it on top of the troll,
and one step closer gets you knocked back". Testing DIZZY instead lets
his own 24px width contribute to the overlap, so the puzzle fires from
x=164 onward -- comfortably before the troll's zone begins at 180.
Measured with the knockback active: fires at x=166, no launch.

The jug is the same story: its window went from a couple of positions to
x=32-64, and the loaf's from a narrow band to x=40-208, essentially the
whole of the rat's corridor.

**The other half of the mechanic, which cost a wrong first attempt**: a
first version checked the boxes every frame, and the apple then fired the
instant a new game started -- the apple is already lying in room 36 and
Dizzy now spawns (T0050) inside its box. The original doesn't check
continuously either: a pickupable's routine opens with `ld a,(pickup) /
and a / ret z` (~2302), so it does nothing at all unless the pickup/drop
key is down that tick. So the rule is BOTH halves: **fire on the drop
action, but test Dizzy against the box.** With that, the boot frame is
pixel-identical to before and the pacing is back to 20/sec (the stray
apple message had been blocking the main loop and dragging the measured
rate to 12.3).

Verified after the fix: apple fires at x=166 with the troll active; jug
across x=32-64; loaf across x=40-208 and the rat then walks over, eats it
and leaves; art byte-identical; playtest regression clean.

### T0055: auditing the rest of the collision constants

T0050 (Dizzy's x unit), T0053 (box widths) and T0054 (which thing the box
is tested against) were all the same failure: a number taken from the
original without checking what it meant. Rather than wait for the next
one to surface in play, this went looking for the others.

**The torch flame's kill box was half its own sprite.** The original
carries no box for a flame at all -- `updateflames` does `ld a,115 / call
collidewithdizzy3`, and that looks the frame's real size up through
`findfrmsize`, whose own source comment reads `;4 pixels=1 unit` for the
width it returns. So the flame's hitbox IS the flame, 16x13. This port
used 8x12, meaning the outer half of a visibly burning torch was safe to
stand in. Measured before/after by stepping Dizzy across a torch: the
kill zone was x=24-48, it is now x=24-56, which is exactly his 24px width
overlapping the flame's real 16px. Notably the fire-pit overlay and the
water hazard had BOTH already been corrected to their decoded sprite
sizes, with a comment explaining this very units trap -- the room's own
torches were simply missed at the time.

**The body side probes were insets, not the source's columns.** This
port probed dizzy_x+5 and dizzy_x+18 for wall collision, described in
its own comment as a "collision box inset". The original probes one
column at each edge: `checkleftside` (~6584) `ld a,(x)`, and
`checkrightside` (~6621) `ld a,(x) / add a,eggwidth-1`. With eggwidth=6
and x in 4-pixel units that is dizzy_x+0 and dizzy_x+20 -- the outermost
4px column of his 24px sprite. The old values sat one 4px block inside
each edge, so Dizzy could push 4px into a wall on either side before
stopping.

Checked for traversal regressions before keeping it, since a wider body
box can newly block a gap: room 36 is still walkable end to end (he now
stops at x=196, the real edge of the right-hand structure, instead of
x=224 which was 4px INSIDE it), and room 35's staircase climbs to
exactly the same height on both builds. Everything the routes need is
still reachable.

**Recorded, not changed -- the floor/ceiling probe columns.** `checkline`
(~6672) probes FOUR columns starting at x+1 unit: pixels +4, +8, +12,
+16. This port probes three: FOOT_L/M/R at +6, +12, +17, which land on
the same first, third and fourth columns but skip the second. The
practical difference is a 4px-wide ledge sitting under only that one
column, which no room built so far has; a fourth probe would cost ~33%
on a path that runs several times per frame, and T0052 just spent real
effort buying that time back. Worth revisiting if a room ever appears
with 4px ledges.

**T0055 addendum -- two more items closed while auditing:**

*The troll's launch velocity* is its own number: `proxtrollrou` does
`ld a,-9 / ld (dy),a`, where a player jump is -8. This port had been
reusing JUMP_DY for it. Now `TROLL_LAUNCH_DY equ -9`. The source ALSO
shoves Dizzy 2 units (8px) west at the same instant; that half is
deliberately still not copied, because this port applies a CONTINUOUS
horizontal push for the duration of the flight instead -- a documented
T0030 deviation made because the source's one-time nudge barely read as
a knockback at this port's frame rate.

*T0039 is stale and is closed.* It recorded room 52's down-transition as
unreachable ("no x position clears all three foot probes against its
pyramid stairs"), which was wrong even when written -- room 52's floor
rows are clear across x=176-228. Verified end to end now: jumping at
room 36's ceiling gap arrives in room 52, and falling through its floor
hole returns to room 36's corridor. Room 52 is not a one-way trip.

### T0056: the wall trap, and an over-wide clear that ate its neighbour

Playtest batch, with a screenshot of Dizzy standing on top of room 36's
wall row.

**The "stuck on the wall" trap is the DOWN-transition's arrival y, not
the jump.** T0044 fixed the up-transition threshold and I assumed that
covered it; it did not, and the reproduction shows why. Coming down from
room 52 arrived at y=56, one pixel below room 36's y=48-55 wall row --
and the very next vertical pass LIFTS Dizzy STEP_UP (4px) before scanning
for a floor, which is the step-climb mechanic working exactly as designed
(T0031). The lift lands on y=52, INSIDE the wall row, `check_ground` says
solid, and he is now standing in the wall able to walk its whole span.
No jump path could produce it -- the up-transition fires at y=65, well
below the wall -- which is why looking there found nothing.

The source avoids it by construction: `gonedown` does `ld a,(y) / sub
114` against its own threshold of 182, arriving at 68. This port's
threshold is 188, so the equivalent is 74. Verified by mashing
jump+left+right for ~17 seconds from four different corridor positions:
the old build reached "standing at y=52" every time, the new one never
does.

**`clear_and_blit` was clearing one byte too many.** It always cleared
bpr+1 bytes, with the `+1` justified as "a 4px-shifted sprite spills one
byte right" -- true, but only when the sprite IS shifted. For an aligned
one that extra byte erases 8px of whatever sits immediately to its right,
and nothing repaints it (unlike the rat's save-under, this clear never
restores the static art underneath).

That is what "the railing is not aligned with the others" actually was.
Room 52's removable railing section is an ACTOR at x=216, and the fixed
railings are placements at 184/200/232 -- all correct, all 16px apart.
Drawing the actor cleared x=216-239, wiping the left half of the fixed
piece at 232. Confirmed by dumping the framebuffer bits rather than
squinting at NTSC artifact colour: the band read solid 184-231, a gap at
232-239, then 240-247. With the clear width now conditional on
`cb_x & 4`, the band is continuous 184-247.

**The picture message was gated on carrying something.** T0040 required a
non-empty inventory before checking `proxpicture`. The original's
`tryputtingdown` gates only on `pickup` -- the key being down that tick
-- so walking up empty-handed and pressing DOWN should show it, and
didn't. Gate removed.

**The railing had no name**: the inventory called it "AN OBJECT" because
`item_name_msg` had no entry for frame 192. X-ALL.TXT ~1105:
`railingmess defb "A:PIECE:OF:RAILING"`.

### T0057: coins -- a third interaction mechanism

Playtest: "the railing is not aligned with the others to hide the fact
that there is a coin hiding behind it, also add the coin".

Coins are neither actors nor proximity triggers. `cointable`
(X-ALL.TXT:504) is 30 static `defb x,y,room` triples -- note the column
order is x,y,ROOM, the opposite of movingdata's room-first layout.
`putcoinsinroom` (~5605) draws frame 0 at every uncollected coin in the
room being entered, as part of room setup; `pickupcoins` (~2154)
collects one by doing `set 7,(ix+2)` -- **bit 7 of the ROOM byte is the
collected flag**, so the table doubles as its own save state and needs
no parallel array. That trick is why the port's room test is a plain
`cmpa cur_room`: a collected coin's room byte no longer equals any real
room number.

Coordinates are the usual 4px+32-biased raw x, plain-pixel top-anchored
y. The two coins in this build's rooms:

| room | raw | pixels |
|---|---|---|
| 36 | 82,160 | x=200, y=160 |
| 52 | 86,88 | x=216, y=88 |

Both sit **underneath something**, and that is the design, not a bug:

* room 52's is exactly under the removable railing section (the actor at
  216,88) -- take the railing, find the coin. That is the puzzle the
  playtest was describing.
* room 36's is under the troll, whose 32x40 sprite at (184,136) covers
  x=184-215, y=136-175. Cost 40 minutes: the collect worked (coins went
  1, room byte 36 -> 164) while the framebuffer showed no coin, and the
  region's ink count was a stable 58 either way. 58 turned out to be the
  dungeon wall's own dither; poking the troll's slot to room 255 made
  the count jump to 116, which is exactly the coin sprite's ink. So the
  drawing was always right and the ordering (coins BEFORE draw_actors,
  matching `drawfullroom`'s putcoinsinroom-then-resetroommoving) is what
  hides it.

**Measure the thing you claim to measure.** "Is there ink in this
region" is not "is the coin drawn" when the region already has art in
it -- the same class of mistake as T0052's walking-distance metric.
Counting the sprite's own ink and comparing exactly is the check that
actually discriminates.

Coin counter: the original's `resetcoins` sets `coins` to 255 because
`addtocoins` increments before displaying, so its first coin shows 0.
This port's status strip reads `coins` directly, so it starts at 0 and
counts 1,2,3 -- a deliberate deviation.

Debugging note, cost ~20 minutes: byte counters used as debug
instrumentation are ambiguous at 0 (0 or 256?), and a "never called"
reading was really "the game is blocked in msg_wait_dismiss and the
mainloop is not running at all". A harness that stops tapping SPACE
partway through will sit in a message box for the rest of the run and
every subsequent input reads as ignored.

### T0058: the crocodile, and the memory layout that had to move first

**The gator** (room 53, `crocodilerou` at X-ALL.TXT ~2747). Three
things about it are load-bearing and easy to miss:

1. It ANIMATES every 8th tick (`inc delaycounter / and 7 / jr nz`) but
   tests for a bite on EVERY tick.
2. The bite is gated on `bit 0,(ix+movefrm) / ret nz` -- frame 123 is
   odd, 124 is even, so **only the open mouth kills**. That single bit
   is the fairness mechanic: the animation telegraphs the danger.
3. The two boxes are different sizes and mean different things. The big
   one (raw 74,80 w=20 h=100 -> pixels 168,80,80x100) only decides which
   way it FACES -- the original rotates the collide result straight into
   bit 7 of the colour byte with `ld a,8+16 / rra`. The small one (raw
   70,140 w=6 h=10 -> pixels 152,140,24x10) is the mouth. Reusing the
   big box for the kill would make room 53 unplayable.

Cycle is var1 0..7 with the mouth open on 3, 5, 7 (`cp 3 / jp c` then
`bit 0,a / jp z`). var1 == 255 means TIED, set by `proxcrocrou` from the
rope's `proxcroc` trigger -- `tiecroc equ -16+var1` reaches BACKWARDS
one 16-byte slot, i.e. the rope's trigger writes the CROCODILE's var1,
because the croc is the slot immediately before it. The rope is not in
any room this build contains, so the state is honoured but unreachable.

On the kill the original drops Dizzy into the mouth first (`ld a,69-32 /
ld (x),a` -- his x is in 4px units, so 148 pixels -- `ld a,160 /
ld (y),a`) and sets sequence 7, the death ANIMATION. This port does the
teleport but has no death animation yet, so Dizzy falls during the
countdown. That is the next task, not a bug in this one.

`kill_dizzy_msg` now carries the hazard's own message into the death
box, which is what `killdizzy` does with HL -- the T0034 note said
wiring this up was out of scope then. The gator's `croceatenmess` is
the first one that reads as a real loss.

**The layout.** Adding four sprites (frame 124 plus three mirrors, 192
bytes) reset the machine about a second after boot. The cause was not
the crocodile at all:

* `shared_sprites_data.asm`'s tail crossed $7E00 into `nibswap`, which
  `start:` fills at boot -- so `blit` read a garbage width/height and
  wrote wherever it liked.
* `room2_data.asm` had ALREADY been sitting 225 bytes inside
  framebuffer B, for several sessions, undetected.

Both are the same failure: **the audit checked symbols, and a symbol is
the last LABEL in a file, not the last BYTE.** room 2's last label is at
$5F61, safely below $6000; its data runs to $60D9. Nothing in a map file
can show that. `tools/memaudit.py` now reads the DECB image's block list
instead, which is ground truth, and it is what regen_art.sh points at.

Fixing it needed more room than existed, and the unlock is worth
remembering: **the $8000 staging area does not have to be low RAM.**
Staging only has to be somewhere CLOADM can write that nothing touches
before `start:`'s relocate loop runs -- and framebuffer A is 6KB of
exactly that, where $0100 had 228 bytes left. Moving the staging origin
to $4000 is a one-line change (the copy loop is already
label-relative), and it cascades:

| region | holds | free after |
|---|---|---|
| $0100-$0DFF | room 36 + room 35 art (freed by the staging move) | 1722 |
| $0E00-$3FFF | code + data | 1594 |
| $4000-$57FF | framebuffer A, and the staged $8000 image at load time | 1655 |
| $5800-$5FFF | dizzy tail, message VM, font, message text | 225 |
| $7800-$7DFF | actor data | 643 |
| $8000+ | rooms 52, 53, 2 and the shared sprites, after the boot copy | ~27K |

The $0E00-$4000 region was down to SIX bytes before dizzy_frame35 would
have started overwriting framebuffer A again -- the exact corruption
dizzy_frames_all.asm's own header describes. It has 1.5KB now.

### T0059: the death animation

Playtest: "we are missing the neat death animation."

X-ALL.TXT's `updatedizzy1` (~6356) replaces the normal
sequence-from-floor-and-direction pick while `killed` is nonzero:

| sequence | what happens |
|---|---|
| 6 | left alone, keeps bobbing |
| 7 | when `animation` reaches 7 it is pinned back to 6, so the last two frames HOLD instead of looping |
| 0 | `animation = 0`, `sequence = 7` -- the keel-over starts here |
| anything else | `and a / jr nz,notdeadyet` -- carry on as normal |

That last row reads like an oversight and isn't: dying mid-stride
finishes the stride first, and dying in mid-air keeps falling, which is
why death in the original never snaps. Confirmed in the port -- eaten by
the gator while airborne, Dizzy stays in seq 3 for the whole countdown.

seq6/seq7 are `defb 4,5,5,6,6,5,5,4` ("bob upside down") and
`defb 0,1,8,8,7,6,7,7` ("fall over backwards"), both recovered into
dizzy_seqtab. seq6 is unused so far but the table has to stay dense for
the `seq*8` index. `checkkeys` also has its own `ld a,(killed) / ret nz`,
so nothing responds to the keyboard while dying -- reproduced by
clearing keyflags for the pass.

`killdizzy` itself turns out to be exactly what T0058 built: `ld a,10 /
ld (killed),a / ld (killedmess),hl` -- a countdown plus a message
pointer. `death_msg` IS `killedmess`.

### T0060: the map

"It's hard to keep referencing the different rooms as 'the one with the
stairs'." Fair, and it had already cost time: the stair room is 52, THE
ENTRANCE HALL, and nothing in any note said so.

**There is no room-connection data in the original at all.** The entire
map is four routines (X-ALL.TXT ~6298):

```
goneleft   roomno - 1   x := 56      gonedown   roomno - 16  y := y - 114
goneright  roomno + 1   x := 2       goneup     roomno + 16  y := y + 118
newroom    and 127
```

So **room = row x 16 + column**, 8 rows of 16, and **up is +16** --
higher numbers are higher in the world. Room 36 (THE CASTLE'S DUNGEON)
is row 2 column 4; 52 (THE ENTRANCE HALL) is directly above it; 53 (THE
SNAP HAPPY GATOR) is east of 52; 35 (SMUGGLER'S HIDEOUT) is west of 36.
The x/y assignments in those routines are also where T0044/T0056's
transition thresholds come from.

Adjacency is therefore ARITHMETIC, not reachability: every room has four
neighbours whether or not you can walk between them, and only the room's
own art decides. The map says so rather than drawing edges it cannot
justify.

Rooms 0-3 are not places. They hold art and look like rooms in any
extraction, but nothing walks into them -- code selects them:
0 is the title screen, 1 is room 58 redrawn with the beanstalk grown
(`checkbeanstalk`), 2 is room 36 redrawn with the fire out
(`checkfireout` -- this port builds it as the fire overlay), 3 is the
heart demo on reaching Daisy. They are passed to the generator as
`--special`, because no extraction can find them.

`tools/roommap` + `tools/genmap.sh` generate
`games/dizzy/recipe/MAP.md`: the grid with names, the built slice as a
Mermaid graph with its frontier, and a per-room index joining the actor,
proximity-trigger and coin tables. 52 live rooms, 49 named, 5 built.
Room names decode with T0010's punctuation convention (`:`=space,
`;`=apostrophe, `<`=comma, `=`=hyphen, `>`=period, `@`=exclamation).

### T0061: Dizzy was running at 1.6x the original's speed

Playtest: "when going to 53, the margin of error for the ledge is tiny.
it wasn't this hard in the original."

It wasn't the ledges. **The original has two clocks, and this port had
been running everything on the faster one.**

| what | routine | rate |
|---|---|---|
| Dizzy: position, physics, animation | `updatedizzy` (~6339), 50Hz interrupt with an `eggcount` divider of 4 | **12.5 Hz** |
| the world: rat, troll, gator, flames, water, pickups | `maingamelp` (~1344), `clocklp` waits 3 ticks of the same 50Hz clock | **16.7 Hz** |

One step is 1 unit = 4px (`ld a,(x) / sub (left) / add (right)`), so the
original's Dizzy walks at exactly **50 px/sec**. This port ran its whole
loop at FRAME_FIELDS=3 = 20 Hz, so he walked at **80 px/sec** -- same
pixels, same jump arc, 60% less time to react to any of it. Measured in
MAME by walking him right for 1.5s: 74.7 px/sec before, 58.7 after.

Every "this is harder than the original" report traces back here, and no
amount of collision tuning would have fixed it, because the geometry was
already right -- verified this session by rendering rooms 36 and 52 from
rooms.json and diffing against the port's own framebuffer: identical
except for the actors and flames the port draws on top.

FRAME_FIELDS=4 is 15 Hz: Dizzy +20%, the world -10%, both even. Exact
needs two clocks (Dizzy every 4.8 fields, the world every 3.6 -- in
fifths of a field, periods 24 and 18) which is real work AND risks
uneven motion, since at any single pass rate some passes must skip
Dizzy's step: at 15 Hz that is 5 steps in 6, a 133ms hitch every 400ms.
`harness/pacetest.sh 5` builds the alternative (12 Hz: Dizzy within 4%,
world -28%) to feel side by side.

Also fixed here, from reading `checkline` (~6672) properly: **the source
uses ONE routine for the floor and ceiling probes**, reading four
contiguous 4px columns at x+1..x+4 units = pixels x+4..x+19.

* the floor probes were 6/12/17 -- columns +1, +3, +4, skipping +2. A
  ledge covering only x+8..x+11 held Dizzy in the original and dropped
  him here. Now 4/8/12/16, the source's own four.
* the ceiling probed x+0 and x+20, which are `checkleftside`/
  `checkrightside`'s columns, not `checkline`'s. Wrong in both
  directions at once: it blocked on ink 4px OUTSIDE the source's span,
  making room 36's gap up to room 52 two whole steps narrower than the
  original's (x=192-208 against 188-212), and it never felt an overhang
  in the middle 8px at all.

**Harness lesson, cost about an hour.** Two "clean" sweeps were both
measuring a frozen game. Symptoms to recognise:

* `keyflags` updates every frame while nothing else moves -- that is
  `msg_wait_dismiss`, which scans keys but runs no game logic. Dismiss
  SPACE for the WHOLE run, not just through the boot messages.
* SPACE left held from the boot loop reads as a stuck key.
* **Poking `cur_room` does not change rooms.** `load_room` is what
  repoints the placement list and the collision mask, so a poked room
  number leaves the previous room's geometry in place and every result
  after it is fiction. Warp by setting `respawn_room`/`respawn_x`/
  `respawn_y` and `killed`, which goes through the game's own path.

`harness/playtest_script_example.lua` is frame-timed and now covers
proportionally less ground per frame; its timeline wants scaling by 4/3
if it is to reach room 35 again.

### T0062: Dizzy drawn mid-stack, and the coin peeking through the railing

Playtest screenshot (XRoar, the CoCo2 port): a lozenge of white visible
through the stair room's grille where the removable railing hides the
coin. "You are only supposed to know there is a coin because you
pressed the down cursor key in front of that railing" -- the coin was
readable before the puzzle was solved.

**redraw()'s single serial pass drew Dizzy too early.** Order was
placements -> coins -> **Dizzy** -> flames -> fire overlay -> water ->
actors -> UI. Anything drawn after him (the troll, the rat, a flame
tile) painted straight over him with no way for his own ink to win
back -- confirmed by standing him exactly where the troll parks and
dumping the framebuffer; before the fix his silhouette was cut by
whatever the troll had already drawn there. The source doesn't have
this problem because Dizzy is drawn by `prtdizzy`, called off the 50Hz
interrupt independently of the main loop's actor updates -- he gets
redrawn on his own cadence regardless of what the room just did. This
port's redraw is one linear pass, so "always on top" only has one
meaning here: drawn last. Moved `jsr blitdizzy` to just before
`refresh_ui_text`/`draw_ui`. Verified: standing him over the parked
troll, his own ink now reads clean with nothing showing through.

**The coin bug was T0057's own draw-order reasoning failing under
`blit`'s OR-only compositing.** `draw_coins` ran before `draw_actors`
on the theory that "coin drawn first, actor drawn on top, actor wins" --
true only if the covering actor is redrawn on the SAME pass the coin
is. `blit` never clears; it only ORs ink on. Once Dizzy's own damage
rect touches the coin's box on a pass where the (unmoving) railing's
own box ISN'T also touched -- ordinary once he's walked away from
both -- `draw_coins` draws the coin fresh with nothing scheduled to
paint over it again, and it shows through the railing's gaps
permanently. Confirmed the leak is exact, not approximate: measuring
ink in the coin's 16x16 box before pickup gave exactly 100 bits, the
railing sprite's OWN ink count (`aspr_192`'s literal bytes sum to
100) -- proof the coin itself drew no ink there before the fix broke
that invariant, i.e. the leak really was a stray extra draw pass, not
a compositing accident every frame.

Fix: `coin_covered` (actors.asm) -- a real geometric test, not a draw-
order assumption. Given a coin's box, it scans every LIVE actor in
`cur_room`, looks up that actor's CURRENT sprite (`actor_sprite`) and
CURRENT position (straight from `actor_ram`, so a moving actor is
always current), and tests overlap with a new `boxes_overlap` (plain
top-left AABB, not `aabb_hit`'s feet-anchored one -- coins and actors
both use sprite-top y). `draw_coins` skips drawing when covered;
`pickup_coins` skips collecting when covered, so the coin can't be
grabbed blind before it's ever been seen. Both call it identically, so
"visible" and "collectible" can't drift apart.

This also fixes room 36's coin under the troll PROPERLY instead of by
luck: previously it depended on the troll's sprite happening to have
enough ink over that exact spot on every pass that mattered. Now it's
tracked by his actual position -- verified by moving the troll actor's
x off its resting spot (simulating the tumble) and back: coin-box ink
went 58 (only the wall dither under the troll) -> 116 (the coin
sprite's own ink, exact) -> 58 again on return, matching "covered while
parked, revealed while tumbling, covered again on landing" exactly.

Pacing unaffected (15.0/15.0/14.3), verbatim art clean, memaudit clean.

### T0063: dropped items drawn over a black hole, not the scene

Playtest: "if I drop an item like the bread, it is drawn as over a black
background... any chance we can draw the object over the scene without a
black background."

`clear_and_blit` (used for every static actor -- apple, jug, loaf, the
removable railing, plus the moving/animating troll and crocodile) does
exactly what its name says: black-fill the sprite's own bounding box,
THEN blit its ink on top. For a non-rectangular sprite (a round loaf on
a square bbox) that leaves a black margin wherever the sprite itself has
no ink -- and nothing repaints it, since `blit` only ever ORs ink in.

That clear is genuinely needed for two of `clear_and_blit`'s callers:
the animated flame/water tiles (different frame every cycle -- the OLD
frame's ink has to be erased or it merges with the new one) and the
crocodile (frame 123/124 toggling while it stays roughly in place, same
reason). It is NOT needed for a plain pickupable that never reanimates
and never moves: by the time `draw_actors` runs, `redraw_placements_dmg`
has ALREADY restored the real floor/wall art under its box THIS SAME
PASS -- clearing again just wipes that back to black for no reason.

Fixed by splitting `clear_and_blit`'s tail into a separate `blit_only`
entry point (cb_spr/cb_x/cb_y pre-set, no clear) and routing
`ROU_PICKUPABLE` actors straight to it, leaving the troll and crocodile
on the clearing path. Verified with a byte-exact framebuffer diff of a
dropped loaf against the pre-fix build: same 16 differing bytes are
every one of them the floor's own dither pattern reappearing around the
loaf's silhouette, nothing else changed. Crocodile's 123/124 cycle and
the troll's tumble both still redraw cleanly through `clear_and_blit`,
unaffected by the split.

### T0064: a real profiler, and 20% off room 36's frame

Playtest: "I still feel like 36 is less responsive, until I solve the
puzzles so there is less moving things in the scene."

**First: stop guessing.** `harness/profile.lua` + a `PROFILE=1` build
gives the exact microsecond cost of every mainloop and redraw phase in
one run. Each phase stamps an id into `prof_slot`; MAME's
`install_write_tap` timestamps the writes with the emulated clock. That
replaces ABLATION (comment a phase out, diff the frame rate), which cost
an earlier session most of an afternoon and produced confident nonsense
twice -- the pacing wait quantises every result to whole fields, and a
substitution silently failed while still yielding plausible numbers.

**MAME gotcha that reads exactly like "the tap never fired": the handle
returned by `install_write_tap` must be kept referenced.** Drop it and
Lua's GC removes the tap, silently, and every phase reads as zero.

**What it found.** The port relies on the SAM's 2x speed-up
(`OVERCLOCK`), and everything had been measured with it on. At 1x --
which is the real-hardware case, and possibly what the player's
emulator does -- room 36 with the fire lit and the rat alive cost
**59.8ms of a 66.7ms frame**. Six point nine milliseconds of headroom.
Any spike (a room transition, a message, the rat's own placement
rescan) tips the pass into a fifth field: 12 passes/sec instead of 15,
felt as exactly the reported stutter. Solve the puzzles and it drops to
39.1ms, comfortable, smooth. The perception was precisely right.

| | 1x CPU, fire lit | 1x, solved | 2x, fire lit | 2x, solved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 59.80ms | 39.13ms | 29.90ms | 19.34ms |
| after | **47.55ms** | **30.42ms** | **23.73ms** | **15.21ms** |

Headroom at 1x went from 6.9ms to 19.1ms. Room 35 also went from 14.3
to a flat 15.0 passes/sec, because the extra room absorbs the
room-transition spike it used to lose a pass to.

**The four cuts, in order of size:**

1. **Flame variants were redrawing identical pixels.** The flame table
   has 4 entries, but 0/1 and 2/3 are BYTE-IDENTICAL -- checked against
   the generated data. In the original those pairs differ only by
   `printflame`'s `xor 6+64`, which recolours the ATTRIBUTE cell: free
   on a Spectrum, meaningless in mono PMODE4. The variant was keyed on
   the counter's bit 0 as well as bit 1, so every pass looked like a
   change and forced all four fire-pit tiles and both torches through a
   full clear+blit for provably identical output. Now keyed on the
   mirror bit alone -- the only bit that changes pixels.
2. **`clear_and_blit` recomputed its row address every row** -- a `mul`,
   a reload of the sprite header, a re-derivation of the byte column
   AND of the shifted-width adjustment, ~70 cycles, to clear three
   bytes. All of it loop-invariant. Same fix for `redraw`'s prime clear.
3. **The placement scan walked all 63 of room 36's placements every
   pass** (11.3ms at 1x), whether or not anything was near Dizzy.
   roompack now emits them SORTED BY Y with a 12-entry index of "first
   placement that can reach this 16px band"; the scan starts at the
   damage rect's band and stops as soon as a placement starts below its
   bottom. Sorting is safe because `blit` composites with OR, so draw
   order cannot change the pixels -- and that was verified, not assumed
   (below). 11.3 -> 7.4ms.
4. **`blitdizzy` reloaded X/U/Y from memory every row**, wrote two back,
   recomputed the row address and re-tested the loop-invariant shift --
   ~65 cycles a row against 21 rows. Split into one loop per shift case
   with the registers live across rows. The compositing math was moved,
   not rewritten. 7.4 -> 5.9ms.

Also retired `FRAME_PULSES`: two unconditional vsync waits from before
T0051's pacing loop existed. The budget loop already holds each pass to
FRAME_FIELDS boundaries and COUNTS those waits, so they changed nothing
in the normal case -- but being unconditional they still cost their full
time on a pass that had ALREADY overrun, which is the pass that could
least afford it.

**Verification: every rendering change is byte-identical.**
`harness/framedump.lua` dumps the displayed framebuffer at a
deterministic point; rooms 36, 52 and 53 all compare to zero differing
bytes against the pre-optimization build. Getting that comparison
meaningful took three tries, and the lessons generalise:

* Pin the animation's INPUTS, not its outputs -- `dizzy_ff` is
  recomputed from `dizzy_seq`/`dizzy_anim` every pass, so pinning it
  just gets overwritten, and the two builds land one animation frame
  apart (which reads as a 1px vertical offset, because frame heights
  differ).
* Pin every independent animation phase: `flame_ctr`, `water_ctr`, the
  rat's RNG-timed walk. Room 53 "differed" until the water was pinned.
* A one-shot poke of `bufA_last_x`/`bufB_last_x` can land MID-redraw,
  after that pass read the flag and before it writes its own value
  back -- so the pass draws a small damage rect and clears the request.
  Hold the flag across several frames. This produced a convincing fake
  regression (one buffer keeping a stale railing) that reproduced on
  the unmodified build once tested properly.

**Still on the table**, in size order: the fire pit's four tiles are
still the single biggest item (11.8ms at 1x) because they sit at floor
height where Dizzy's damage rect keeps landing, so they genuinely
redraw every pass; fusing `clear_and_blit`'s two passes over the same
bytes into one store-based copy would roughly halve them. Beyond that,
the real architectural answer is the original's own: a save-under for
Dizzy (`ruboutdizzy`), which would delete the prime clear, the
placement rescan and most of the actor redraw in one go -- T0052
already did exactly this for the rat.

**Worth a decision:** the port sets the SAM's 2x speed bit, documented
as marginal on some real CoCo2s. At 47.6ms of a 66.7ms frame it no
longer needs it -- turning `OVERCLOCK` off would make the port safe on
real hardware at no cost to smoothness.

### T0065: dropped items sank into the floor, by exactly one anchor

Playtest: "when dizzy drops an object, it sinks into the floor a bit,
we are missing some sort of offset."

`dropobject` (~5877) is `ld a,(y) / and %11111000 / sub 8`, and this
port had rejected that formula (T0053) in favour of a `-12` fudge
because it "yields 168 standing on room 36's floor", which looked wrong.
It IS wrong -- when fed this port's y. The formula is right; the anchor
differs by one pixel:

`checkbottomside` (~6524) offsets its two cursors by different amounts
-- `looky` by 3 and `y` by 4 -- so the row it actually PROBES is `y+1`.
The original's `y` is therefore the last CLEAR row, one above the floor.
This port's `dizzy_y` is the first SOLID row, because that is what
`check_ground` tests. On room 36's floor (top ink row 176) the original
holds y=175 and drops at (175 & $F8) - 8 = **160**, so a 16px item's
bottom lands on 175: resting exactly on the floor. Feeding 176 into the
same formula gives 168 -- eight pixels buried. The `-12` fudge split the
difference and still left it 4px under.

`lda dizzy_y / deca / anda #$f8 / suba #8` puts this port on the
source's anchor. Verified through the real pickup/inventory/drop path in
MAME: the jug now occupies rows 160-175 against a floor whose top row is
176. The 8px quantisation is the original's own and is kept -- an item
taller than 16 floats, one shorter sinks, exactly as it does there.

Worth remembering as a class: **an off-by-one in an ANCHOR convention
shows up as an 8-pixel error** once a formula quantises. Neither number
looked wrong on its own.

### T0066: room 53's chop was the crocodile repainting the whole room

Playtest: "room 53 is slow and a bit choppy, needs tuning."

Profiled it (T0064's harness, PROF_ROOM=53): **82.8ms of work against a
66.7ms budget, 10.2 passes/sec**, with the two biggest entries being the
prime clear at 29.5ms and the placement pass at 24.5ms. Those numbers
are diagnostic on their own: 29.5ms is exactly what clearing all 6,144
bytes of a framebuffer costs, and room 53 has only 29 placements, so
24.5ms means all of them were being BLITTED rather than rejected. The
damage rect was the whole screen.

Counting them: **14% of room 53's passes were full-screen redraws**,
against 0% in room 36. The cause was T0058's own line -- when the gator
changes frame, it set `bufA_last_x`/`bufB_last_x` to 255, repainting the
entire room in both buffers to animate one 16x32 sprite. Two ~80ms
passes every eight: slow, and choppy exactly on the gator's cycle.

The mechanism to do this properly was already in the codebase --
`draw_flames` has kept a per-buffer record of the variant it last drew
since T0033, precisely because the two buffers alternate and each needs
its own. `draw_actors` now does the same for the crocodile: remember
what each buffer last drew for it, and when that differs, force just its
own box through clear_and_blit. The record packs the FACING into bit 7
(free -- frames 123/124 don't use it) because a facing flip changes the
sprite without changing the frame number.

Room 53: **82.8 -> 29.5ms, 10.2 -> 15.0 passes/sec.** Verified both
buffers stay in step, by ink count against the sprites' own (163 for
frame 123, 174 for 124, both exact) and by dumping the mirrored form.

Generalises: **an actor that animates in place cannot rely on the
damage rect**, which only answers "did something else scribble on me".
It needs a per-buffer record of what it drew. Reaching for a full
invalidation instead is a whole-screen repaint to move a few dozen
bytes, and it will not look like a rendering bug -- it looks like the
room being slow.

### T0067: the four adjacent rooms -- and a three-session-old crash

"Lets implement the adjacent rooms." Per games/dizzy/recipe/MAP.md the
built slice's live neighbours are exactly four: **51 MOAT AND
PORTCULLIS** (west of 52), **54 THE WIDE-EYED DRAGON** (east of 53),
**68 THE BANQUET HALL** (above 52) and **69 THE EAST WING** (above 53).
The port now has eight rooms.

**Staging needed a second window.** The $8000 image went past 11.5KB and
one staging window is only as big as one framebuffer (6KB). Framebuffer
B is free at load time for exactly the same reason A is (T0058: nothing
draws until after the relocate), so it carries a second block, copied to
the address straight after the first -- computed, not hardcoded. The two
blocks must NOT be one contiguous org: the $5800 gap between the buffers
holds real resident data. Capacity now: 6KB + 6KB against 11.5KB used,
so **there is room for perhaps one more room before a third window is
needed** -- $0100-$0DFF has 1.6KB spare and would be the place.

**load_room and the transitions were per-room copy-paste.** Eleven
hand-written stores per room, and a `cur_room` compare chain at every
screen edge; eight rooms would have meant eight of each. roompack now
emits a `room_desc` record per room in exactly the order of the `room_*`
variables, so load_room is a table scan plus a 19-byte block copy, and
the transitions run the ORIGINAL'S ARITHMETIC once -- roomno -1/+1/
+16/-16, `and 127` -- gated on "does this build have that room",
answered from the same table load_room reads. **An unbuilt neighbour is
an edge you can't walk through**, which is also what it looks like in
play. Adding a room is now: generate the data, include it in a staging
block, add one `fdb` to room_desc_table.

**The crash: `blit` had no vertical clip, and never has.** Room 53 has a
24-row sprite (frame 132) placed at y=176 -- eight rows past the bottom
of a 192-row screen. `blit` just walks rows, so for three sessions it
has been writing those eight rows into whatever follows the framebuffer.
Nobody noticed because they landed in the middle of a sprite's BITMAP,
where a few corrupt bytes look like nothing. Growing the actor table put
a sprite HEADER at that address instead, so the same eight rows started
rewriting a width/height/bpr triple -- and the next blit through that
header ran away across all of memory, into the PIA and SAM registers,
and took the machine down about a second after entering the room.

Both `blit` and `clear_and_blit`'s clear now clip to row 191.

Two lessons, both expensive:

* **A latent out-of-bounds write is dormant until the memory behind it
  changes.** This one survived every previous audit because memaudit
  only checks what the IMAGE loads, and this is a RUNTIME overrun. The
  giveaway in the end was a MAME write tap on the corrupted address,
  which named the routine in one run after an hour of reasoning had
  named the wrong three.
* **An early-out label placed in front of a fall-through is not an
  early-out.** The first version of the clip put `blit_offscreen: puls y
  / rts` immediately before `blit_rowdone` -- and blit's SHIFTED row
  path FALLS THROUGH into that label. Every 4px-shifted sprite drew its
  top row and returned. Caught by the framebuffer diff (139 bytes in
  room 36), which is the only reason it did not ship.

Also fixed in the harness: `framedump.lua` parked the rat by a hardcoded
slot index, and slot order shifts whenever a room joins --actor-rooms;
and it invalidated 6 frames before the dump, which is inside the ~8
frames a full repaint takes, so it sometimes compared a half-drawn
screen.

Rooms 51/54/68/69 come with their actors: the portcullis and its switch,
the dragon, the dagger, the rope and Denzil. **Their behaviour routines
do not exist yet** -- they draw as static sprites and do nothing. That
is the next obvious body of work, along with `proxsleep` (54) which the
extracted trigger table already carries.

### T0068: the up-transition only fired from a jump, never from a climb

Playtest: "we have a problem with the upper limit on 51 and 53... on 51 I
cannot get dizzy to jump to the room above" and "on 53 he can climb over
the top edge and drop on the other side of the crocodile, this is not
how it is supposed to work."

Not a rendering bug: rendering both rooms from `rooms.json` and diffing
against the port's own framebuffer confirmed the art matches (rooms 51's
and 53's blank rows above y=48 are real -- the original's own art doesn't
extend there either). And the up-transition mechanism itself was fine --
jumping from the topmost step of room 53's staircase correctly
transitioned into room 69, verified directly in MAME before touching any
code.

The actual bug: `ml_moveup` (the JUMP path, `dizzy_dy < 0`) tests
`TOP_TRANSITION_Y` before landing, but the GROUNDED path
(`ml_downlp`/`ml_down_notrans`, walking and step-climbing) never did.
X-ALL.TXT's `checkbottomside` (~6524) -- the routine BOTH paths in this
port are modelled on -- runs the exact same test from ITS OWN landing
point too: `floorfound: ld a,(y) / cp 66 / jp c,goneup` (~6559). A
staircase whose steps are each shallow enough for `STEP_UP` (walked, not
jumped -- exactly room 51's and room 53's) lets Dizzy's feet cross below
`TOP_TRANSITION_Y` while `dizzy_dy` never goes negative, and this port
then just left him standing there, below the threshold, with nothing to
stop him walking off across the top of the level.

Added the same test to the grounded landing path (`ml_floorfound`),
matching `floorfound`'s own three-way split (y<66 -> transition up; else
-> land normally, folding the source's one-pixel `y==66` no-op case into
"land" rather than replicating it exactly).

Room 51's up-neighbour (67, THE WEST WING) isn't built, so climbing to
that height there now means he simply can't rest there -- `floor` never
gets set, gravity pulls him back down next pass -- rather than the
previous silent "stand on nothing, walk off the edge" state. Consistent
with T0067's own rule (an unbuilt neighbour is something you can't pass
through), just applied vertically this time.

### T0069: whiskey bottle's name, and room 51's gate

**Bottle name**: frame 18 (room 53's `whiskeyhere`) was never in
`item_name_msg`'s dispatch, so it fell through to "AN OBJECT" -- same
class of gap as T0056's railing. Added `FRAME_WHISKEY equ 18` and
`msg_name_whiskey` ("A BOTTLE OF WHISKEY", X-ALL.TXT's `fullwhiskeymess`
~1089, verbatim). Verified with a before/after inventory-screen
framebuffer diff: the item name's ink now extends across roughly twice
as many glyph columns as "AN OBJECT" did, matching the longer string.
The source's OTHER bottle text (`emptybottlemess`, "AN EMPTY BOTTLE")
toggles once Dizzy actually drinks it (`checkifdrunk`) -- not
implemented, same simplification the jug's own full/empty state already
accepts.

**The gate**: X-ALL.TXT's `portcullisrou`/`portswitchrou` (~3186/3208).
Two things about it are easy to miss:

* The visible lattice in the screenshot is ordinary WALL PLACEMENT art,
  static and harmless. The actual mechanism is a separate 8x8 sprite
  (frame 120) that starts completely inert -- the source's own routine
  opens with `ld a,(ix+var1) / and a / ret z`, so an unthrown gate is
  never even redrawn or collided against.
* The switch (frame 122) is one-shot, and the source SAYS so in its own
  text: "[X-ALL.TXT line 879] [X-ALL.TXT line 880]' [X-ALL.TXT line 881]". Once thrown, the
  gate oscillates between y=96 (open) and y=136 (closed) forever,
  killing Dizzy on contact for as long as it's moving
  (`collidewithdizzy16`, reused here as `actor_hit` against the gate's
  own current sprite box -- same idea T0058 uses for the crocodile's
  mouth).

`update_portcullis` (gameplay.asm) finds both actors by scanning
`actor_ram`, throws the switch on a DOWN-key hit against its own sprite
(gated on its own v1, needing no separate edge-detection since going
from 0 to permanently-1 is itself the one-shot), and moves the gate
1px/mainloop-pass -- this port's own rate, not a literal copy of the
source's -2px/interrupt-tick, since the two run on entirely different
clocks (T0061) and matching the FEEL mattered more than a tick count
that wouldn't mean the same thing here anyway.

Caught one real bug in my own first pass at this: the two threshold
reversals had their directions swapped (setting the STILL-RISING delta
again at the top instead of reversing to fall, and vice versa at the
bottom), which let the gate sail straight through y=96 to y=1 before
ever turning around. Found by logging the gate's own y every ~10
frames rather than trusting the oscillation "looked" plausible from a
handful of samples.

The gate moves, so a plain single-box `clear_and_blit` at its new
position each frame would leave a trail of itself at every position it
passed through -- the exact problem the rat's save-under (T0052) exists
to prevent. Rather than build a second copy of that machinery, this
reuses `rat_clear_and_blit`/`rat_save`/`rat_restore` directly for the
gate: the mechanism is already fully generic (saves/restores whatever
sits under wherever it's told to draw, no rat-specific assumption baked
in), the gate's 8x8 sprite fits comfortably inside a buffer sized for
the rat's larger one, and the two are never live in the same room at
once (rat: room 36, gate: room 51) -- so sharing carries none of the
risk `da_clear`'s own comment warns about for a STATIC actor doing the
same. Verified no trail: with Dizzy moved well clear (his own sprite
was the first thing that looked like a false trail -- measure the thing
you're actually trying to measure), ink at a row-band the gate had just
vacated dropped to exactly zero.

### T0071: the dragon, animated in full

Full implementation of X-ALL.TXT's `dragonrou`/`dragonfire`/`findnecky`
(~2540-2830), replacing T0070's deliberate static-hazard placeholder.

**State**, as globals rather than packed into the 8-byte actor record
the way the source overloads `oldmovex`/`delaycounter`/`var1` --
there's only ever one dragon, so the fields are just easier to read
this way:

| variable | meaning |
|---|---|
| `dragon_swing` | the source's `oldmovex`. Triangle wave 0..16 while awake, decrementing toward -8 once asleep. Head Y = 152-swing; neck segment b (1..6) sits at 152-b*swing/8 (`findnecky`). At swing=0 every segment collapses to y=152 -- that's the source's own geometry (not a bug): the neck visibly "uncurls" as swing rises from its low point. |
| `dragon_delay` | 0..31, wraps; drives the triangle wave (`delay<16 ? delay : 32-delay`). |
| `dragon_asleep` | latched permanently by the `proxsleep` trigger (pixel 112,150,40,30). Once set AND swing has decremented to -8, `update_dragon`/`draw_dragon` both stop touching the dragon at all -- matching the source's own `cp -8/ret z`. The LAST frame drawn (swing=-8, head sunk to y=160, neck flattened downward) just stays on screen forever after, like any static placement -- there's no explicit "hide" step in the source and none was needed here. |
| `dragon_fire` | 0 = not breathing. 1..47 = a breath cycle, this port's own per-tick rate (T0061 -- the interrupt-driven original and this port's mainloop don't share a clock, so matching the FEEL mattered more than a literal tick count). While breathing the NECK IS NOT DRAWN AT ALL -- the source calls `dragonfire` INSTEAD of `printneck` once `breathingfire != 0` -- only the head and the flame plume. |

**The flame plume's extent** (`printdragonflame`'s own arithmetic, `pos
= frame*2 - dragon_fire + 68`, visible only for `50<=pos<68`) turned
out to be a fully deterministic "grow then retreat" sequence once
simulated in Python before writing any 6809 -- `dragon_fire` 1-2 is a
silent windup, 3-20 the plume grows from one puff to six sweeping
outward, 21-30 it retreats, 31-47 is a silent cooldown. Reproduced as a
direct 6-iteration loop matching the source's formula exactly (cheap
enough, at 6 iterations every several seconds, that a lookup table
wasn't worth the memory it would cost). What's NOT reproduced: the
yellow/red colour flip between the two `printdragonflame` passes --
inert on this monochrome target the same way every other attribute
byte already is.

**Rendering problem specific to this actor**: SEVEN independently-
moving sprites (six neck segments + head) every single pass while
awake, plus up to six more (flames) while breathing -- nothing else in
this port has that shape. A save-under per piece (T0052's rat
mechanism) would need seven separate per-buffer buffers; a plain clear-
only-the-new-position blit (a static actor) would leave a trail of
every position passed through. Cheaper than either: clear ONE fixed
rectangle generous enough for every piece in every reachable position,
then blit everything fresh into it every pass -- `draw_dragon`
(room36.asm), gated only on `cur_room==54` and the "fully retracted"
early-out.

Profiled (T0064's harness) at 1x CPU: the clear was easily the biggest
single cost, 21.4ms of a 66.7ms frame at the first (deliberately
generous, 128x56) box size. Recomputed the ACTUAL union of every
piece's reachable position exactly rather than re-guessing -- neck
72-184 x / 140-175 y, head 144-160 x / 136-176 y, flames 72-156 x /
144-168 y -- landing on 112x48 (72-184, 132-180), about 25% less area,
which measured out to 18.5ms. Room 54 still holds 15.0 passes/sec with
~17ms of headroom to spare at 1x CPU.

**Bug found and fixed during this session, each caught by testing
rather than review:**
* the two threshold reversals (swing hitting -8 or +16... wait, +16 has
  no reversal, only the CLOSED/OPEN-equivalent -8/16 boundary for
  asleep-retract) -- actually the one real bug was in
  `dragon_necky`'s sign handling: an unsigned `bhs`/`blo` clamp-to--8
  check silently mis-clamped anything already in the awake range
  (0..16) because -8 and 16 sort backwards as unsigned bytes (248 vs
  16). Fixed with signed `bge`.
* `dd_headptr`'s frame-pointer selection clobbered the very register
  (D) it was about to store, because the branch test (`lda
  dragon_headfrm`) landed in the middle of a `ldd #aspr_109_w ...
  ldd #aspr_110_w` pair -- taking the "no branch" path left the low
  byte of D pointing at the WRONG sprite. Fixed by doing the comparison
  in B first, loading D cleanly in each branch.
* label collisions with `draw_flames`'s own `df_*` locals (this file
  reused the same short prefix for the flame-position loop) --
  caught immediately by the assembler, renamed to `dgf_*`.

All three verified fixed by direct memory inspection in MAME: the
triangle wave, the freeze-during-breath, the head-frame swap (110 for
the first third of a breath, 109 otherwise), the flame plume's
grow/retreat matching the Python simulation exactly, and the kill on
contact for both the head and a flame -- each confirmed with `killed`
actually counting down. One test-harness lesson along the way: `aabb_
hit` (used for the switch/proxsleep proximity tests) checks Dizzy's
FULL 24px sprite width, not the narrower body box `actor_hit` uses for
per-actor collision -- a test standing 2px "outside" the sleep box by
that narrower measure was still comfortably inside it by aabb_hit's,
which looked exactly like the trigger firing on its own until traced.

### T0072: memory optimization -- gap1 was down to 28 bytes

The dragon's three new messages (~180 bytes) had nowhere to go: the
gap between the two framebuffers (dizzy frame tail, message VM, font,
message text) was down to 28 bytes free after T0070. Moved
`gap_messages.asm` out of there entirely, into the `$0100` region
(room 36/35's own art) alongside T0067's other tenants there -- that
region still had 1.6KB spare. Pure data reached only by absolute `ldx
#label`, so where it lives is arbitrary; this is just the region with
room left. Net: gap1 28 -> 296 bytes free, "low data" 1634 -> 1366 (a
smaller loss there than gap1's gain, since less padding/alignment is
wasted in the bigger region). Verified byte-identical rendering and
15.0 passes/sec unchanged before adding a single line of dragon code
on top of the freed space.

### T0038 scoping (no implementation) -- the well shaft is smaller than its name suggests

Asked to scope this out before building anything. The task title
("upside-down world rooms 7/23/39/55") overstates it -- there is no
area-wide inverted-gravity world. Read every one of the seven
`upsidedown` references in X-ALL.TXT (there are only seven); here is
what they actually do.
