and assert (v & $F0) == $F0 for RG6, then read bit 3 for the colour set.
Confirmed $F4 for green and $FC for buff.

## Colour on the CoCo2: measured, then REVERTED. Do not redo this.

Asked whether the port could use green. Everything below was measured on
the machine, not quoted, and then backed out at the user's call as not
worth the trouble. The reason it is here is so nobody spends the day
re-deriving it.

    RG6/PMODE4 CSS=1   black + buff/white         256x192 1bpp  <- SHIPPING
    RG6/PMODE4 CSS=0   black + green              256x192 1bpp
    CG6        CSS=0   green, yellow, blue, red   128x192 2bpp
    CG6        CSS=1   buff, cyan, magenta, orange

Green as the ONLY ink is one bit (PIA1 $FF22 bit 3, the colour-set
select) and costs nothing -- but it makes the whole game green, which is
not what was wanted.

**CG6 HAS NO BLACK.** All four slots are colours and the border renders
green. That, not the halved resolution, is what kills it for this game:
converting the real title art turned every black background red or blue
and looked garish. Rendered before believing it.

**The split-screen idea, abandoned unverified.** Both modes are 32
bytes/line, 192 lines, 6144 bytes -- the same memory read two ways -- so
a banner in CG6 over a play area in RG6 would need NO framebuffer
change. It could not be validated: **MAME's coco2b renders each frame
with the last $FF22 value written, not per scanline**, so a mid-frame
split is invisible to it. Proven both ways -- switching to CG6 and
staying there renders solid yellow, while switching to CG6 and back
renders the whole screen RG6, and four different switch delays gave
byte-identical captures. Verifying it needs XRoar or real hardware and a
human looking.

**THE TWO-PHASE PREDICTION WAS WRONG.** I argued that the artifact
palette is two opposite subcarrier phases, so dithering them could only
average to grey and green was unreachable. The chart says otherwise: on
the user's XRoar, bands 6 and 9 read GREEN, and cyan, magenta and orange
are there too. The palette is much richer than two hues. Not pursued --
the user called it not worth the trouble -- but do not repeat the claim
that PMODE4 artifacting cannot make green. It can.

**Two probes lied before they were believed**, both worth remembering:
the first pointed the SAM at $0200 (wrote $ffc7 = F0) instead of $4000
($ffd1 = F5) and showed uninitialised RAM; the second built all four
mode variants identically, because `-DMODE=\$$1` in bash expands `$$` to
the PID. Both produced confident, plausible pictures. Check that N
variants have N distinct checksums before reading anything into N
captures.

## T0097 FIXED -- collision uses the LAST attribute painted into a cell

The port keyed solidity off each placement's OWN colour byte. The
original doesn't. `checkattri` (X-ALL.TXT ~6705) is called only when the
pixel byte is non-zero and then reads the attribute straight off the
screen:

        checkattri  ld a,(lookx) / ld e,a / ld a,(looky) / ld l,a
                    call findattriloc / ld a,(hl)
                    bit 6,a / ret nz          ; dull -> no hit

Screen attributes are per 8x8 cell and every placement repaints the
cells it covers, so **a later decorative placement drawn over a solid
one makes those cells non-collidable**. Collision is therefore
`ink AND (final cell attribute).bit6 == 0`, not
`ink AND (this placement's attribute).bit6 == 0`.

Room 67 is where it showed: the barrel (frame 154, 24x24 at 216,152,
attr $02 = solid) is immediately overdrawn by frame 215 (24x26 at
216,141, attr $44 = dull), which covers all but its bottom 8px. The real
game leaves an 8px step you walk over; this port built a 24px wall and
sealed the room. Reported from a playtest.

roompack now paints an 8x8 attribute map in placement order, then marks
a 4x4 block solid only if the placement that drew the ink was ITSELF
solid AND the cell's final attribute is still solid.

**INTERSECTION, not replacement -- and this is the whole lesson.** The
first version replaced the per-placement test with the final-cell test.
That is arguably the more faithful reading of plotattris (which paints
whole rectangles, and drawfullroom calls it unconditionally for every
placement), and it BROKE ROOM 51: 59 blocks of new solid mass appeared
on the left (x=0..28, y=80..135) where a decorative sprite's ink sat in
a cell a later placement re-attributed as solid, walling off a level
that worked. Reported from a playtest, one build later.

Intersecting can only ever REMOVE solidity, which is all room 67 needed,
and cannot wall anything off. Verified both ways: room 51's mask is now
byte-identical to pre-T0097, and room 67's barrel is still cut to its
bottom 8px. If the fuller model is ever wanted, the open question is
which cells plotattris really paints -- do not assume whole rectangles. Verified: Dizzy now walks past the barrel and on into room
68; room 35's walkable surfaces are byte-identical; the --above-line
stranding report is unchanged; lzverify and all 36 sweep trials match.

Frame 154 is decorative (attr 66/69) in rooms 35/45/46/47/68/69/85 and
solid (attr $02) only in 23 and 67 -- that asymmetry is what made the
data look wrong before the overdraw explained it.

## T0098 -- the portcullis is genuinely an 8x8 sprite in the source

Not solved. What the data says, so the next session starts here:

* `porthere` (X-ALL.TXT 1556): `defb 51,portcullis,76,136,120,...` --
  room 51, x=76 (pixel 176), y=136, frame 120, travelling between y=96
  and y=136, colour 7.
* **Frame 120 is 8x8 pixels.** Confirmed by unit: frames 65/66 are the
  letters A/B, also width=2 height=8, and letters are 8px wide, so the
  width field is in 4px units.
* Its bitmap IS a portcullis lattice texture (`#.##.##.` / `##.##.##`),
  i.e. a TILE, not a gate.
* `printmoving` (X-ALL.TXT 2038) draws exactly ONE frame at
  (movex,movey). There is no tiling loop in it.
* Room 51's scenery has no tall lattice placement near x=176 either.

So the source appears to describe a single 8x8 tile, which contradicts
the playtest report that the real game shows a continuous barrier. One
of those is wrong and it is probably my reading. Unchecked leads: the
`addtoflame`/`addtowater` repeated-draw lists (room 51 does have flames),
and whether some other routine redraws the gate as a column. Settle it by
LOOKING at the original -- harness/zx_orig.sh boots the tape -- rather
than by reading more assembler.

## The banner repaint is NOT optional -- and the sweep cannot see it

I removed draw_ui's 1536-byte banner repaint on the argument that the
title screen had already painted rows 0-47 into both framebuffers and
nothing ever clears them (clearplayarea starts at y=48, every other blit
is clipped to win_top). The argument was wrong: the eggs and the border
disappeared in play, reported from a playtest.

**Nothing I ran could have caught it.** harness/sweep.lua compares
physics and never looks at pixels; rate.lua reported 15.0 passes/sec
either way; lzverify checks the $8000 room image, which was untouched.
Every check stayed green while the screen was visibly wrong -- the same
shape as T0028. **A change to what is DRAWN needs a framebuffer capture
and a human-visible render, every time.** grabgame-style: pull the
buffer the SAM is actually displaying (draw_base tells you which is the
back one) and convert it.

The repaint is restored and stays. The routine that clobbers the band is
NOT identified -- `clear_and_blit` is the suspect, since it clears actor
damage rectangles with only a >=192 clip and no win_top clip, so a rect
reaching above y=48 would erase banner rows -- but that is a hypothesis,
not a finding. Prove it before optimising the repaint away again.

## T0100/T0101/T0102 -- one root cause: ACTORS ARE INVISIBLE TO COLLISION

Three playtest reports that look unrelated share a single architectural
gap. Worth reading together before fixing any of them.

**The original has no collision mask.** `checkattri` reads the ATTRIBUTE
off the live screen (X-ALL.TXT ~6705), and the screen contains whatever
has been drawn into it -- including moving actors, which `printmoving`
paints with their own colour byte. So an actor whose colour has bit 6
clear is *automatically solid*, with no extra code anywhere. This port
precomputes a STATIC room mask from scenery placements only, so no actor
has ever been collidable. That is the gap.

* **T0101, the gator (room 53, THE SNAP HAPPY GATOR).** Its colour byte
  is 12 -> bit 6 CLEAR -> solid in the original, which is exactly why you
  can land on its nose to reach the rope. Here it is drawn and nothing
  more, so Dizzy falls through.
* **T0102, the portcullis (room 51).** Colour byte 7 -> bit 6 clear ->
  solid, so the closed gate blocks and the moving gate crushes. Ours
  blocks nothing.

**And the portcullis is a COLUMN because it is never erased.**
`portcullisrou` calls plain `printmoving`; `crocodilerou` and the other
movers call `rubprintmoving` (erase-then-draw, X-ALL.TXT 2033). So the
8x8 lattice tile (frame 120) deliberately leaves a TRAIL as it travels
between y=136 and y=96, painting a continuous lattice column. That
resolves the T0098 puzzle -- the source really does describe an 8x8
sprite, and the barrier is the trail it leaves, not a big sprite. Do not
"fix" the portcullis by giving it a tall frame.

* **T0100, Denzil (room 68).** Not a collectible at all. Compare the two
  `defw` fields in movingdata:

        ropehere    defb 68,pickupable,76,160,14
                    defw ropemess,proxcroc          ; message + prox routine
        denzilhere  defb 68,pickupable,80,155,33
                    defw denzilrou,denziltalking    ; ROUTINE + talk routine

  Both use the `pickupable` id, but Denzil's first word is a routine, and
  `denzilrou` is `ld hl,stereoess / jp windowrou` -- it opens a message
  window. So the routine id alone does not tell you whether a thing is
  picked up or talked to; the first defw does. Anything the port imported
  as "pickupable" needs re-checking against that word.

## T0100 FIXED -- frames 32..39 are PEOPLE, and play.sh takes a room

Denzil went into the inventory as "AN OBJECT". The rule is the
original's own, keyed on the frame number in `pickupablerou`
(X-ALL.TXT ~2302):

        cp 32 / jr c,notpickingupbag     ; frame < 32  -> pick up
        cp 40 / jp c,talkingtopeople     ; frames 32..39 -> TALK

The routine id does NOT distinguish them -- denzilhere carries
`pickupable` exactly as ropehere does. Frames 32..39 are Dozy 32,
Denzil 33, Dylan 34, Daisy 35, Doug 36; only Denzil is in a built room
so far. The rope is now named too ("A PIECE OF ROPE", X-ALL.TXT
`ropemess`) instead of falling through to the generic name.

**Denzil's box is CONDENSED to two lines.** The source's three lines in
its own 26x5 box at y=96 render truncated -- line 2 stops mid-word and
line 3 never appears -- so this port's message VM limits a box more than
the original's does. Not chased. Geometry and pens are msg_troll's,
which is the known-good pairing: pen numbers are Spectrum INK colours
and on 1bpp only ink-vs-paper survives, so the source's 4/3 drew white
text on a white box.

### The test lied three times before it told the truth

Worth reading before trusting any actor test:

1. A fixed spawn never reached Denzil and reported "not pocketed" for a
   build that pocketed him fine. **It gave the right answer for the wrong
   reason.** Fixed by sweeping past him and printing closest approach, so
   a null result is distinguishable from a miss.
2. The "empty box" screenshots were the ROPE's inventory screen. The
   rope sits at x=176, inside reach of Denzil at x=192, and tp_loop
   returns the FIRST matching actor -- so the rope was picked up and its
   box photographed. The test now removes the rope first.
3. A run reported nothing at all because a previous `./play.sh 99`
   (testing the not-built warning) had left the binary starting in an
   unbuilt room. Rebuild the default before measuring anything.

## play.sh: a room number and a starting inventory

`./play.sh 51` drops Dizzy into room 51 at boot instead of making you
walk there. START_ROOM is a build-time define, so it cannot be combined
with --no-build, and play.sh warns if the room is not in roomview.py's
BUILT list.

**The spawn point comes from the room's own mask** (tools/start_pos.py:
widest walkable surface safely below TOP_TRANSITION_Y, stand in the
middle). A fixed drop point does NOT work -- x=128,y=80 is inside room
69's geometry, where the grounded step-climb walks Dizzy out of the top
of the room and you arrive in 85 having asked for 69. Room 36 keeps its
real opening position (x=184, inside the troll's box) so a normal run
still opens with the knockback.

### ...and a starting inventory

`./play.sh 53 rope` or `./play.sh 68 rope,whiskey`. Names map to FRAME
ids (rope 14, apple 17, whiskey 18, jug 19, loaf 20, railing 192) and at
most three are taken, because inv_cap is 3 without the bag.

**`inv` holds an actor INDEX+1, not a frame**, so seeding has to find the
actor carrying that frame, take it OUT of the world (room=255, exactly
what tp_take does) and push its index. Seeding the frame directly, or
skipping the room=255, leaves the item both in your hands and lying in
the room. seed_inventory runs after actors_init (which populates
actor_ram) and before load_room.

Verified on the target, not just at the build: the inventory resolves
back through actor_ram to frames 14 and 18 with room=255 on both, the
inventory screen reads "A PIECE OF ROPE / A BOTTLE OF WHISKEY", and a
default build is byte-for-byte unchanged in the sweep.

### ...and it works out the items a room's puzzle needs

`./play.sh 53` starts you holding the rope, with no list given. The
requirement is DERIVED FROM THE ORIGINAL, not from anyone's memory:
every pickupable's movingdata entry carries a `prox` routine, and a prox
routine's data block opens with the room its trigger box lives in.

    proxcroc  defb 53      ;;room
              defb 68,140  ;;;x,y
              defb 10,20   ;;;w,h

`ropehere`'s prox is proxcroc, whose box is in room 53 -- so the rope is
what room 53's puzzle wants, straight out of X-ALL.TXT. tools/room_items.py
reads all 23 prox boxes every run, so a room built later picks up its
items with no table to maintain. 20 item->room links exist today,
including several this build cannot use yet (room 54 wants the sleeping
potion, 55 the crowbar, 84 the door key) -- those are reported on stderr
rather than silently dropped, because `inv` stores an actor index and an
item whose actor is not in the 20-slot table has nothing to point at.

Explicit lists still win (`./play.sh 53 whiskey`), and `--no-items`
suppresses seeding. Note `./play.sh 36` is NOT the same as `./play.sh`:
naming the room explicitly seeds its puzzle items (apple, jug, loaf),
while a bare run starts a normal game.

## T0101/T0103 FIXED -- actors are solid, and it is ink not a box

The gator now holds Dizzy up so he can reach the rope from its nose.

**The original has no collision mask and no actor/scenery distinction.**
checkattri reads the attribute off the LIVE SCREEN, and a moving actor
paints its own colour byte there via printmoving -- so any actor whose
colour has bit 6 clear is solid for free, with no code. This port
precomputed a static scenery mask, so no actor had ever been collidable.

Hooked into `cmask_test`, which is the single choke point every probe
goes through (ten call sites, floor and wall alike), so actors became
solid everywhere at once rather than in one hand-picked check. Four
actors have bit 6 clear in this build: the gator (colour 12), the
portcullis (7), the rat (29) and the well lid (2).

**INK, not the bounding box.** Box-only left Dizzy standing in mid-air
on the gator's empty top-left corner -- frame 123 is 16x32 and its ink
sits to one side. checkattri only runs when the pixel byte is non-zero,
so the ink test is what the original does anyway. Verified by capturing
the screen and looking: contact moved from x=140 (thin air) to x=152
(on the sprite).

**Collision must use the sprite that is actually DRAWN.** The gator
faces Dizzy, and draw_actors swaps in aspr_123_mirror when colour bit 7
is set. Testing the unmirrored ink would put the nose on the wrong side,
so draw_actors' selection is factored into `actor_sprite_for` and both
callers share it.

### The list is built once a PASS, not once a probe

The first version scanned all 20 actor slots inside cmask_test and cost
room 36 nearly a fifth of its frame rate: **15.0 -> 12.2 passes/sec**.
cmask_test has ten call sites and the floor search walks downward
through it, so "once per probe" is far more often than it sounds.
`build_solid_actors` now collects the short list at the top of the
mainloop, and the common case -- a room with no solid actors -- is a
single byte test. Back to 15.2.

That regression was caught by rate.lua and would NOT have been caught by
the sweep, which reports positions rather than speed. Run rate.lua after
anything that touches a collision probe.

**The mouth-open rule was already right** and needed no change: the
original's justcroccoll does `bit 0,(ix+movefrm) / ret nz`, so the kill
box is only tested on an EVEN frame -- 123 closed is odd, 124 open is
even. Only the open mouth kills.

## T0104 -- the $0E00-$4000 region overflowed, and I missed the audit

T0103's actor collision pushed code+data 195 bytes past $4000, into
framebuffer A's staging block. memaudit caught it and printed
OVERLAPPING BLOCKS; **I missed it because I piped stage_pack.sh's output
through `grep -iE "error"`**, and the audit does not use that word. The
build went out and the user hit it on the next pull.

Two lessons, and the second is the one that matters:

* A filtered build log is not a read build log. stage_pack.sh ends with
  the audit for a reason -- read its last lines, or grep for "OVERLAP"
  too, never just "error".
* **The T0095 guard did not fire, and could not.** It checks the two
  STAGING blocks against their windows. This overflow was the resident
  code region growing into a staging window from the other side, which
  memaudit sees (it compares the actual DECB blocks) and an assembler
  `ifgt` on staged sizes never will.

Fixed by moving boot-only code into the $0100 region, the same move
ui.asm and gap_messages.asm already made: the LZSS unpacker, the
START_ITEM seeder, and the T0092 title sequence (lifted out of `start:`
into a `show_title` subroutine -- straight-line boot code, so it costs
one jsr/rts). target/boot_code.asm.

    before   code+data   0 free, overlapping by 195
    after    code+data 166 free, low data 101 free

Verified after the move, because relocating boot code is exactly the
kind of change that breaks quietly: staged image byte-exact, title screen
byte-exact against its source, gator still solid, items still seed,
Denzil still talks, 15.2/15.0/15.0 passes/sec, 36/36 sweep trials
identical to the pre-move build.

## T0105 CONFIRMED BY PLAYTEST -- dropping the rope ties the gator

Dropping an item is not the point; WHERE you drop it is. The original
runs the check straight after `dropobject` in `justexitinvent`
(X-ALL.TXT ~5848, its own comment: "CHECK DROPPING OBJECT BY TRIGGER"):
the item carries a prox routine in its movingdata entry, and if Dizzy is
inside that box when it lands, the routine fires.

`proxcroc` is room 53, raw x=68,y=140,w=10,h=20 -> X=(68-32)*4=144,
W=10*4=40, y/h unchanged, so the box is x=144..184, y=140..160. Standing
on the gator (y=152) is inside it; standing on the room floor (y=176) is
NOT, which is the whole puzzle.

`proxcrocrou` sets the CROCODILE's var1 to 255 -- `tiecroc equ -16+var1`
reaches back from the rope's record to the crocodile's, 16 bytes earlier
in movingdata -- and crocodilerou then does `cp 255 / jr z,hestied`,
freezing it on frame 123 with its mouth shut. The rope is consumed.

Wired for the rope only; the other 19 item->room links (bean, egg, rock,
sleeping potion, crowbar, bucket, keys) follow the same shape when their
rooms exist. tools/room_items.py already lists them all.

**Confirmed working by the user's own playtest.** The build was already sound (staged image byte-exact,
15.2/15.0/15.0, gator still standable, 36/36 sweep identical) but
harness/tiecroc.lua never managed to drive the drop, and I stopped
rather than keep bending the harness. What it did establish is worth
keeping:

* Standing on the gator when the mouth opens KILLS -- correct, and it
  ended several runs before the drop could happen.
* **A 16px sprite can fall between Dizzy's two foot probes.** They sit at
  x+0 and x+20 and the gator is 16 wide, so from x=148 both straddle it
  and he drops straight through. Landing on it needs a probe to actually
  cross the sprite (x<=147 or x>=152). That is a real gameplay quirk of
  probe-pair collision, not a harness artifact, and may deserve a third
  centre probe if narrow platforms become common.

## Why a 64K machine is tighter than the 48K original -- measured

Asked, fairly, why this port fights for bytes when the Spectrum game fit
102 rooms in 48K and we are full at thirteen. The answer is not "6809
code is fatter". Measured:

    13 room files          12008   of which 4992 is COLLISION MASK
    dizzy frames            4719
    shared sprites          4082   (1165 + 2917 overflow)
    actor data              1374
    font                      689
    messages / UI / names     721

**We are not out of RAM.** Above $8000 there are ~6.3KB genuinely unused
($b83c-$bfff and $ee00-$feff), plus 10KB of title scratch that is
boot-only and reusable. The 64K is not full; the sub-$8000 regions are.
That is a LOADING constraint, not a memory one: CLOADM cannot write
$8000+ before all-RAM is engaged, so everything must arrive below $8000,
and resident code must live there.

**Two things the Spectrum got free from its hardware, which we pay for
in bytes:**

1. **Collision masks -- 384 bytes per room, 4992 for thirteen. The
   original has NONE.** checkattri reads the attribute map, which exists
   anyway as a side effect of colour, so the Spectrum's collision data
   IS its colour data. The 6847 has no per-cell attributes at all
   (factory/platforms/coco2.toml says so explicitly), so we must store
   an explicit mask. At 102 rooms that is 39KB -- more than the entire
   Spectrum game. This is the single biggest structural cost of the
   port and it scales linearly with rooms.

2. **Double buffering -- 12288 bytes against the Spectrum's single 6912
   screen**, +5376. The original redraws in place.

So the comparison is not 64K vs 48K. It is "48K where the display
hardware doubles as your collision map and your colour" against "64K of
which only the bottom half is loadable, and you store the collision map
yourself".

**The relief valve, when the sub-$8000 regions fill again:** resident
code can be staged to $8000+ exactly as room data already is -- the
unpacker does that every boot. Nothing about code makes it special; it
just has to arrive through the window like everything else. That is the
move to reach for before shaving bytes.

### Dead-data audit: there is no litter (checked, so nobody re-checks)

Asked whether an old title screen or similar was still being compiled in.
It is not, and neither is anything else:

* **Only one title exists.** target/title_lz.asm is regenerated from the
  PNG on every build; the .SCR loading-screen path in mktitle.rs is dead
  code in the TOOL, not bytes in the binary. The title buffers
  (TITLE_LZ_BUF $c000, TITLE_RAW_BUF $d000, BANNER_BUF $e800) are `equ`
  addresses above $8000 -- reserved address space, not loaded bytes.
* **Every include is live.** hello.asm, pm4test.asm and room36_cart.asm
  sit in target/ but nothing includes them. dizzy_frame0.asm (127 bytes)
  is included ONLY by room36_cart.asm and is absent from room36.map --
  do not "clean it up" thinking it is in the build, and do not panic on
  seeing it in a naive `grep include target/*.asm`.
* **No unreferenced sprites**: 29 shared + 55 overflow + 27 actor
  sprites, all referenced.

So the pressure is structural, not litter -- see the measurement above.
The 10KB of title scratch above $8000 IS idle after boot, though, and is
the obvious place to stage resident code when the low regions fill.

## Collision masks: pack them, do not derive them (measured)

Asked whether the masks could be split and loaded on demand. They can,
and the numbers are good -- but note WHERE they live first: masks are in
the $8000 image, and $8000+ is not the scarce region. Today's pressure is
resident code BELOW $8000. This is a scaling fix, not a fix for that.

The masks are extremely sparse -- 14% of bits set, 77% of bytes $00:

    LZSS, per room, decoder ALREADY EXISTS   1193   (23%)
    sparse rows (6-byte row bitmap)          2718   (54%)
    RLE, per room                            2700   (54%)
    zlib, all masks together                  559   (11%, needs Huffman)

**LZSS wins and costs nothing new**: lz_unpack is already on the target
for the staged image and the title. Store each room's mask packed, unpack
the current one into a single 384-byte buffer on room entry -- 384 bytes
is a trivial unpack, and rooms already do far more work than that when
they load.

    13 rooms   4992 -> 1193 + 384 buffer = 1577   saves 3415
    102 rooms 39168 -> 9360 + 384 buffer = 9744   saves 29424

That second line is the point. 39168 bytes of masks is more than the
entire 48K Spectrum game; packed it is 9.4KB, which is the difference
between "this map cannot fit" and "it fits".

**Do NOT derive the mask at room-entry from the placements instead.** It
is tempting -- zero storage, and it is how the Spectrum gets collision
free -- but it roughly doubles room-load work (every placement's ink
walked again, ~4500 sprite bytes in room 51 alone) and it has to
reproduce roompack's ink-AND-final-cell-attribute rule exactly, including
the T0097 intersection. Packing gets most of the benefit with a decoder
that already exists and no behavioural risk.

**And the fix for the CURRENT squeeze is different**: resident code
staged to $8000+, where ~6.3KB is free plus 10KB of idle title scratch.

## What actually fills the two tight regions (measured from the listing)

Attributed per source file by walking lwasm's listing, not guessed.

**code+data $0E00-$4000, 12747 of 12800 used -- the tightest:**

    4125  32%  dizzy_frames_all.asm   <- Dizzy's own animation frames
    3712  29%  room36.asm             (engine: blit, physics, boot, main loop)
    3158  24%  gameplay.asm
    1682  13%  actors.asm

**low data $0100-$0E00, 3286 of 3328 used** (byte-column figures, which
undercount bulk data slightly -- the span method is wrong here because
boot_code.asm ends on an `org` jump):

     753  room35_data.asm     \ 1486 together, of which 768 is
     733  room36_data.asm     / COLLISION MASK for just these two rooms
     448  ui.asm
     349  boot_code.asm
     314  gap_messages.asm
     175  ui_room_names.asm

**The single biggest occupant of the tightest region is Dizzy's sprite
frames, at ~4.1KB.** They are pure data reached only through
`dizzy_frame_maskptrs` / `dizzy_frame_spriteptrs` / `dizzy_frame_heights`
-- a pointer table plus numbered blobs, which is exactly the shape room
data already has. So they can be STAGED to $8000+ through the existing
window, `phase`d like the rooms, and the pointer tables will resolve to
their final addresses with no code change. That one move frees roughly a
third of the region.

Second-biggest lever: T0106's mask packing would take rooms 35+36's 768
bytes in the low region down to ~180, freeing ~590 more. So the masks DO
touch the scarce region after all -- rooms 35 and 36 live there, unlike
the other eleven which are staged to $8000+.

## T0107 DONE -- Dizzy's frames staged, and a real bug found doing it

code+data went from 52 free to 1192 free by staging the main body of
Dizzy's animation frames (dizzy_frames_body.asm, split from the
existing dizzy_frames_all.asm) to $8000+ through the r8000/r9800
windows, same mechanism room data already uses. Its resident TAIL
(frame36 on -- split out in an earlier session specifically to live at
$5800, see that file's own header) is untouched.

**The body had to be split BETWEEN r8000 and r9800**, not dropped whole
into either: at ~4188 raw bytes it doesn't fit either window's spare
alone. Split at frame 8 (bodyA = frames 0-7 -> r8000, bodyB = frames
8-35 -> r9800) by direct measurement through the real packer, not
estimated -- LZSS ratios aren't linear across a concatenated stream, so
"spare packed bytes / expected ratio" undershoots. Final: r8000 packed
4793/6144, r9800 packed 6099/6144, both fit with a few bytes to spare.

**Two build-tooling bugs found and fixed getting here, both about the
same root cause: an address happening to fall in a range that was
meant to identify something else.**

1. `stage_pack.sh`'s symbol harvest takes everything in
   `[$8000, dest_end)` from the raw pass's map and treats it as a
   staged room-data label. Once the raw image grew past 8KB, the block-
   boundary labels' OWN real (unphased) addresses ($6000+lenB, etc.)
   started falling inside that range by coincidence of magnitude and got
   re-harvested as if they were staged data -- "Multiply defined
   symbol", since room36.asm already defines them. The STAGE_GEN scratch
   addresses chosen for title chunks ($c000+) hit the exact same trap.
   Fixed by excluding both classes BY NAME (the four block-boundary
   labels, and anything starting `title_lz`), not by trying to out-guess
   the address range.

2. **The one that actually corrupted the game, and the one lzverify
   exists for.** TITLE_LZ_BUF/TITLE_RAW_BUF/BANNER_BUF were hardcoded
   ($c000/$d000/$e800) on the assumption the room image would stay
   below them. Staging Dizzy's frames grew it past $c000, so
   show_title's own boot-time scratch write silently clobbered the tail
   of the staged room image -- specifically the back half of Dizzy's own
   animation frames -- every single boot. The game still ran (short test
   sessions never happened to need the corrupted frames), title screen
   still rendered fine, sweep and rate stayed green. Only lzverify,
   which checks literally every byte, caught it.

   Made IMAGE_END symbolic instead of a fresh hardcode, and that took a
   second attempt: R9800_DEST-based formulas mean DIFFERENT things in
   the two build branches (r9800_staged_end brackets a packed blob's own
   length in STAGE_LZ, the raw content's true length in the else
   branch), so a single top-level formula silently used the WRONG one in
   the packed build -- IMAGE_END came out $BC10 instead of the real
   $C898, landing INSIDE the image rather than after it. Fixed the same
   way R9800_DEST itself already handles this: a per-branch definition,
   with the packed branch's correct value computed by stage_pack.sh from
   the RAW pass (target/image_end_lz.asm) and the raw branch computing
   it directly from its own (correctly-scoped) labels.

   BANNER_BUF now REUSES TITLE_LZ_BUF's address rather than taking its
   own 1536 bytes: the packed stream is dead by the time the banner copy
   runs (from the framebuffer, after unpacking), so their live ranges
   never overlap in time, only in address -- which is exactly what makes
   sharing safe.

**Verified end to end, not just "it built"**: lzverify OK across all
18584 bytes (not just the room data -- this is what actually caught
both bugs above), title screen byte-exact against its source image,
15.2/15.0/15.0 passes/sec, 36/36 sweep trials identical to the
pre-T0107 baseline, gator still solid, Denzil still talks, items still
seed correctly.

## T0102 DONE -- the portcullis is now a real column, not a hopping block

**A previous session had it exactly backwards.** X-ALL.TXT's
`portcullisrou` calls plain `printmoving` while every other mover calls
`rubprintmoving` (erase-then-draw) -- the ORIGINAL DELIBERATELY LEAVES A
TRAIL as the 8x8 lattice tile rises 1px/pass from PORT_CLOSED_Y(136) to
PORT_OPEN_Y(96), so the gap reads as a solid column after the first full
rise, not a single block hopping between two positions. A previous
session found the trail, read it as a leftover-sprite BUG, and put the
gate on `rat_clear_and_blit` (erase old position, draw new) specifically
to STOP it -- the opposite of the source's own mechanism. Checked
against X-ALL.TXT before touching this a second time, not just against
how a screenshot looked.

**Fix, two halves:**

1. **Draw**: the gate now calls `blit_only` (draw with no pre-clear)
   unconditionally while active, instead of `rat_clear_and_blit`. No new
   draw code -- `blit_only` already existed for pickupables.
2. **Collision**: T0103 already makes the gate's CURRENT 8x8 sprite
   solid (colour 7, bit 6 clear), but that only blocks wherever it
   happens to be sitting -- the visual column needs the WHOLE gap solid,
   not one 8x8 slice of it. `up_gatecheck` now latches a "filled" flag
   (v2, offset 6 -- unused by the source's own movingdata entry for this
   actor) the first time the gate reaches PORT_OPEN_Y. `build_solid_actors`
   checks that flag and, when set, swaps the gate's real sprite for a
   synthetic one (`gate_col_hdr`: 8px wide, 48 rows of solid $FF ink,
   pinned at y=PORT_OPEN_Y) instead of its actual 8x8 frame -- so once
   filled, the WHOLE column collides, permanently, regardless of where
   the moving 8x8 sprite currently sits.

**Verified on the target, both halves separately**, since a screenshot
alone would only prove the draw side:

* Framebuffer capture after a full rise shows a continuous lattice
  column from y=96 to the floor -- the trail (harness/portcullis.lua).
* With the gate poked into its post-fill state, Dizzy holding RIGHT from
  the left side plateaus at x=152 and stays there for 90+ frames (his
  body's right edge, +20, lands at 172 -- 4px shy of the gate's face at
  176) -- genuinely blocked, not just slow (harness/portcullis_block.lua).

**The crush hazard is untouched and still correct**: `up_kill`'s
point-check against the gate's own current sprite (regardless of fill
state) is exactly what it was before this task; only the draw call and
the NEW filled-column addition to collision changed.

### The test itself lied first, walked into an already-documented trap

`harness/portcullis.lua`'s first few runs all reported the switch never
threw, even though the switch WAS in reach. Two separate bugs, both
worth remembering:

* My lookup for "the gate actor" matched the first actor with routine
  byte 0 -- but zero is also ROU_PORTCULLIS's OWN id, so that part was
  right, except I hadn't also filtered on frame==120, and a wrong first
  match would have silently watched the wrong slot. Filtering on both
  fields is what made the reads trustworthy.
* **The real one**: my script stopped toggling SPACE once inside room 51
  (copied from an earlier test where that was fine). The switch-throw
  message uses `msg_wait_dismiss`, which BLOCKS the mainloop without
  SPACE -- exactly the T0061 trap this file already has a section on.
  The gate's v1 latched to "rising" correctly on the very first press,
  and then sat frozen for 200+ frames because the whole game was frozen,
  not because anything about the portcullis was wrong. Toggle SPACE for
  the WHOLE run, always -- there is no room-specific exception where it
