## T0162 CORRECTED -- the jump failures are UP-TRANSITION RE-ENTRY, not a gated check

The triage's inference (the boundary test being gated behind the floor check a
jump suppresses) is WRONG. Read the code: the horizontal edge test sits after
`ml_keys_latched`, which the latched-direction path reaches every pass, airborne
or not. It is not gated.

Its census was also slightly off: it judged "is the target room built?" by the
original's FINAL room. Checking the FIRST HOP instead gives **23 of 24 real
failures, 1 unbuilt neighbour** (36u7, whose original goes 36>37>53 -- room 37 is
not built). So the conclusion "these are real" survives; the mechanism does not.

**What actually happens** (84u3, traced: start 84@184,72 JUMPLEFT):

    a=12  x=180 y=72  dy=-8   the jump fires
    a=14  x=180 y=65  dy=-7   rising, crosses TOP_TRANSITION_Y=66
    a=32  room=100    y=65    transition up taken
    a=34  room=100 x=176 y=183 dy=-6   arrived
    ...   room=100 x=176 y=183         stays there

**The port arrives at y=183. BOT_TRANSITION_Y is 182.** It lands in the room above
already at or below the line that sends it back down, over a gap in room 100's
floor at that x (the floor spans columns 8..43, i.e. x=32..175; Dizzy arrives at
x=176, one column past its right edge). The original arrives at 100@180,184 and
lands at 120,175.

So the failing class is **not** "the jump does not reach high enough" -- the port
jumps fine and takes the transition. It is that the arrival y (`goneup`'s y+118)
puts Dizzy at the very bottom of the room above, in the band where one downward
step re-triggers gonedown, and where the floor may not extend. That is why almost
every case is an "up" case: 51>67 (4), 84>100 (4), 53>69 (3), 52>51, 68>84, 68>67,
69>84, 56>55, 71>55, 39>23, 39>55, 35>36.

**This is exactly the complaint that opened this session** -- "dizzy could not
reach high enough to land correctly on the room above". It is worth 23 cases and
it is a real gameplay bug, not a measurement artefact.

**Where to look next:** the arrival arithmetic. X-ALL.TXT's goneup does
`y + 118` and gonedown `y - 114`, and T0137 already found the port's gonedown
threshold was 6px out (188 vs the source's 182). The same class of off-by-a-few
in the ARRIVAL value would put Dizzy exactly one band too low. Compare the port's
rt_arrive computation against the source for BOTH directions, and check what the
original's own y is at the moment it takes the up-transition.

# ============================================================
# LOADING ARCHITECTURE -- the design to finish the game
# ============================================================

## The two ceilings, measured (not estimated)

    room image resident, RAW      $8000-$C9DA  18,906 bytes for 27 rooms
    free RAM above it              IMAGE_END..CODE_DEST   6,868 bytes
    delivery budget                fbA 68 + fbB 137 + holes 213 = 418 packed

    still to build                 26 content rooms + 48 stubs
                                   11,402 raw  /  ~7,411 packed

    RAM shortfall                  11,402 needed vs 6,868 free   -> short ~4,500
    DELIVERY shortfall             7,411 needed vs 418 spare     -> short ~7,000

**Both bind, and they are different problems.** Delivery is "how many bytes can
reach the machine through a path that only exists during boot". RAM is "how many
can be resident at once". Fixing one does not fix the other. Every lever tried so
far (packer, code moves, dropping the title) moves hundreds of bytes against
shortfalls of thousands.

## PART 1 -- rooms live PACKED in RAM, unpacked one room at a time

Today every room's data sits UNPACKED at $8000+ for the whole game: 18,906 bytes
to have 27 rooms available, when only one is ever on screen.

**The mechanism already exists in this port.** load_room unpacks the current
room's collision mask into CUR_ROOM_CMASK (384 bytes) on every room change, and
has since T0106. This extends that to the whole room record.

    rooms resident today, raw            18,906
    the same rooms packed (~65%)         ~12,300     frees ~6,600 immediately
    all remaining rooms, packed          ~7,411      instead of 11,402 raw
    total packed-resident, whole game    ~19,700  against ~25,700 available

That closes the RAM ceiling with room to spare, and changes the per-room price
from its raw size to its packed size for every room built from here.

**Cost:** one unpack per room change, of ~250-700 bytes. lz_unpack is already on
the boot path for far larger blocks; a room is a fraction of a frame.
**Risk to check first:** room records contain ABSOLUTE pointers -- each placement
is `fdb <sprite header>` plus x,y. Sprite headers live in the shared pool, which
stays resident and unmoved, so those pointers survive relocation. Rooms with
PRIVATE sprites would not; T0144 already removed all 27 of those, so the
precondition holds today and must be kept (a room that grows the pool is fine, a
room that keeps a private copy is not).

## PART 2 -- deliver in MULTIPLE PASSES, using BASIC as the loader

Even packed, ~19,700 bytes must reach RAM through a path that is 12,288 (the two
framebuffer windows) + 4,388 (holes) = 16,676 bytes at its absolute maximum, and
is nearly full. One pass cannot do it. The windows must be REUSED.

**The trick needs no ROM-cassette poking, no interrupt work, and no new hardware.
Split the tape into two files and let BASIC drive it:**

    CLOADM"DIZZY1" : EXEC &H<relocate> : CLOADM"DIZZY2" : EXEC &H<start>

`EXEC` calls our code as an ordinary subroutine and BASIC continues when it
RTSes. So the first EXEC engages all-RAM, unpacks/relocates everything the first
file put in the windows up to $8000+, **switches ROM back in, and returns**. BASIC
is then intact and loads the SECOND file into the very same windows. The second
EXEC relocates that payload and starts the game.

**Every mechanism this relies on is already proven in this port.** T0041's own
diagnostics established that toggling the SAM's TY bit moves $8000+ between ROM
and RAM, leaves $0000-$7FFF completely untouched in both directions, and that the
SAM and PIA decode stays live throughout. Returning to BASIC needs only that the
ROM is back and the stack is as we found it.

Capacity becomes 12,288 packed bytes PER PASS, and passes can be added. Two is
enough for the whole game; the design does not forbid a third.

**What this costs the player:** the load is two files instead of one. On real
hardware that is a continuous tape with a brief pause; whether it needs a second
PRESS PLAY depends on the setup, which is exactly what the spike must establish.

## Staging, each step independently verifiable

1. **Prove the BASIC round-trip** in isolation: a throwaway program that engages
   all-RAM, writes a sentinel above $8000, restores ROM, RTSes to BASIC, and lets
   BASIC print the sentinel back. This is the whole architecture in miniature and
   it either works or it does not. **Do this first; everything else depends on it.**
2. **Pack the room records** (Part 1) with the room set as it stands. Verify with
   tools/roomrender.py (renders from data, no emulator, no timing), the room
   sweep, and the differential holding at its reference.
3. **Split the build into two files** and move the newest staged block into file
   two. Nothing new gets built; the game must be byte-identical in behaviour.
4. **Then build rooms**, in batches, until the game is complete.

## What could still kill it

- **Step 1 failing.** If BASIC cannot survive the round trip, Part 2 falls back to
  the ROM-cassette route with its four unknowns, or to our own tape loader.
- **Tape behaviour on the user's own setup** (XRoar, MAME, real hardware) may
  differ on whether a second file needs manual intervention.
- **The six missing actor behaviours** (hawk, log, dozyfloat, miner, daisy,
  switch1) are a separate cost this architecture does not address; their code
  needs delivery space like anything else.

## LOADING ARCHITECTURE, REVISED -- single load, everything resident

**The two-file tape design above is REJECTED by the user: no loading rooms from
tape, one load, everything in memory.** That constraint turns out to be
satisfiable, and the answer is better than the one it replaces -- but only by
storing less, not by squeezing harder.

**The arithmetic for the WHOLE GAME (52 content rooms, 49 empty slots):**

    placements, every room in the game   2783 x 4 = 11,132 raw -> ~7,235 packed
    collision masks                      DERIVED, 0 bytes stored
    the 49 empty slots                   ~100 (ONE shared record, not 49 copies)
    new scenery frames                   ~600
    -------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHOLE-GAME ROOM TOTAL                ~7,935 packed

    today, for 27 rooms (staged A+B)      5,706 + 5,748 = 11,454 packed

**The entire game costs LESS than what 27 rooms cost today**, against a
single-pass delivery path of 12,288 (windows) + 4,388 (holes) = 16,676 bytes.
It fits, with thousands to spare for code, title and music.

### Change 1 -- DERIVE the collision mask at room load (saves 3,276 packed)

Every room currently ships a packed 384-byte mask (~63 packed each). But the port
ALREADY draws every placement when the room loads, and the mask is nothing more
than "which 4px cells does the non-decorative art cover". Build it from the same
placement walk that blits the room, into the CUR_ROOM_CMASK buffer that has
existed since T0106.

This is also closer to the original, which has no collision map at all --
checkattri reads the screen it just drew.

**The decorative flag has to ride along:** roompack skips placements whose
attribute has SOLID_DULL_BIT when building the mask (that is why room 52's 18
mirrored railings never collided). Placement x is a multiple of 4, bit 0 is
already T0142's mirror flag, so **bit 1 is free for "decorative"** -- zero extra
bytes per placement, same trick, same place.

Cost: one rasterise pass per room load, over the placements we are already
blitting. Risk: it must reproduce the current masks EXACTLY -- and that is
checkable offline with tools/roomrender.py plus a mask comparison, no emulator.

### Change 2 -- ONE shared record for the 49 empty rooms (saves ~4,753 raw)

48-49 of the original's rooms are empty map slots that exist only so a fall or a
walk passes through them. They do not need 49 copies of "nothing": one shared
empty-room record, referenced by every empty slot in room_desc_table.

### Change 3 -- rooms live PACKED in RAM, unpacked one at a time (Part 1 above)

Unchanged from the earlier design and still needed: it is what keeps 52 rooms'
data resident at once. The mechanism is T0106's, already in load_room.

### Order of work, each step verifiable on its own

1. **Change 1** on the current 27 rooms. Masks must come out byte-identical to the
   stored ones -- verify offline, then the room sweep and the differential.
2. **Change 2**, then build a handful of stub rooms to prove the shared record.
3. **Change 3**, verified with roomrender + sweep + differential.
4. **Then build the remaining 26 content rooms**, in batches.

The six missing actor behaviours (hawk, log, dozyfloat, miner, daisy, switch1)
remain a separate cost, unaffected by any of this.

## Change 1 PROVED OFFLINE -- every mask derives exactly, with one ordering catch

`tools/derive_cmask.py` rebuilds each room's collision mask from its PLACEMENTS
plus attribute bytes, decoding sprites straight from FRAMES.DAT with the same
decode/mirror functions verify_verbatim.py already uses, and diffs against the
LZ-unpacked mask actually shipped in target/roomNN_data.asm.

**All 27 built rooms: 0 bytes, 0 cells different.** No tuning, no special cases.
Run `tools/derive_cmask.py`; exit 0 means every room still derives.

**THE CATCH, and it is a real design constraint.** roompack's mask build is two
passes: pass 1 paints 8x8 attribute cells with each placement's effective
attribute (LAST WRITER WINS), pass 2 rasterises ink for non-dull placements
intersected with the FINAL attribute of the cell it lands in. The per-cell test
only changes the answer in 2 of 27 rooms -- room 67 (22 cells, the overdrawn
barrel main.rs already documents from a playtest) and room 23 (44 cells,
previously unknown) -- but pass 1's LAST-WRITER-WINS makes it **order-sensitive**.

The target ships placements Y-SORTED, for T0064's band-skip draw optimisation.
Deriving with that order instead of source order breaks **6 of 27 rooms** (23, 55,
56, 67, 68, 87 -- up to 56 cells in room 23). Ink drawing is order-independent
because it ORs; the attribute pass is not.

**Resolution for the 6809 side:** ship placements in SOURCE order and build the
y-band index AT ROOM LOAD by sorting into a separate index array. A ~70-entry
insertion sort once per room change is cheap, the draw path keeps its per-frame
optimisation (which T0128 just showed is worth protecting), and the attribute
pass gets the order it needs. Cost: a small sort plus ~70 bytes of RAM index,
against 63 packed bytes per room saved -- still a clear win, and it scales to
every future room.

**A landmine found on the way.** roompack's ink loop casts `t.pixel_x as usize`;
rooms 51 and 84 have 4 placements with NEGATIVE pixel_x (-4..-16, an original
portcullis mechanism this port's blit cannot clip). In a --release build the
negative wraps to a huge u64 and the later `+ px_i` wraps again, back to the
correct on-screen value -- so those placements are dropped from the DRAWN list
(roompack says so on stderr) yet still contribute to the collision mask. It works
by accident. **If roompack is ever built in debug this becomes an overflow
panic.** Do not "fix" the cast without checking what rooms 51 and 84 collide with.

## Change 1 runtime -- CORRECT but 40x TOO SLOW, and the fix is known

The 6809 derivation works: harness/cmaskverify.lua compares the derived mask
against the stored one in RAM for all 27 rooms and gets **23 byte-identical**.
The 2 that differ are rooms 51/84, and by exactly the documented landmine: their
negative-pixel_x placements are filtered out of the shipped placement table, so
NOTHING derived from that table can recover their contribution (2 and 4 bytes).
2 more rooms (39, 70) leave the warp room before the check settles, which the
Room sweep section already documents as the original's own behaviour.

**But it costs 189 frames -- 3.15 SECONDS -- per room load** (room 36, 63
placements). That is a visible freeze on every transition and it is not
shippable. Steady-state frame rate is untouched at 15.0; the cost is purely
one-time, which is why it also broke the differential: every exit case's frame
budget (150-220) is shorter than the freeze, so cases sample Dizzy's landing
before the mainloop resumes. MATCH went 200 -> 0 for that reason alone, not a
collision regression -- proved by rebuilding the pre-change commit in a worktree
(200 again) and by padding budgets +300 (recovers MATCH/SETTLED).

**The cause is rasterising PER PIXEL.** ~63 sprites x ~40 bytes x 8 bit-tests is
~20,000 pixel operations per room load.

**The fix, and it is the same trick T0137 already used for collision probes:
rasterise PER BYTE.** The mask is 4px cells and every placement x is a multiple
of 4, so one source byte (8 pixels) covers exactly TWO mask cells: test the high
nibble, set one cell; test the low nibble, set the next. That is ~2 operations
per byte instead of 8 bit-tests per byte -- roughly 40x fewer inner iterations,
which should put a room load at a handful of frames rather than 189.

**Also: the delivery budget is down to 3 bytes** because the new code grew while
the stored masks are still shipped (this step deliberately kept both). Removing
them is the next step and returns ~63 packed per room.

## Decision: remove the stored masks NOW, and inline the rasteriser with the space

**My "40x" estimate was wrong** and the agent was right to say so: 8 bit-tests
becoming 2 nibble-tests is 4x, and 4.1x is what it measured (189 -> 46 frames,
3.15s -> 0.77s). Correctness held exactly: 23 rooms byte-identical, 51/84 off by
the documented 2 and 4 bytes.

**Is deriving even worth it?** Checked, because 0.77s per transition is a real
cost. Whole-game delivery arithmetic:

    today's staged A+B                    11,454 packed
    + remaining placements (~5,132 raw)   + 3,335
    + 25 more stored masks @63            + 1,575
    + stubs deduped to one record         +   100
    + new frames                          +   400
    WHOLE GAME with stored masks          16,864 packed

    capacity (12,288 windows + 4,388 holes)  16,676
    less title/music/block C/block D         -4,371
    available for staged rooms               12,305

    SHORTFALL, stored masks                   4,559
    SHORTFALL, masks derived                  1,283

So deriving is NECESSARY (it removes 3,276) but not SUFFICIENT -- the last 1,283
is what dropping the title screen (2,666) would cover. The work stands.

**Why it is still slow, and why it cannot be fixed at 2 bytes of budget.** 46
frames over ~2,500 source bytes is **~270 cycles per byte** to test two nibbles
and set two bits. That is not the algorithm; it is a JSR per nibble plus address
recomputation. An inlined, row-hoisted version should be 5-8x faster again --
single-digit frames -- but inlining COSTS code space, and the delivery budget is
2 bytes because this step deliberately kept the stored masks as a comparison.

**The two problems solve each other: remove the stored masks (returns ~1,700
packed) and spend part of it inlining the rasteriser.**

**Rooms 51/84 need a decision when the stored masks go.** Their negative-pixel_x
placements are dropped from the shipped table, so the derived mask loses 2 and 4
bytes of collision the stored one has -- collision the port never DRAWS, because
blit cannot clip them, but which the original does have (it clips and draws the
visible part). Cheapest honest fix: ship those few cells as a tiny per-room mask
patch. 6 bytes total against 1,700 recovered.

## T0166 -- stored masks removed, rasteriser inlined, rooms 51/84 patched

**Delivery budget (tools/memaudit.py target/room36.bin), before/after in
this one session, everything else held constant:**

    before (stored + derived masks both shipped, T0163's state)   530 packed
    after  (stored masks gone, rasteriser inlined+hoisted)       2784 packed
    net change                                                  +2254 packed

roompack (tools/roompack/src/main.rs) no longer emits `room_cmask_lz` at
all -- the whole attr_cells/cmask rasterise-and-LZSS-pack block is gone,
and the room descriptor record is one field shorter (`room_cmask_ptr`
removed; ROOM_DESC_LEN shrinks with it). room36.asm's load_room no
longer unpacks a stored mask; CUR_ROOM_CMASK is now the ONLY mask
buffer, filled in place by derive_room_cmask (which used to fill a
separate DERIVED_ROOM_CMASK alongside the stored one for comparison --
that second 384-byte buffer is gone too, RAM only, not ROM budget, but
one less thing to keep in sync).

**Runtime cost, harness/cmasktime.lua, room 36 (63 placements, 48
solid), same three hoists/inlines applied in sequence:**

    T0163 baseline (per-nibble, row-hoisted CMASK addr only)   46 frames
    + hoist ATTR_CELLS row addr (was a MUL per ink nibble)     44 frames
    + hoist mirror flag + basecc (dc_xm>>2, was relcell*4+xm
      pixel-domain shift/add/shift chain per ink nibble)       43 frames
    + inline dc_p2_cell (remove JSR/RTS per ink nibble)        42 frames

**This did NOT reach single-digit frames, and I'm reporting that
honestly rather than declaring the target met.** A one-off profiling
script (bucketing PC samples by routine range, not kept -- not a
harness) showed pass2 rasterisation (dc_pass2_place's own body) is
~29 of the 42 frames; pass1 (dc_pass1_place, walked for ALL 63
placements including dull ones) plus dc_load_placement is ~4; the
y-sort/band-build (rd_sortplaces) is ~4-9 (some of that bucket is
sp_addr, whose code happens to sit between dc_patch and rd_sortplaces
in memory and gets miscounted into the wrong bucket -- a labelling
quirk of the profiling script, not a real cost). **Pass2 is still the
dominant cost even after inlining and hoisting every redundant
per-nibble computation this session found** -- 2571 ink-bearing nibbles
for room 36 alone, each still costing on the order of 90-100 cycles for
the ATTR-skip + CUR_ROOM_CMASK-set sequence itself (not the addressing
around it, which is what got hoisted/inlined). Getting further would
need a different representation, not more micro-optimisation of this
one -- e.g. a precomputed nibble->cell-pair OR-mask table indexed
straight off the source byte (trading code space for removing the
bounds-check/mirror-reflect/shift chain entirely), or accepting a
coarser mask granularity. Neither attempted this session.

**Rooms 51/84, the negative-pixel_x landmine, patched (not derived):**
their off-screen-at-spawn placements are dropped from the SHIPPED
room_placements table by roompack's own `(0..256).contains(pixel_x)`
filter, so nothing walking that table can recover their contribution.
Computed the exact patch by diffing tools/derive_cmask.py's own "full"
derivation (all placements, including negative pixel_x, exactly
roompack's algorithm) against a second derivation that drops the same
placements the shipped table drops, keeping the FULL attribute-
inheritance chain intact for both (dropping an entry from the actual
`things` list, rather than skipping it in place, corrupts
`same_colour_as_previous` for everything after it -- tried that first,
got 70 bytes of "diff" for room 84 instead of the real 4; the fix was a
custom derive that skips indices during the walk but computes
`effective_attrs` from the untouched full list). Result: room 51 needs
2 bytes back (offsets 272/280, OR $f0/$10), room 84 needs 4 (offsets
256/264/272/280, all OR $f0) -- 6 bytes total, matching the number this
session's plan already predicted. Both are purely ADDITIVE (never a bit
that needs clearing) so a small hardcoded OR-table (dc_patch, 4
bytes/entry: room, offset, orbyte) applied once after derive_room_cmask
is exact and cheap. Verified: both rooms PASS harness/cmaskverify.lua's
byte-for-byte check with the patch applied.

**harness/cmaskverify.lua rewritten** (its whole reason for existing --
diffing CUR_ROOM_CMASK against DERIVED_ROOM_CMASK -- went away with the
second buffer): now diffs CUR_ROOM_CMASK against an EXTERNAL ground
truth, `target/cmask_expected.bin` (tools/derive_cmask.py
--dump-expected, 27 rooms x 384 bytes, BUILT_ROOMS order), regenerated
offline from rooms.json + FRAMES.DAT rather than from anything the
target ships. **Result: 24 of 26 tested rooms PASS byte-for-byte
(including 51 and 84); 39/70 SKIP** (the same documented original-
behaviour drift T0163 already found: Dizzy leaves those rooms before
the settle window, not a Change 1 regression).

**Found in the process, out of scope for this task, recorded so nobody
re-derives it: room 2 is not a real room.** It is 4 flame placements
used ONLY as data for room 36's fire-pit overlay (`draw_fire_overlay`,
see this file's "the real fire mechanic" entry) and has NO entry in
room36.asm's `room_desc_table` -- `load_room` can never load it
(`lr_unknown`, leaving the previous room's CUR_ROOM_CMASK untouched).
tools/derive_cmask.py's BUILT_ROOMS and the OLD cmaskverify.lua's ROOMS
both included it anyway. The old harness's design (diff CUR_ROOM_CMASK
against DERIVED_ROOM_CMASK, both filled by the SAME load_room call)
made this invisible: forcing cur_room=2 leaves both buffers stale from
whatever the previous room left, so they agreed BY COINCIDENCE and the
old harness reported PASS for a room that was never actually derived.
Comparing against an independent ground truth (this session's rewrite)
turned that into a FAIL (120/384 bytes), which is what surfaced it.
Fixed by excluding room 2 from cmaskverify.lua's own ROOMS list (with
this explanation inline) -- NOT by wiring room 2 into room_desc_table,
which would be a real behaviour change nobody asked for and might not
even be valid (nothing suggests Dizzy should ever stand IN the fire pit
as its own room).

## Change 1 checkpoint -- masks gone, budget won, speed still the blocker

**Won:** delivery budget **530 -> 2,784 packed bytes** (+2,254, better than the
~1,700 predicted, because deleting the stored-mask emission and the comparison
buffer cost more than the inlining added). Mask correctness proven independently:
cmaskverify now diffs the live CUR_ROOM_CMASK against tools/derive_cmask.py's own
offline derivation, and **24 of 26 rooms are byte-exact including the patched 51
and 84**; 39/70 skip by their documented drift.

**Not won: 46 -> 42 frames only.** Inlining the per-nibble call and hoisting the
ATTR row address bought 4 frames, not the 5-8x I predicted. Profiling says pass 2
is still ~29 of the 42 frames and each of room 36's 2,571 ink nibbles costs
~90-100 cycles in the ATTR-skip + mask-set sequence itself. **That is the work,
not the overhead -- my diagnosis was wrong.**

**Differential fell 200 -> 178**, and PORT-STUCK rose 24 -> 38, all of them jumps
(the same signature T0162 documents). Consistent with the 42-frame freeze eating
case budgets across multi-hop cases rather than a collision fault, since the mask
is independently proven correct -- but it is a real open regression, not a
rounding error.

**THE BETTER FIX, and it is the original idea done properly: fold pass 2 into the
room's own draw.** At room load the port ALREADY blits every placement into the
framebuffer -- it walks exactly the same sprite bytes pass 2 walks. Setting the
mask cells while that byte is already loaded costs a few cycles on top of work
being done anyway, instead of a second full traversal. Pass 1 stays separate and
is cheap (2 frames). Gate it to the load-time FULL redraw, never the per-frame
damage-rect redraws.

**Also found, and worth keeping:** room 2 is not a real room -- 4 flame
placements used as data for room 36's fire pit, with no room_desc_table entry, so
load_room can never load it. The OLD harness compared two buffers both filled by
the same load_room call, so room 2 sat stale-equal and reported PASS. Comparing
against an independent ground truth turned it into a real failure. A test that
compares a thing to itself will agree forever.

**Unattributed:** roomsweep now flags room 54 at (128,176) with 1 death and 80%
floor, where the historical run had 98% and none. Room 54's own mask is
byte-exact, so it is probably the warp spot's fall path crossing the dragon's
hazard -- but nobody has proven that. Do not dismiss it.

## The fold was reverted, and the differential is NOT a timing-change oracle

**Fold result:** correct (cmaskverify still 24/26, rooms 51/84 included) but 42 ->
**41 frames** -- one frame -- and it cost 125 packed bytes. It removed only the
separate traversal's placement-decode overhead, not the per-nibble rasterisation,
because the pass-2 routine was CALLED from the draw loop rather than merged into
blit's own byte loop. Merging into blit was judged too risky to attempt unasked,
and that judgement was right: blit is the ubiquitous per-frame render path.
**Reverted** -- 125 bytes for 1 frame is not a trade worth keeping.

**THE METHODOLOGICAL FINDING, which matters more than the fold.** The exit
differential moved 178 -> 172 and PORT-STUCK 38 -> 53 for a ONE-FRAME change in
room-load cost, scattered across a dozen unrelated rooms with no locality. The
same instability appeared earlier at 46 -> 42 frames (200 -> 178, "all jumps").

**The differential is chaotically sensitive to per-transition frame counts.** It
is a scripted-input harness: shift when the mainloop resumes and later keypresses
land on different frames, across every multi-hop case at once. So:

- It remains a good oracle for LOGIC changes at constant timing (it caught the
  T0137 lift work, T0142's mirroring, T0143's collision shapes).
- It is NOT a valid oracle for changes that alter frame pacing, and reading a
  drop as "a regression" -- which I did twice today -- is a mistake. The mask is
  independently proven byte-exact by cmaskverify against an offline derivation;
  that is the evidence that counts here.
- Anything that changes room-load cost must be judged by cmaskverify plus the
  behavioural harnesses, and the differential re-baselined afterwards rather than
  compared across the change.

**Still open: 42 frames (0.7s) per room load.** Next idea, untried: a table-driven
rasteriser. Index a 256-entry table by the source byte to get which of its two
4px cells carry ink, then OR that pattern into the mask -- roughly one lookup and
one OR per byte instead of ~90-100 cycles per nibble. That is a ~5x candidate
that does not touch blit. Budget is 2,784 packed, so a 256-byte table is
affordable now in a way it was not two rounds ago.

## 42 frames is the FLOOR for this rasteriser -- four rounds, measured

    per-pixel                                189 frames
    per-byte nibble tests                     46
    inline the per-nibble call, hoist rows    42
    call it from the draw loop instead        41   (reverted, cost 125 bytes)
    cc-indexed bit/byte-offset table          40   (reverted, cost 117 bytes)

**I over-predicted all four rounds** (40x, then 5-8x, then "nearly free", then
single digits). Each measurement came back smaller. The reason is in the last
agent's breakdown of the ~90-100 cycles per ink nibble:

1. **mirror-reflect + bounds-check + basecc add** (~8-10 instructions) -- depends
   on runtime placement state, not on the source byte, so no static table reaches it.
2. **the ATTR decorative-cell test** (~5 instructions) -- runs per NIBBLE although
   ATTR granularity is 8x8 pixels, so one test could serve both nibbles of a byte
   when they fall in the same attribute cell. **This is the only remaining
   candidate worth real money (~20%)**, and it is a control-flow change needing
   its own correctness proof (parity of basecc, interaction with mirroring, the
   last-byte padding nibble) -- not a lookup table.
3. **the mask-set tail** -- the smallest third, and the only part a table reaches,
   which is exactly why the table bought 2 frames.

Both reverted: 125 bytes for 1 frame and 117 bytes for 2 frames are bad trades
when the delivery budget is the thing actually gating the game. **The floor stands
at 42 frames / 0.70s per room load.**

Whether that is shippable is a judgement about the game, not the code: it is a
visible hitch on every room transition, against a port that previously had none.
The alternative is going back to stored masks, which costs 3,276 packed bytes
across the game -- the very thing Change 1 exists to avoid.

  sprite size/complexity too. Room 60 (a volcano scene, lots of large
  rock/terrain sprites) is denser than room 36 per solid placement.
  **This answers the open "does it scale badly" question from the
  floor entry above: yes, for a content-dense room it can exceed room
  36's own number**, not just track it.

**Projection.** Budget remaining: 1,166 packed bytes. Measured cost
this session: 423/524/671 (avg ~539, worst 671). 26 - 3 = 23 content
rooms remain unbuilt. At the average, **~2.2 more rooms fit**; at this
session's worst (671, room 60), **~1.7**. Either way: **not all 23
remaining rooms fit in the current budget** -- roughly 2 more at best,
then the memory work (T0121's remaining levers: better compression, or
the pass-2 representation change flagged in "42 frames is the FLOOR")
has to happen again before the game can hold the rest of its own
content. This was already implied by the T0159 line's own "~2-3 more
rooms" note; this session's measurement confirms the same order of
magnitude in the post-Change-1 regime rather than finding it improved.

Change 1 removed the shipped `room_cmask_lz`, so roomview.py's `--surfaces` (and
`start_pos.py`, which imports its `load_mask`) were reading data that no longer

attempt duplicated the FRAMES.DAT decode and the two-pass derivation into
roomview -- ~180 lines -- and described the result as "guaranteed to stay in sync
forever", which is exactly backwards: two copies of a subtle two-pass rule drift,
and then there are two offline ground truths and no way to tell which is right.
That matters more here than usual, because derive_cmask.py IS the ground truth
harness/cmaskverify.lua checks the live 6809 buffer against.

Verified: roomview's mask is bit-identical to derive_cmask's for rooms 36, 60 and
22 (752, 975 and 272 solid cells); `--surfaces` works again for old and new rooms
alike; start_pos.py works through it; an unbuilt room exits non-zero instead of
printing something stale. Zero copies of the algorithm remain in roomview.

Note `derive()` returns a **(mask, attr_cells) tuple** -- taking it as a bytes
object is a TypeError, which is how the duplication was caught.

## T0166 -- the room-54 "dragon death" is the DEATH BOX, not the dragon

Traced: `killed` reads 1 continuously from the warp through load_room and the
respawn tune; `dragon_fire` stays 0 and `death_msg` stays $0000 throughout, so
nothing ever called kill_dizzy. A canary that forces `killed=0` on arrival makes
the stage pass completely (swing 0..16, fire seen), proving the dragon's own
logic was never at fault.

**The mechanism is the harness, and Change 1's longer room load is what exposed
it.** actorlife's `warp()` pokes `killed=1` to force a respawn -- which produces
a REAL death, including the death box, which blocks on a keypress. The teleport
stage presses SPACE only until it has seen three clear ticks, then stops. With
room loads now taking 42+ frames (room 54 has 57 placements, the most of any
built room), the box is still up when the pressing stops, so nothing dismisses
it, `killed` never clears, and the dragon never gets to animate.

That also explains the gradient the diagnosis found: room 53 (29 placements) never
stalls, room 50 (54) self-heals in ~4 ticks, room 54 (57) never recovers.

**The agent's reading was "leans real engine race"; I think that is wrong.**
`warp()` pokes once, not per frame, and the canary shows nothing re-kills him --
both consistent with the game simply sitting in the death box. A real player
dying in room 54 dismisses the box themselves and respawns normally.

Fixed in harness/actorlife.lua by clearing `killed` once on arrival, which is
warp bookkeeping and touches none of the assertions (swing/fire are untouched,
so the stage can still fail if the dragon stops animating). **A cleaner fix
exists and is worth doing next time this is opened: gate dismissal on
`msg_active`, the state byte T0154 added for exactly this -- press until the box
is really gone instead of counting ticks.**

**Break-proof still owed** (needs a rebuild, so it was not run): neuter
update_dragon's swing advance in target/dragon_code.asm, rebuild, and confirm the
stage fails with `swing_changed=false` -- NOT with "died settling into room 54".
If it fails with the old message, this fix regressed.

## T0172 — the title screen froze with no music, and every harness was green

**Symptom (playtest, not a test):** the game reaches the title screen and
freezes there; no music. `harness/titleverify.lua` passed the whole time.

**Cause.** `room36.asm`'s `RELOC_BOOT_BYTES` pad (T0153, which pins the
STAGE_GEN and STAGE_LZ boot branches to the same byte count so no symbol
drifts between passes) padded with **`rmb`**. `rmb` reserves space without
emitting bytes, so the DECB output *splits into two segments there* —
`$0E00+82`, then `$0E5E+2561`, with `$0E52-$0E5D` **not written by the
loader at all**. Boot falls straight through those 12 bytes and executes
whatever the machine happened to have in RAM.

MAME's `coco2b` clears RAM to something benign, so it booted correctly for
months. xroar's `coco2bus` does not: the garbage there decoded into a store
that cleared **PIA0 CRA bit 2** ($FF01: `$34` → `$BB`), the DDR-select bit.
After that `lda $ff00` reads **DDRA (= $00)**, not the keyboard — so
*every* key scans as held down. Hence both symptoms at once: the title
mixer checks SPACE, sees it down, returns immediately (no music), and
`ti_release`, which waits for SPACE to come back *up*, spins forever.

**Fix.** Pad with `fill $12,N` (NOP) instead of `rmb`, guarded by `ifne` so
a zero-length pad is legal. The load file is then one contiguous segment
and the pad is executable by construction.

**Two break-proofs, because this class of bug hides:**

1. `tools/memaudit.py` now enumerates every gap in the DECB load file,
   resolves the symbol at each gap's start from `room36.map`, and **fails
   the build** for any gap not in `KNOWN_DATA_GAPS` (`solid_list`,
   `blit_revbuf`, `rat_sv_col`, `inv`, `coin_ram` — all `rmb` for
   variables, never executed). Verified by reverting the `fill`: it
   reports `$0e52 +12 at _rb_end` and exits 1.
2. `harness/bootreal.py` (new) boots **the real DECB load path** under
   xroar (`-run`), not a poke-into-RAM harness, and asserts (a) $FF01 keeps
   its DDR-select bit and (b) the sampled PC stays inside the mixer blob
   with no key pressed. On the reverted build it prints exactly the user's
   two symptoms.

**The general lesson, and it is the important part:** every MAME harness
here writes the DECB segments into RAM itself. That silently writes the
bytes an `rmb` hole leaves out, and it inherits MAME's RAM-clear pattern.
**No test that loads the binary by hand can see a load-path bug.** That is
why 20-odd green harnesses coexisted with a game that would not boot.

**xroar gdb-stub gotchas** (cost an hour; `harness/bootreal.py` encodes
them): the stub does not answer `?`; and with the rate limiter ON in a
headless run (no audio device) it answers `g` but never answers the `0x03`
interrupt, so every halt times out — `-no-ratelimit` is *required*, not an
optimisation, which is why bootreal's sleeps are fractions of a second.

## T0175 — room 51's lever: where it can be thrown from, and why not from the ledge

Playtest: "dizzy cannot trigger the lever on 51." **The mechanism is not
broken** — it is a reach question, and the answer is geometric.

The lever is the `portswitch` actor, `fcb 51,1,136,78,122,0,0,69`:
routine 1 (ROU_PORTSWITCH), **x=136, y=78**, frame 122. Colour 69 has bit
6 set, so `build_solid_actors` treats it as decorative — it is NOT solid
and does not block Dizzy. `draw_actors` does not filter on that bit, so it
is still drawn.

Room 51's relevant geometry (`tools/roomview.py 51`, cells 4px):

| y | solid x | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| 72–84 | 96–135 | the ledge. Its TOP is y=72 |
| 88–92 | 112–199 | the lower floor. Only **exposed from x=136** rightward — left of that the ledge sits on top of it |

So the lever hangs off the ledge's right face: **above** the lower floor,
**below** the ledge top.

**Measured trigger window** (sweep of dizzy_x at y=88, pressing DOWN and
reading the switch's v1): **x=120..148, 32px wide.** The part Dizzy can
actually stand in is **x=136..148**, since the ledge covers x<=135 at that
height. Walking LEFT along the lower floor he comes to rest at exactly
x=136 — inside the window — and DOWN throws it. Verified end to end.

**Standing on the ledge does NOT throw it, and that is faithful.**
`actor_hit` rejects any actor whose top is at or below Dizzy's feet
(`lda ah_ay / cmpa dizzy_y / bhs ah_miss`): 78 >= 72. X-ALL.TXT's
`collidewithdizzy16` does the same thing — its vertical half computes
`actor_y - (dizzy_y - eggheight)` = 78 - 54 = 24 and rejects on
`cp eggheight` with eggheight=18. Both miss. The original is not more
forgiving here; do not "fix" this without deciding it is a deliberate
deviation.

**`pickup` in the original is the KEY-PRESS flag, not the held item.**
`portswitchrou` opens `ld a,(pickup) / and a / ret z` and later clears it
with `xor a / ld (pickup),a` — that is the one-shot guard on the pickup
key, which this port maps to DOWN. So gating the throw on `keyflags`
bit 1 is right, and it does NOT require Dizzy to be carrying anything.

**DOWN at the lever also opens the inventory** (try_pickup's `tp_noninv`
fallback, since there is nothing there to pick up). try_pickup runs at
room36.asm:850 and update_portcullis at :879, so the inventory box comes
up first and the lever message second — both in the same pass, and the
throw still lands. Confirmed in the probe, which goes through exactly that
path. Worth knowing before reading "the inventory opened instead" as a
failure.

### The test that could not have caught this

`harness/portcullis.lua` respawns Dizzy at x=140 — **already inside the
hit box** — and presses DOWN. That proves the switch→gate wiring and
nothing about reachability. Same shape as T0172's load-path blindness.
`harness/lever51.lua` (new) WALKS instead: holds LEFT until Dizzy stops,
asserts he came to rest inside x=136..148, asserts DOWN throws it, and
carries the ledge position as a negative control.

**Its own trap, hit on the first run:** the throw is one-shot and
permanent ("it breaks") and `actor_ram` is NOT reloaded by a respawn, so
the second case read the first case's `v1=1` and passed a lever it had
never touched. `start_case` now un-throws the switch and parks the gate
before each case. That first run is also the harness's break-proof — it
reported FAIL.

## T0176 — "jumps to a higher room always fall short": the arc is fine, the ARRIVAL is the suspect

Playtest: "rooms where you need to jump from an edge to a higher room,
the jumps always fall short — e.g. the left edge of the dining table to a
rock ledge in the room above." Reported across several rooms, so treat it
as systemic, not one room's geometry.

**The jump arc is NOT the problem. Measured, not assumed.** Sampling
`dizzy_y` through a single UP tap on room 36's floor:

```
176 -> 169 -> 163 -> 158 -> 154 -> 151 -> 149 -> 148     rise = 28px
deltas: 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1
```

That is X-ALL.TXT exactly. `tryjump` sets `dy=-8`; the vertical step does
`ld a,(dy) / inc a / ld (dy),a` **before** moving `|dy|` pixels, so the
first move is 7, not 8, and the total is 7+6+5+4+3+2+1 = **28**. The port
matches per-tick, not just in total. (The comment above TOP_TRANSITION_Y
saying "a jump rises 32px" is wrong — it is 28. Harmless there, since the
argument it supports only needs "less than 40".)

**The arithmetic that looks wrong.** `goneup` fires when feet would pass
below TOP_TRANSITION_Y=66, and arrival is `y+118` computed from the
PRE-decrement y — so arrival is **y=184**, with only the tail of the rise
left. Worked example, jumping from room 68's table top (y=88):

| tick | dy | y after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | -7 | 81 |
| 2 | -6 | 75 |
| 3 | -5 | 70 |
| 4 | -4 | 66 |
| 5 | -3 | crosses 66 -> **goneup, arrive y=184** |

That leaves ~5px of rise (2 of tick 5, then 2, then 1) — apex about
y=179 in the room above. **BOT_TRANSITION_Y is 182.** So unless there is
floor directly under the arrival x, Dizzy falls the 5px straight back
through 182 and `gonedown` returns him to the room he came from. From the
player's seat that is exactly "the jump fell short".

Room 84 (above 68) has floor at y=176..183 spanning x=8..31 and x=80..255,
with a **hole at x=32..79** — and room 68's own ceiling gap, the only
place a jump is not blocked, is x=32..76. So the one x-range you can rise
through is the one x-range with nothing to land on.

**What is NOT yet established, and must be before changing anything:**
whether the ORIGINAL bounces the same way. On paper it does — same 28px
arc, same 66, same `y+118`, same 182 — which would make this faithful and
the real route something else entirely. But "on paper it does" is exactly
the reasoning that has been wrong here before, and the user reports it
across several rooms. **Settle it with the differential** (harness/
exits_zx.lua + the committed baselines), not with more reading: drive the
same up-jump in the ZX original and in the port and compare where Dizzy
ends up. This is the same territory as the open T0162 (up-transition
re-entry, 23 cases) and should probably absorb it.

**Room 68's left-edge block is real, by the way.** The solid at y=48..55,
x=8..31 over the table's left edge is `frame 134 @ pixel_x=8, y=48` with
`same_colour_as_previous`, inheriting `attribute_byte=2` — bit 6 clear, so
solid in the original too, not a decorative sprite this port got wrong.
The clear run to jump through is x=32..76.

## T0177 — the up-jump differential was measuring the harness, not the port

Following T0176 ("jumps to a higher room fall short"), the committed
baselines say the port refuses **70 of 258** jump cases the original
makes — across 13 rooms, and lopsided: JUMPLEFT 52, JUMPRIGHT 13, plain
JUMP 5. That looked like the systemic bug. **It was the test.**

`harness/exits_port.lua`'s `stand` stage gives up after 120 frames and
enters `run` with `c.stood=0`. `run` then presses UP for at most **16
frames from the start of the move** — so on a slow settle the entire UP
window was spent MID-AIR, where the jump is correctly refused (it needs
`dizzy_floor`, exactly as X-ALL.TXT's `tryjump` does). The case walked
instead and logged `jumped=0`, which reads as "the port refuses this
jump".

Even with `stood=1` a 16-frame press often failed, and my first
explanation for that was a sampling race (keys read once per mainloop
pass, heavy room = long pass). **That explanation is wrong and was
measured wrong.** `harness/rate.lua` says room 68 runs at **15.0
passes/sec, identical to room 36 and room 84** — a pass is ~67ms, so a
16-frame (267ms) press spans about four passes and cannot be missed.

The real reason is simpler: at the start of `run` the mainloop is often
BLOCKED — the respawn plays the death and new-life tunes and puts up a
message box, and `msg_wait_dismiss` does not return until SPACE. No
passes run at all, so the UP window elapses in wall-clock frames while
the game is frozen, and by the time the game is live again UP is
released. Starting the window on the first grounded frame and widening it
to 60 fixes exactly that.

**With that fixed, the port matches the original on the user's own case:**

| case | start | strat | PORT rooms | ZX rooms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 68u6 | 68@32,88 | JUMP | 68>84>68 | 68>84>68 |
| 68u9 | 68@56,88 | JUMP | 68>84>68 | 68>84>68 |
| 68u10 | 68@56,88 | JUMPLEFT | 68>84 | 68>84 |

And a hand-driven probe of 68u10 lands Dizzy at **84@24,176** against the
original's **84@24,175** — the known 1px feet offset, on the rock ledge.
So the arc (28px, T0176), the transition, and the landing all agree.

`68>84>68` for a STRAIGHT-up jump is **correct**: room 84's floor has a
hole at x=32..79, which is exactly room 68's only unblocked ceiling gap,
so jumping straight up drops you back. You have to jump LEFT to drift
onto the floor at x=8..31. The original does the same.

### Corrected: there is no input-latency bug here

I filed one (and a task) off the 16-frame observation before measuring
the pass rate. Room 68 is 15.0 passes/sec, the same as everywhere else,
so a normal keypress is sampled several times and nothing is being lost.
Task withdrawn. Recording it because the wrong version was written down
first, and the lesson is the usual one: the pass-rate number took one
run, and I reasoned for several paragraphs before getting it.

**The baselines are now stale for every jump case** — they were produced
by the broken press. Re-run both sides before quoting any jump number.

## T0180 — the reported jump is the LEFT transition (room 67), not the up one

Playtest screenshots settle what T0176/T0177 had wrong from the start.
Dizzy jumps from the left edge of the banquet-hall table and lands in
**"THE WEST WING" = room 67 = roomno-1**, the room to the LEFT. Room 84
("THE CASTLE STAIRCASE") is the room above and is not involved. So the
mechanism under test is `goneleft` crossed **mid-jump**, not `goneup`.

The player's own reading — "it lost the height of the table" — matches
what the screenshot shows: he ends up on the floor at the bottom of room
67 instead of on the ledge the red arrow points at.

**Room 67's geometry explains the fall, and names the target.** At the
arrival x (`goneleft` sets x:=224) there is **no floor at table height**:

```
y 88 .................######################.........####........####
y 92 ................########################........####........####
      cols 48-51 = x=192..207     cols 60-63 = x=240..255
```

x=224 (col 56) is clear at y=88 and below. The ledge the arrow points at
is **x=192..207**. So arriving at x=224 and simply falling is correct for
that x — you have to keep drifting LEFT after the transition to reach
192..207. The original does exactly that: `68u4` (68@8,88 JUMPLEFT) gives
ZX `68>67 land=67@224,87 final=67@204,111`, i.e. it arrives at 224 at
table height and drifts to the ledge at x=204.

**The port has never been tested on this.** Its own baseline line for the
same case is:

```
EXIT id=68u4 ... rooms=68>67 land=67@224,88 ... final=67@224,88 jumped=0
```

`jumped=0` — the old broken UP press (T0177) meant the port WALKED off
the table instead of jumping, so that line describes a walk, not a jump.
Every 68u*/68l* JUMPLEFT verdict has the same problem.

**Next step, concretely:** re-run `68u4`/`68u7` with the fixed press and
compare the drift after the transition. The mechanism to scrutinise is
whether `dizzy_dir` keeps carrying Dizzy left on the passes AFTER
`room_transition_left` — the code says it should (`rt_horizontal` ends
`lbra ml_dirdone`, y and dy untouched, and `dizzy_dir` is latched, only
rewritten by the grounded `ml_keys_floor` branch), and a trace of the UP
case across `goneup` does keep drifting (x 36->32->28->24). But that is
the up path; the left path is unverified.

**Probe note / dead end:** a standalone respawn probe into room 68 at
x=8..32 never settles — Dizzy dies repeatedly there, and the ORIGINAL
dies too (`killed=1` on both 68u4 and 68u7). `harness/exits_port.lua`
also hangs on those cases with no output at all, which is its own bug
(no per-case timeout when a case never reaches a verdict — cf. T0174,
the same shape in cmaskverify). Fix that before trying again.

### T0180 resolved: the port matches the original; the direction must be held AT TAKEOFF

With the T0177 press fix and T0181's harness fixes, the reported case runs
clean and agrees with the original:

| case | start | PORT | ZX |
|---|---|---|---|
| 68u4 | 68@8,88 JUMPLEFT | 68>67 final **67@208,112** | 68>67 final **67@204,111** |
| 68u7 | 68@32,88 JUMPLEFT | 68>67 final 67@208,112 | 68>67 final 67@204,111 |
| 68u10 | 68@56,88 JUMPLEFT | 68>84 final 84@24,176 | 68>84 final 84@24,175 |

67@208,112 IS the ledge the playtest screenshot's red arrow points at.
The 4px/1px deltas are the walk-step granularity and the known feet
offset.

**What changes the outcome is WHEN the direction key is held.** Same three
cases with LEFT pressed 25 frames AFTER the jump starts:

| case | LEFT at takeoff | LEFT pressed late |
|---|---|---|
| 68u4 | 67@208,112 (the ledge) | 67@224,88 (stranded at the arrival x) |
| 68u7 | 67@208,112 | 68>84>68, back where it started |
| 68u10 | 84@24,176 | 68>84>68, back where it started |

That is T0136's air-control latch doing exactly what X-ALL.TXT does:
`bettercheckkeys` reads keys only on a floor, and `cantstop` then applies
the LATCHED left/right for the whole arc. No mid-air steering, in either
version. So a jump made by pressing UP first and steering afterwards
cannot reach the ledge — and lands you at the bottom, which is what the
screenshot shows.

**Not a port bug.** If we ever want it friendlier, the deviation would be
to re-latch `dizzy_dir` mid-air; that is a design call, not a fix.

### Two harness bugs fixed getting here (T0181)

1. **The boot gate hardcoded room 36.** A build made with `START_ROOM=N`
   — which is what a debug/playtest build in `target/` often is — never
   opened it, and the run produced **no output at all**. That reads as
   "the harness hangs" and cost a round. Now any live room opens it;
   every case warps anyway.
2. **The `warp` stage had no timeout**, unlike every other stage. A case
   whose predecessor keeps dying could spin there and suppress the whole
   run's output, including verdicts already earned. Now prints
   `WARP-STUCK` and moves on.

**Do not rebuild `target/room36.bin` without checking what is in it** —
`grep 'Symbol: START_ROOM' target/room36.map`. It may be the user's own
debug build, and `tools/stage_pack.sh` overwrites it in place.

start at y=40/48/88/128/176. The dining table is at **y=148, x=48..167**
(`tools/roomview.py 68`). The thing at y=88 that earlier work jumped from
is the railing shelf, a different platform — which is why T0180's "the

Three new cases from the table's left edge, JUMPLEFT, both sides with the
jump press fixed (T0177 for the port, T0182 for the ZX side — the ZX
harness had the identical bug: a 12-frame window from the START of the
move, so unsettled cases logged `jumped=0`, a verdict about nothing):

| case | PORT | ZX ORIGINAL |
|---|---|---|
| TBL48 68@48,148 | `68>67>51` final 51@168,182 (air) | `68>67>51` final 51@156,85 (air) |
| TBL52 68@52,148 | **NEVER-ARRIVED** (room 51, x=168, y=88) | `68>67>51` final 51@168,67 (air) |
| TBL56 68@56,148 | `68>67` land 67@212,168, final 67@172,182 (air) | `68>67>51` final 51@168,67 (air) |

2. **TBL52**: the port NEVER-ARRIVED — it ends up in room 51 at x=168,

### Process note, because this cost five rounds

Three wrong diagnoses in a row, each confidently argued: (a) the
up-transition arrival y, (b) a key-sampling race, (c) "the port matches
the original" from the wrong platform. Every one of them was reasoning
running ahead of a cheap measurement that was available the whole time —
`roomview.py 68` would have located the table in seconds, and the
playtest screenshot showed it. **When a playtest names a place ("the
dining table"), find that place in the collision mask BEFORE forming any
theory about the mechanism.**

## T0185 — CONFIRMED: jumps across screens fall short. Within-room jumps do not.

The playtest said "this is not the only case where a jump across screens
falls short, there is a problem here." It is right, and the split is
sharp. Computed from the committed baselines, restricted to cases where
**both sides really jumped** (`jumped=1`, i.e. not the T0177/T0182
press bug):

| | cases | divergent |
|---|---|---|
| jumps that stay in one room | 39 | **0** — horizontal travel is pixel-identical, mean 12.6px both sides |
| jumps that cross a screen | 79 | **18** (a 19th, 36u7, is a room this build does not have) |

So the arc is not the problem — T0176's 28px measurement stands, and
within a room the port and the original move Dizzy the same distance to
the pixel. **Everything that goes wrong, goes wrong at the crossing.**

Seven of the eighteen are literally "falls short" — the original carries
Dizzy over a boundary and the port leaves him behind:

| case | start | strat | PORT | ZX ORIGINAL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35u6 | 35@228,80 | JUMP | `35` | `35>36` |
| 36u4 | 36@116,80 | JUMPRIGHT | `36` | `36>2>36` |
| 39u14 | 39@8,96 | JUMPLEFT | `39` | `39>23` |
| 51u13 | 51@136,88 | JUMPRIGHT | `51>67>51` | `51>67>51>52` |
| 53u7 | 53@56,88 | JUMPRIGHT | `53>69` | `53>69>53` |
| 83r3 | 83@208,176 | JUMPRIGHT | `83>84` | `83>84>68` |
| 84u22 | 84@152,88 | JUMPRIGHT | `84` | `84>100>84` |
| 86r0 | 86@216,176 | JUMPRIGHT | `86>87>71` | `86>87>71>87>71` |

Four more cross into a DIFFERENT room than the original (39u6/17/21/23
all go `39>55` where the original goes `39>23`; 67u4 goes `67>68` where
the original goes `67>51`), and five cross MORE than the original.

**Where to start — revised after checking the edge values.** `35u6`
starts at **x=228, which is past DIZZY_MAXX=224**: the harness warped
Dizzy to an x the port will not let him stand at, and with strat=JUMP
(no direction) he cannot move, so that case says nothing about crossings.
`84u22` is the real one: JUMPRIGHT from 84@152,88, the port ends at
84@184,72 (it moved right and apexed at 72) while the original goes
`84>100>84` — an UP crossing the port never reaches. From y=88 a 28px
rise reaches y=60, well past TOP_TRANSITION_Y=66, so the port is losing
rise to something — a ceiling bonk is the first thing to check
(`ml_uplp`'s `check_ceiling` runs BEFORE the transition test, so a
ceiling one pixel into the gap would block a crossing the original
makes). Prime suspects, in order:
1. ~~`DIZZY_MAXX`/`DIZZY_MINX` vs `cantstop`'s `cp 57`/`cp 1`~~
   **CHECKED AND WRONG — do not spend time here.** DIZZY_MINX=8 and
   DIZZY_MAXX=224 are exactly the source's x=2 and x=56 in pixels, and
   with WALK_STEP=4 the port's before-the-step test (`cmpa #DIZZY_MAXX /
   bhs`) fires at the same x as the source's after-the-step equality
   (`x+4 == 228` i.e. `x == 224`). The two tests agree at the boundary.
   Written up so the next session does not re-derive a dead end.
2. `room_transition_*` returning to `ml_dirdone` vs `ml_vertdone`, i.e.
   which parts of the pass still run after a crossing.

**Do not touch the arc.** 39/39 within-room cases are exact; changing
GRAVITY/JUMP_DY would break what is currently right.

### How five rounds were spent missing this

The endpoint differential kept reporting "match" because it was dominated
by within-room cases, which are perfect, and because the jump press was
broken on both sides (T0177/T0182) so most cross-screen cases logged
`jumped=0` and compared nothing. Splitting the SAME data by "did it cross
a screen" took one script and no emulator, and it separated a clean
subsystem from a broken one immediately. **Partition the differential by
the mechanism under suspicion before running anything.**

### T0185 attempt 1: the ceiling head offset — fixes the reported case, breaks nine others. REVERTED.

**The measurement that made it look right.** Per-frame trajectories for
case `84u22` (84@152,88 JUMPRIGHT), port vs original, are identical until
one pixel:

| step | ORIGINAL | PORT (before) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | x=156 y=81 dy=-7 | x=156 y=81 dy=-7 |
| 2 | x=160 **y=75** dy=-6 | x=160 **y=77 dy=0** (bonk) |
| 3 | x=164 y=70 dy=-5 | — |
| 4 | x=168 y=66 -> room 100 | — |

`check_ceiling` probed `dizzy_y - dizzy_h - 1`, and `dizzy_h` is the
CURRENT frame's height (up to 21), so the probe row was **y-22**.
X-ALL.TXT `checktopside` uses a fixed **`sub 20`**. Two pixels of extra
head, and room 84's ceiling (y=48..55, x=32..167, gap x=168..207) catches
it 8px short of the gap.

**Changing it to the source's fixed 20 fixed that case exactly** — port
`84>100>84`, same as the original.

**And broke nine within-room cases that previously matched the original
to the pixel:**

| case | was (== ZX) | after the change | ZX |
|---|---|---|---|
| 53u16 | 53@72,88 | 53@24,104 | 53@72,87 |
| 53u19/22 | 53@72,88 | 53@32,104 | 53@72,87 |
| 84u31/34/37/40/43/46 | 84@184,72 | 84@140..148,88..104 | 84@184,71 |

Reverted. **The middle values do not help either**: with probe `y-21`,
84u22 still bonks at y=76 (the original reaches 75), so there is no
single offset that satisfies both sets.

**What that means — the offset is a symptom, not the cause.** A fixed 20
is right *by the source*, and with it the port matches the original on
84u22 but not on the nine. So the disagreement is in what the probe
lands ON, i.e. **our sprite heights and/or the derived mask are not the
original's** — `y-h-1` was accidentally compensating in those nine cases.
Next step is to compare our frame heights against the original's
`findfrmsize` table, and the derived mask rows against the original's
attribute map, rather than tuning the probe offset. Do NOT re-try
offsets; that ground is covered.

### T0186: the frame heights are NOT the problem — ruled out by measurement

Theory was that this port's hand-redesigned Dizzy is taller than the
original's, so `y - dizzy_h - 1` probes higher than the source's fixed
`sub 20`. **Wrong.** The extracted original frames are:

```
frame 00: 24x21   frame 03: 24x14   frame 06: 24x18   frame 09: 24x21
frame 01: 24x20   frame 04: 24x18   frame 07: 24x14   frame 10: 24x21
frame 02: 24x18   frame 05: 24x20   frame 08: 24x17   frame 11: 24x20
```

and `dizzy_frame_heights` is `21,20,18,14,18,20,18,14,17,21,21,20,...`
— **identical**. The art is the same size as the original's. Do not
re-open this.

So the difference really is only the probe offset, and its meaning:
with feet at y and height h the sprite occupies rows `y-h+1 .. y`, so for
the tallest frame (h=21) the head-top row is **y-20** — exactly what the
source probes, for EVERY frame. The source therefore treats Dizzy as
always 21 tall for ceiling purposes; this port probes `y-h-1`, which is
2 rows above the head for h=21 and varies per frame.

Matching the source exactly (`probe_y = y-20`) is therefore the right
change on paper, and it fixes 84u22 — but it regressed 9 within-room
cases that previously matched (above). Since the heights are confirmed
identical, **what the probe lands on must differ**: the remaining suspect
is the derived collision mask (T0166's runtime derivation), not Dizzy.
Next step: dump the port's `CUR_ROOM_CMASK` rows for room 84 y=48..56,
x=152..200 and compare against the ORIGINAL's attribute map for the same
cells, read out of the ZX machine — the one comparison that has never
been made, and the only thing left that can explain both results.

## T0187 — ROOT CAUSE: the collision mask is 4px-quantised VERTICALLY; the original tests one pixel row

`tools/derive_cmask.py` rasterises with `cc, cr = px // 4, py // 4` — a
single ink pixel anywhere in a 4x4 cell marks the whole cell solid. The
target's `CUR_ROOM_CMASK` is 64x48 cells over 256x192 for exactly that
reason (384 bytes).

**The original is not 4px vertically.** X-ALL.TXT `checkline` walks
`lookx` across `eggwidth-2` = 4 steps calling `getbyte`, which fetches a
**screen byte** — 8 pixels wide, **ONE PIXEL ROW** — and only calls
`checkattri` when that byte has ink. So the original's collision is
1px vertical; ours rounds to 4.

**Measured on the case that started this.** Room 84, columns x=164..179
(what `check_ceiling` probes with Dizzy at x=160):

| row | true ink | our 4px cell |
|---|---|---|
| 48,49,50 | INK | SOLID |
| 51 | — | SOLID (false) |
| 52,53,54 | INK | SOLID |
| **55** | **—** | **SOLID (false)** |
| 56 | — | clear |

The ceiling's real bottom edge is **y=54**; our mask says **y=55**.

**Two errors compound, and together they are the bug:**
1. `check_ceiling` probes `dizzy_y - dizzy_h - 1` = **y-22** for the
   tallest frame; the source probes a fixed **y-20** (the head-top row).
   2px too high.
2. The mask's bottom edges are up to **3px too low** (1px here).

Port at y=78: probe 56, clear, move to 77. At 77: probe 55 — our mask
says solid, the truth is clear — **bonk**. The original at 77 probes 57,
then 56, then 55 (clear in truth), and keeps rising to 66 and out of the
room. That is the whole of "jumps across screens fall short": a jump
needs its full 28px of rise to clear a gap, and we steal 2-3px of it.

It also explains why fixing only (1) regressed nine cases (T0185 attempt
1): with the mask still fat, lowering the probe moves it into cells that
are falsely solid at their OTHER edge.

**The fix is a memory/time decision, not a code tweak** — see the options
recorded with T0187 in tasks.toml. Do not attempt another probe-offset
tune; (1) alone cannot work while (2) stands.

### T0187 attempt: 1px mask built and measured — NOT shipped, and the control was invalid

Implemented the full 1px-vertical mask (CM_ROWS 48 -> 192, CMASK_BYTES
1536, `cmask_test` loses its two `lsra`, `dc2_rowlp` stores py directly,
attr row becomes py>>3, `dc_patch` paints 4 rows per cell-granular entry).
**It fits and costs nothing shipped**: the mask lives in TITLE_RAW_BUF
scratch, which had 1466 bytes spare; the delivery budget stayed at 1671.
My earlier "4x derive cost" estimate was also wrong — the rasteriser
already walks every ink pixel, so only the clear-loop grows.

**It fixes the reported case**: 84u22 gives `84>100>84`, the original's
own path.

**But the measurement underneath all of this was invalid.** I compared
new runs against `baselines/exits_port.log`, which was produced BEFORE
the T0177/T0181 harness fixes. Reverting the source entirely still left
9 of 39 cases "changed" against that baseline — proof the difference was
the harness, not the code. With a same-harness control:

| build | room path == original | mean \|final-orig\| |
|---|---|---|
| control (current code) | 39/39 | 16.8px |
| 1px mask only | 38/39 | 21.6px |
| 1px mask + y-20 probe | 38/39 | 21.6px |

Only **2 of 39** cases differ from the control (36l4, which gains a room
transition it should not have, and 53u16 by 4px). The "10 regressions"
that killed attempt 1 were largely harness noise.

So the 1px mask is **not** obviously wrong — it is one room-path
regression and ~5px of mean error against a control that is itself 16.8px
off the original. **That control is too noisy to judge a collision change
by.** Reverted and left unshipped for that reason, not because it was
disproved.

**Hard prerequisite before any further collision work: regenerate BOTH
baselines with the fixed harnesses (T0179).** Every comparison in T0176,
T0177, T0180, T0185 and T0187 rested on logs whose jump verdicts were
produced by a press that never fired. Nothing about jumps should be
concluded from `baselines/` as committed.

## T0179/T0188 — baselines regenerated on the fixed harnesses; the bug is confirmed on a valid control

Both baselines re-run with the T0177/T0182 jump-press fixes (the window
starts on the first GROUNDED frame). The ZX side needed a second pass:
a 40-frame SPACE window gave **213 NEVER-ARRIVED of 358**, because on the
Spectrum SPACE is BOTH jump and window-dismiss and a long hold cascades.
Back to 12 frames, moving only the START: **0 NEVER-ARRIVED, 210 real

WARP-STUCK.

**The result, on cases where BOTH sides genuinely jumped (136):**

| | cases | divergent room path | mean \|final-orig\| |
|---|---|---|---|
| jump stays in one room | 48 | **0** | **1.9px** |
| jump crosses a screen | 88 | **16** | 58.1px |

The playtest report is confirmed on evidence that holds: within a room
the port matches the original almost exactly; across a screen boundary it

Superseded numbers: the earlier "18 of 79" (T0185) reached the same

## T0188 — SHIPPED: the 1px collision mask. And derive_cmask.py is NOT ground truth.

`CUR_ROOM_CMASK` is now **64 columns x 192 rows of 1px** (1536 bytes),
not 64x48 of 4px. `cmask_test` drops its two `lsra`, `dc2_rowlp` stores
`py` directly, the attr row becomes `py>>3`, and `derive_cmask.py`
matches. It lives in boot-transient TITLE_RAW_BUF scratch (1466 bytes
were spare), so **the delivery budget is unchanged at 1669**, and the
rasteriser already walked every ink pixel so only the clear-loop grew.

**Measured against the regenerated baselines (T0179):**

| build | all cases | within-room jumps | cross-screen jumps | mean \|final-orig\| | NEVER-ARRIVED |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 264/346 | 48/48 | 72/88 | 38.2px | 12 |
| **after** | **268/351** | **48/48** | **75/89** | **37.8px** | **7** |

Fixes `84u22` (the playtest case: port now `84>100>84`, the original's
own path) and `83r3`. **Breaks nothing.**

### The part that matters more than the fix

**`tools/derive_cmask.py`'s "full" derivation is NOT ground truth, and
this port has been treating it as such.** Regenerating `dc_patch`
per-row so the target matched that derivation byte-for-byte made **all
fifteen room-51 cases NEVER-ARRIVE** — Dizzy could not stand where the
ORIGINAL stands him (the ZX log completes every one). The coarse 4-row
patch "over-paints" relative to the offline model and matches the REAL
GAME better.

So the 11 differing bytes in rooms 51/60/84 are now `KNOWN_DEV` in
`harness/cmaskverify.lua` — counted and printed, not failed. The open
question (T0189): **why** does the offline derivation lose those cells?
It is the negative-`pixel_x` sliver emulation; the target is right and
the model is wrong, which means any future claim of the form "the mask
matches ground truth" is worth nothing until this is understood.

Every earlier note in this file saying the mask was verified against
ground truth was comparing our derivation against itself. The ZX original
is the only authority.

### Deliberately not shipped

`check_ceiling` still probes `dizzy_y - dizzy_h - 1` where X-ALL.TXT
`checktopside` uses a fixed `sub 20`. With the 1px mask in, switching
measures EXACTLY neutral on all 358 cases — same 268/351, same two fixes,
no breaks. Left out as unnecessary risk, documented at the call site.

## T0190 — "dizzy spawns in the fireplace": the 1px mask broke every tool that read it

Playtest, right after T0188 shipped: `START_ROOM=68` spawns Dizzy in the
fireplace and he dies at once. Two separate faults, both the same shape.

**1. `tools/roomview.py` kept its own copy of the mask geometry.**
`CM_ROWS, CM_COLS = 48, 64` / `CM_LEN = 384`, hardcoded, while
`derive_cmask.py` had gone to 192 rows / 1536 bytes. `load_mask` decoded
only the first 384 bytes — **the top 48 PIXEL rows, i.e. sky** — and
returned an all-clear mask for most rooms. This file's own header already
warns that a second copy is how the T0106 decoder broke; the constants
were the copy nobody had removed. Now taken from `_dc` (import hoisted
above the constants that need it).

**2. `tools/start_pos.py` fell back to its "no mask" default of 128,80**
— which in room 68 is inside the fireplace. Exactly the failure its own
docstring describes for a fixed point ("any fixed point is inside a wall
in some room"), reached by a different route.

**And a third, found while fixing those:** `CELL` conflated row height
with column width. Rows are 1px now, columns are still 4px, so scaling x
by `CELL` put every spawn against the left wall (x=8..29). Split into
`ROW_PX` (192//CM_ROWS) and `COL_PX` (256//CM_COLS).

**`tools/stage_pack.sh` now asks `start_pos.py` itself** when START_ROOM
is set and START_X/START_Y are not. `play.sh` already did this for its
room argument; the bare `START_ROOM=N tools/stage_pack.sh` path used the
ASM's fixed 128,80 fallback, so the two disagreed — and that bare path is
the one a debug build usually takes.

Verified: `START_ROOM=68` now spawns at 100,168, settles to y=176 with
`floor=1`, `lives=2`, `killed=0`, **0 deaths in 15s**.

**The lesson is the one this port keeps relearning.** T0188 changed the
mask's shape and I checked the things that *write* it (the target,
derive_cmask, cmaskverify) and not the things that *read* it. Before
changing a shared data structure, grep for every consumer of its
dimensions — `CM_ROWS`, `CM_LEN`, `CELL` — rather than only the code that
produces it.

## T0191 — the jump is pixel-identical across a room transition. Traced, both sides.

Playtest hypothesis: "is it possible we are losing some pixels in the
room transition?" **No.** Traced case TL80 (68@80,148 JUMPLEFT) per pass
on the port and per tick on the ZX original:

```
   ORIGINAL                PORT
   80,148                  80,148
   76,141                  76,141
   72,135                  72,135
   68,130                  68,130
   64,126                  64,126
   60,123                  60,123
   56,121                  56,121
   52,120                  52,120     <- apex, both
   48,120                  48,120
   44,121                  44,121
   ...                     ...
   12,162                  12,162
    8,169                   8,169
 [67] 224,169            [67] 224,169  <- same arrival, to the pixel
```

18 horizontal steps of 4px, identical y at every one, identical arrival.
`goneleft` sets x:=224 and the arc continues unchanged. The ~37-frame
`load_room` stall does not cost steps because the whole mainloop is
frozen during it, so the arc resumes where it stopped.

A full sweep of the dining table (15 positions, both sides) agrees too:
from x=80 to x=152 the final positions match within 1-4px (the known 1px
feet offset plus the 4px walk step). **And the ORIGINAL also lands at
y=167 — the floor — not on the ledge at y=142.** So jumping left off the
dining table does not reach that ledge in either version.

Real divergences remain only at the table's LEFT END (x=48..72), where
the two take different room paths.

Four rounds of this session were spent guessing which platform a playtest

## T0192 — FIXED: a horizontal room transition ran a vertical step the original skips

The playtest's own hypothesis ("is it possible we are losing some pixels
in the room transition?") was right, and vertical rather than horizontal.

X-ALL.TXT's `newroom` sets **`dontupdatedizzy=1`**, and the main loop then
does `ld a,(dontupdatedizzy) / and a / call z,updatedizzy` -- the original
runs **no movement, gravity or animation on the tick it changes room**.
`room_transition_up`/`down` in this port already skipped the rest of the
pass (`lbra ml_vertdone`); `rt_horizontal` fell through to `ml_dirdone`,
which runs the jump test and the whole vertical section. So the port came
out of every SIDE crossing one vertical step ahead of the original.

Traced on 68@32,148 JUMPLEFT -- the playtest's own position, read off the
DEBUG_XY banner -- identical to the pixel until the crossing:

| | ORIGINAL | PORT (before) |
|---|---|---|
| x=8 | 121 dy-2 | 121 dy-2 |
| x=224 | 121 dy-2 | **120 dy-1** |
| x=212 | 121 | **123** |

Two pixels. Room 67's ledge there is a **dithered rock face** (frames
132/152, attr 2), so `check_wall`'s probes -- `y-10/y-14/y-18`, which are
`checkleftside`'s own three rows, verified against the source -- hit ink
at y=123 and miss it at y=121. The original steps left onto the ledge and
step-climbs to y=111; the port was blocked and fell 57px to the floor.

Fix: `lbra ml_dirdone` -> `lbra ml_vertdone` in `rt_horizontal`.

**Measured on the full 358-case differential:**

| | all | within-room | cross-screen | mean \|final-orig\| |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 268/351 | 48/48 | 75/89 | 37.8px |
| after | 267/350 | 48/48 | **75/84** | **27.7px** |

Five cross-screen divergences fixed (51u28, 55u2, 56u8, 67u4, 71u8),
**none broken**, within-room untouched, mean error down 27%. The
playtest case now lands `67@208,112` against the original's `67@208,111`.
cmaskverify 27 PASS / 0 FAIL, memaudit clean, bootreal passing.

### Why this took so long, for the next session

Four reproductions missed because I inferred the starting position from
screenshots instead of measuring it: the railing shelf at y=88, the
table's left edge, a sweep from x=48. The real spot was **x=32**, left of
the table's left edge (the table starts at 48) with only Dizzy's
rightmost foot probe on it. `-DDEBUG_XY=1` (T0191) exists so this is two
numbers off the screen next time. **Ask for them first.**
